Intermediate and poor CYP2D6 metabolizers had a high chance of 3.32 [1.58-6.99] to present with a fall, while normal and ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers had not (1.19 [0.71-1.98]). CYP2C19 metabolizers were not found to be associated with a higher chance of falls (1.10 [0.59-2.04]).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This hypothesis-generating-study identifies pharmacogenetic slow CYP2D6 metabolizers as high‑risk patients for falls with the use of AC drugs. Our study may help to individualize recommendations on anticholinergic drug treatment to optimize drug safety in older adults.

articles.title: Discussing lung cancer management options in the emergency department.
Healthcare provider and patient perspectives on barriers and facilitators to accessing maxillofacial injury care in Lesotho: a qualitative study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Maxillofacial injuries encompass a wide spectrum of trauma to the face and jaws, with facial fractures forming a major component. Between 1990 and 2017, the global incidence and prevalence of facial fractures increased by 39.45% and 54.39%, respectively, carrying severe risks. In sub-Saharan Africa, healthcare gaps cause significant under-reporting of maxillofacial injuries. Systemic barriers in low-resource settings hinder coordination. This study explored the barriers and facilitators to accessing maxillofacial injury services in Lesotho from both healthcare provider and patient perspectives.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: This qualitative study, guided by grounded theory, used in-depth interviews with healthcare providers and patients in Lesotho. The data were analysed thematically using NVivo V.14 software. The process followed Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) reporting guidelines.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: This study was conducted across key maxillofacial care departments, dental clinics, emergency units and surgical wards in three strategically selected facilities in Lesotho. These comprised two secondary-level district hospitals (north and south) and the country’s sole tertiary-level surgical referral hospital in the capital, Maseru, ensuring broad population coverage and accessibility.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This study employed purposive sampling of healthcare providers with at least 4 years of injury management experience from various disciplines, alongside patients who accessed maxillofacial services. Recruitment occurred from November 2023 to April 2024 across the three healthcare facilities.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In-depth interviews identified systemic barriers to maxillofacial care in Lesotho across four domains: access, referrals, treatment and care and maxillofacial injury preventive measures. Participants viewed the availability of ambulances and subsidised medical fees as insufficient, with some participants expecting services to be entirely free. Other systemic issues identified included fragmented communication from absent referral protocols, restricted access, severe resource constraints, shortages of healthcare professionals and inadequate emergency and diagnostic services. These inefficiencies emerged as interconnected factors that participants perceived to be undermining injury management across Lesotho’s health system.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Participants viewed systemic inefficiencies, poor referral protocols, limited access and resource shortages as adversely affecting maxillofacial injury care in Lesotho. Future implementation could integrate trauma care into national frameworks, support specialised expertise and resources and expand education for healthcare workers and the public. Evaluating this approach may help address barriers, improve injury management and strengthen healthcare system resilience.

articles.title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Athletes: A Narrative Review of Diagnostic Challenges, Management Strategies, and Return-to-Play Outcomes.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a compression disorder involving the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, or subclavian vein within the thoracic outlet. Athletes represent a distinct population in whom delayed diagnosis may result in career-threatening injuries.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This review aimed to: (i) identify diagnostic pitfalls in athletes not captured by conventional provocative tests; (ii) evaluate conservative and operative management by TOS subtype; (iii) synthesize return-to-play (RTP) rates, timelines, and clearance criteria; and (iv) highlight methodological limitations and propose minimum reporting standards for future athlete-specific studies.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to July 2026 using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for TOS, its subtypes, Paget-Schroetter syndrome, and athletic populations. Reference lists were hand-searched. Studies addressing TOS diagnosis, classification, pathophysiology, management, or RTP in athletes were eligible regardless of design, reflecting limited randomized evidence. Journal legitimacy was screened using the Kscien's list.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: nTOS is the predominant form in athletes and usually improves with 4-6 months of rehabilitation, whereas refractory cases may require surgery. vTOS/Paget-Schroetter syndrome requires urgent thrombolysis and early first-rib resection; aTOS is rare but limb-threatening and requires prompt surgery. Mixed presentations occur in up to 23% of surgical cases.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Outcomes are favorable with subtype-specific diagnosis and objective RTP criteria. However, evidence is limited by retrospective, single-center studies with pooled subtypes, inconsistent RTP definitions, and selective reporting. Prospective, sport-specific studies using standardized outcomes are needed.

articles.title: Validation of the CARG tool in prediction of chemotherapy completion and side effects in older adults with cancer: A retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Predicting treatment-related toxicity in older adults remains challenging. The Cancer and Aging Research Group (CARG) toxicity tool is one of the most established toxicity prediction tools; however, validation studies have shown variable predictive ability. Our primary objective was to validate the CARG toxicity tool in a cohort of Canadian older adults on systemic therapy. Secondary objectives were to compare the tool's performance with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG-PS), Geriatric-8 (G8), and Vulnerable Elders Survey (VES-13) scales and examine whether these tools could predict treatment discontinuation, emergency room (ER) visits, and hospitalizations.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective analysis included patients aged ≥65 who completed a Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) and received systemic therapy at an academic Canadian cancer centre. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated for the CARG and compared to ECOG-PS, G8, and VES-13. Logistic regression was performed to examine the association of the CARG toxicity tool with Grade ≥ 3 toxicity, ER visits, and hospitalizations.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: One hundred sixty-eight patients were included, 87 (51.8%) female, mean age 79.1 (SD 5.9). At least one Grade ≥ 3 toxicity was observed in 118 patients (70.2%). In toxicity prediction, the CARG toxicity tool had modest performance (AUC 0.64, 95% CI 0.55-0.73) but outperformed the ECOG-PS (AUC 0.57), VES-13 (AUC 0.55), and G8 (AUC 0.54), though this was not statistically significant (p = 0.17). On multivariable logistic regression, the high-risk category on the CARG toxicity tool was significantly associated with Grade ≥ 3 toxicity (OR 2.93 (95% CI 1.10-7.79, p = 0.03). High-risk CARG toxicity scores were correlated with treatment incompletion (OR 2.12, CI 1.04-4.30, p = 0.04) but not with hospitalization or ER visits. ECOG-PS ≥ 2 (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.04-3.80, p = 0.04) and abnormal G8 scores (OR 2.71, 95% CI 1.13-6.51, p = 0.03) showed stronger association with these outcomes, respectively. The CARG tool performed similarly when restricted to chemotherapy regimens alone and for solid vs hematological malignancies.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The CARG toxicity tool demonstrated modest performance in toxicity prediction in a Canadian older adult cohort but appears superior to other tools. It was also associated with treatment incompletion although the ECOG-PS and G8 showed stronger association with hospitalization and ER visits.

articles.title: Electronic health record phenotype choice and real-world outcome estimates: A propensity score-matched comparison of three invasive breast cancer definitions in TriNetX.

abstract.text: Electronic health record-based oncology studies depend on computable case definitions, but different operational definitions may identify different patient populations and change downstream estimates. This retrospective benchmarking cohort study evaluated three definitions of incident invasive breast cancer in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network: at least one malignant breast cancer diagnosis code (Dx1), a repeated diagnosis-code definition within 90 days (Dx2), and a diagnosis code plus breast cancer-directed treatment evidence (DxTx). Female patients aged 20 years or older were identified after a 12-month washout period and exclusion of patients with carcinoma in situ only. Pairwise one-to-one propensity-score matching was performed using 13 baseline covariates. Outcomes were all-cause mortality and time to the first emergency department visits, assessed from day 180 after the index date to 1, 3, and 5 years after the original index date. Appendicitis and femoral neck fracture were included as negative-control outcomes. Dx1, Dx2, and DxTx identified 1,450,233, 678,739, and 578,576 patients, respectively. After matching, more restrictive definitions were consistently associated with higher hazards of mortality and emergency department visits. For mortality, hazard ratios ranged from 1.26 to 1.32 for DxTx versus Dx1, 1.13 to 1.14 for Dx2 versus Dx1, and 1.13 to 1.17 for DxTx versus Dx2 across assessment windows. Emergency department visit estimates showed a similar but attenuating pattern. These associations should be interpreted as differences between phenotype-defined populations arising from selection and ascertainment mechanisms rather than as treatment effects. Negative-control outcomes were generally close to the null; small appendicitis associations observed in comparisons involving Dx1 did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings indicate that plausible electronic health record-based breast cancer definitions are not analytically interchangeable. Phenotype specification should therefore be treated as a core analytic decision and evaluated through transparent reporting and sensitivity analyses.

articles.title: Feasibility of using a mobile cardiotocograph device in an ambulance during maternal transport.

abstract.text: Maternal transfer generally refers to the emergency transportation of a pregnant woman to a medical facility with more advanced capabilities when her condition, or that of the fetus, deteriorates or is expected to deteriorate, thereby ensuring the safety of both mother and fetus. This procedure is frequently performed in Japan, where childbirth at primary obstetric facilities is common. However, no reports have described attempts to remotely monitor maternal and fetal vital signs inside an ambulance during transport and use these data to support clinical care at a remote location. The current study aimed to assess the feasibility of a system that enables real-time remote monitoring (RM) using a small mobile cardiotocograph (CTG) in an ambulance during maternal transport from primary obstetric facilities to a higher-level perinatal medical center. This study included women with singleton pregnancies beyond 22 weeks of gestation who were transferred from nine private clinics to a university hospital because of medical complications. Using a small mobile CTG device, the CTG data were transmitted during maternal transfer to a university hospital. The obstetrician of the university hospital checked the data in real-time using tablets to select the appropriate treatment. A questionnaire survey was conducted on the medical staff of the primary facilities who accompanied the patients during maternal transport. An online survey was also administered to paramedics only after the recruitment period. The study period was from August 2021 to August 2023. In total, 68 pregnant women were enrolled in this study and analyzed. The median time from getting into the ambulance to arrival at the university hospital was 34.5 (range: 15.0-67.0) min. No monitoring sessions were discontinued because of connectivity issues. All 68 fetal heart rate records were legible, and the median proportion of the total legible period in each recording was 91.1% (range: 53.9%-99.8%). Twenty-three (33.8%) women delivered by the next day after the transportation. The questionnaire survey revealed high levels of medical staff satisfaction and paramedical acceptance of real-time CTG RM during maternal transfer. Real-time CTG RM during emergency maternal transport is feasible and useful for making a medical decision more precisely in tertiary perinatal medical centers. Further, the use of the system in an ambulance is also acceptable for paramedics.

articles.title: Triage under pressure: Nursing students' learning and preparedness in a code orange simulation using CTAS.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Preparing nursing students for mass casualty incidents requires more than foundational knowledge; it demands the ability to apply triage principles under pressure. While simulation-based education is widely used, there is limited evidence examining how students integrate established triage frameworks, such as the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), within high-acuity disaster contexts. This study evaluated nursing students' knowledge application, clinical prioritization, and perceived preparedness following a Code Orange simulation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: cross-sectional survey was conducted with undergraduate nursing students (n = 26) following participation in a high-fidelity Code Orange simulation. The survey included multiple-choice knowledge items assessing CTAS and GCS application, Likert-scale measures of perceived knowledge, confidence, and preparedness, and open-ended questions exploring student experiences. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests, while qualitative responses underwent content analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Participants demonstrated strong knowledge of CTAS and GCS principles, with most correctly identifying triage priorities and neurological assessment parameters. Variability was observed in students' ability to distinguish between CTAS Levels 2 and 3, with recognition of vital signs as a key differentiator (χ² = 57.18, p < .001). Likert-scale responses indicated high levels of perceived preparedness, confidence, and knowledge following the simulation. Qualitative findings highlighted the importance of realism, cognitive demand, and teamwork in shaping learning, with students emphasizing the value of applying theoretical knowledge in a dynamic, high-pressure environment.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Findings suggest that high-fidelity disaster simulations extend beyond reinforcing baseline knowledge by promoting the application of triage decision-making in complex clinical contexts. Integrating structured triage frameworks within immersive simulation may enhance preparedness for mass casualty response, particularly in areas requiring nuanced clinical prioritization. These results underscore the role of simulation in bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and real-world emergency decision-making.

articles.title: Integrating personal support workers to support older adults in the emergency department: a quantitative analysis.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Our aim was to describe the pragmatic implementation of personal support workers in an ED setting, evaluating the characteristics of patients who were assigned to and received personal support worker care and the estimated operational impact of the program.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective observational cohort study was performed at a single ED during a pre (September 1/2022-February 28/2023) and post (March 11/2024-March 31/2025) intervention period. Requests were left to the discretion of any ED team member, including personal support workers. Using logistic regression, the primary outcome was patient characteristics. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital delirium rate, ED falls, ED length of stay using propensity score matching, and estimated redistribution of nursing hours with associated costs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: There were 26,757 and 60,737 ED visits made during the control and intervention periods. In the latter group, 6,039 (9.9%) visits received personal support worker care. The three characteristics most strongly associated with care were age ≥ 65 years (OR: 7.1, p<0.001), ambulance arrival (OR: 3.9, p<0.001), and higher acuity triage score (OR: 3.3, p<0.001). After matching the 6,039 personal support worker-attended visits to (1) control period visits and (2) non-personal support worker-attended visits during the intervention period, the personal support worker-attended group was associated with an increased rate of in-hospital delirium (2.2%-2.5%, p<0.001) and ED length of stay (8.5-13.4 h, p<0.001) in both comparisons, and a trend toward increased ED falls in the second comparison (0.1%, p=0.06). In the personal support worker-attended group, an estimated 9 h of nursing time and $287.01Cdn in costs were redistributed per day.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Left to the discretion of the ED staff, patients receiving personal support worker care were older, had longer ED length of stay and higher rate of in-hospital delirium. Personal support worker care was associated with an estimated redistribution of nursing hours, which could be redirected toward providing acute medical care.

articles.title: Confidence in the wild: the educational impact of a wilderness medicine workshop on emergency medicine resident self-confidence and perceptions.

abstract.text: Wilderness medicine education has become an increasingly valued component of emergency medicine residency curricula but remains inconsistently integrated across programs. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a wilderness medicine educational workshop on residents' confidence in their provision of wilderness medicine care and their overall perception of wilderness medicine. A pre-test-post-test design was employed. The intervention of interest was an educational workshop composed of a lecture, rotating skills stations, and multiple simulated wilderness medicine scenarios. Data were collected through a survey completed prior to and immediately following the intervention. Twelve confidence and six perception competencies were assessed by the survey. A total of 22 participants comprised the study sample. Statistically significant differences were found post-intervention across wilderness medicine confidence outcomes as well as the confidence composite score (p < 0.001, r=0.905). All 12 competencies demonstrated moderate to large effect sizes (r > 0.50). Participants maintained favorable perceptions of wilderness medicine training across the workshop, with no significant post-intervention difference detected (p = 0.42). Our study highlights residents' favorable perceptions of wilderness medicine training and demonstrates the effectiveness of a single-day workshop in improving residents' confidence in wilderness medicine skills. This study supports the use of such interventions to further enhance medical residents' learning and self-reported confidence in important medical skills.

articles.title: Opioid-free analgesia for acute renal colic: a randomized, double-blind, head-to-head comparison of intravenous ibuprofen, dexketoprofen trometamol and paracetamol in the emergency department.

abstract.text: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are first-line analgesics for acute renal colic, but comparisons of the intravenous (IV) non-opioid agents used in emergency departments are scarce. In this prospective, single-centre, randomized, double-blind, three-arm trial, 251 adults with acute renal colic received IV ibuprofen 400 mg (n = 86), dexketoprofen trometamol 50 mg (n = 82) or paracetamol 1 g (n = 83) infused over 15 min. Pain was scored on a 100-mm visual analogue scale (VAS) at 0, 15 and 30 min; the primary outcome was treatment success (≥50% VAS reduction at 30 min). Treatment success occurred in 76.7%, 74.4% and 66.3%, respectively (p = 0.280); mean VAS reduction at 30 min was 51.1, 56.5 and 45.5 mm. Baseline VAS was higher with dexketoprofen (85.2 vs 78.0 and 79.8 mm; p = 0.025); after adjustment for baseline, VAS at 30 min was lowest with dexketoprofen (25.6 mm), intermediate with ibuprofen (29.0 mm) and highest with paracetamol (35.1 mm; dexketoprofen vs paracetamol -9.5 mm, 95% confidence interval (CI) -16.5 to -2.5; p = 0.023). Rescue fentanyl was required in 32.6%, 31.7% and 43.4% (p = 0.217); the adjusted odds were lower with dexketoprofen than with paracetamol (odds ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.20-0.84). Mild nausea or dizziness occurred in 3.5%, 3.7% and 3.6% of patients; none was serious. All three agents provided effective opioid-free analgesia; dexketoprofen produced the largest adjusted pain reduction and the lowest need for rescue opioid, ibuprofen was comparable and paracetamol least effective. Trial registration: not registered (see Methods).

articles.title: Rapid identification of severe hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia in hospitalized patients using laboratory-integrated machine learning.

abstract.text: Dysglycemia is common in hospitalized patients and is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Although central laboratory glucose testing is the diagnostic reference, clinically relevant delays may occur between sample processing and result reporting, particularly for critical values requiring urgent intervention. We investigated whether early photometric reaction signals generated during routine enzymatic glucose measurement could enable earlier recognition of severe dysglycemia.We developed a laboratory-based machine learning model to predict plasma glucose concentration using early analyzer-derived photometric absorbance features during the enzymatic reaction. Model development was performed, and performance was evaluated using an internal test split and an independent external validation cohort. Regression performance was assessed using mean absolute error, root mean squared error (RMSE), and coefficient of determination. Clinical risk classification was evaluated for severe dysglycemia defined as glucose <54 mg/dL or >250 mg/dL.In the internal test set, the model achieved high agreement between predicted and measured glucose concentrations (RMSE 7.1 mg/dL; R2 0.990). In external validation, prediction accuracy remained high (RMSE 45.1-52.0 mg/dL; R2 0.904-0.928 across evaluated models). For severe dysglycemia alerts (< 54 mg/dL or >250 mg/dL), multivariable linear regression provided the highest sensitivity (98.6%) with specificity of 90.9%..Analyzer-derived photometric reaction signals can be leveraged to predict glucose concentration and identify severe dysglycemia before routine test reporting is finalized. This laboratory-integrated approach may enhance patient safety by enabling earlier recognition of critical glucose abnormalities and supporting timely clinical decision-making. This approach may shorten the time to recognition of critical glucose abnormalities and facilitate earlier intervention.

articles.title: Economic Evaluation Methods in Post-Injury Care: A Global Systematic Review and Critical Appraisal of Their Suitability for Decision-Making.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND AIM
abstract.text: Over 4 million people (8% of all deaths) worldwide die from traumatic injuries annually. For people aged 5-29 years, three of the top five causes of death are injury related, namely road traffic injuries, homicide, and suicide. Investments in injury care need to consider budget constraints, and economic evaluation studies can be employed to understand the costs and outcomes of competing interventions for injury care. However, these studies should be designed to meet the information requirements of decision makers. This systematic review aims to critically appraise the methodologies used in economic evaluations of injury care, assessing their suitability for informing decision-making.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a global systematic review in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. We searched six databases, from inception to June 2023, for eligible full economic evaluations of injury care. The primary population was persons who have suffered acute traumatic injuries. Only full economic evaluations were eligible for inclusion, and studies that met the inclusion criteria were appraised using the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards statement and critiqued against the decision-making guidelines developed by Sculpher et al. (2009).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 259 studies were included in the final review. An overwhelming majority of the studies (92%) were conducted in high-income countries, and they predominantly evaluated in-hospital interventions (93% vs 1% pre-hospital and 6% post-discharge). Fractures were the most commonly studied injury type, while the provider perspective was the most frequent analytic perspective. We found that just over half of the studies synthesised effectiveness evidence from multiple sources; nearly a quarter of the studies compared more than two competing interventions; and 84% of the studies considered costs and outcomes over an appropriate time horizon.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: We found key gaps in the existing evidence: limited synthesis of evidence to inform treatment effects, inadequate alignment of time horizons with intervention outcomes, geographic disparities in the scope and quality of evidence, and limited coverage across the full patient pathway. These limitations hinder the usefulness of study findings in decision-making. Future economic evaluations should address key gaps to improve the utility of economic evaluations in healthcare decision-making.

abstract.label: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION
abstract.text: PROSPERO: CRD42022351978.

articles.title: NeuroPOCUS: what every intensivist should know.

abstract.text: Ultrasound has become a paramount tool in critical care. Nowadays, it is common for intensivists to use ultrasound to evaluate cardiac function, pulmonary alterations, guide vascular access, and monitor systemic venous congestion through ultrasound-based techniques. However, the brain remains often overlooked in the point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) practice. NeuroPOCUS encompasses cerebral hemodynamic assessment, mainly at the level of the middle cerebral artery, as well as evaluation of hydrocephalus, hematoma size, midline shift and intracranial pressure. Most of these are basic or basic-plus skills. In this manuscript, we present a concise guide on what every intensivist should know about NeuroPOCUS, including basic key concepts, technique and several real illustrative figures.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care ultrasound for proximal lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis in emergency settings: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.text: ObjectiveTo evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of emergency clinician-performed ultrasound for proximal lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and explore variation by scan protocol and operator group.MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis included studies of adults with suspected DVT in emergency settings. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to 8 April 2026, and a targeted literature update was conducted through 20 September 2026 during revision. A bivariate binomial random-effects model jointly estimated sensitivity and specificity. The primary analysis included one dataset per study to avoid duplicate weighting of paired cohorts. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed with QUADAS-2. Protocol and operator subgroup analyses were exploratory. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261361599).ResultsSixteen studies contributed quantitative data, providing 17 protocol datasets because one paired cohort was evaluated with both two-point and three-point protocols. Selecting the three-point result from that paired cohort for the primary overall model yielded 16 independent study datasets comprising 2,781 patient or limb/examination units. Pooled sensitivity was 0.91 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85-0.95), and specificity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.91-0.97). Sensitivity estimates for two-point and three-point/extended protocols were 0.87 and 0.92, respectively. Source-data uncertainties, including a reconstructed diagnostic-analysis table in Jahanian 2019 and a provisional Crowhurst input, were examined in sensitivity analyses. Koylu 2026 was added during the revision-stage targeted literature update.ConclusionsEmergency clinician-performed ultrasound may support proximal DVT assessment within a defined diagnostic pathway. Negative limited examinations require interpretation alongside clinical probability and examination adequacy. Heterogeneity and unresolved source data limit confidence in the pooled estimates. Exploratory subgroup findings do not establish the superiority of any protocol or operator group.

articles.title: Positive Urine Cultures for Enterococcus spp. vs. Escherichia coli in Febrile Infants Younger Than 90 Days: A Matched Cohort Study.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To compare febrile infants aged 90 days or younger with Enterococcus spp. or Escherichia coli in urine cultures, overall and by urine dipstick findings.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Matched cohort study in three Spanish paediatric emergency departments (2011-2023). Infants with Enterococcus spp. were matched 1:1 by age and sex with infants with E. coli and compared using paired tests; dipstick-stratified analyses were exploratory.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 4006 febrile infants, 77 (1.9%) had Enterococcus spp. Abnormal dipstick findings were less frequent than with E. coli (27.3% vs. 80.5%; p < 0.001), and blood inflammatory markers were lower, largely reflecting the higher proportion of normal dipsticks. Abnormal voiding cystourethrogram findings were more frequent with Enterococcus spp., with abnormal (70.0% vs. 27.6%; p = 0.03) and normal dipsticks (33.3% vs. 0%; p = 0.04). With abnormal dipsticks, abnormal dimercaptosuccinic acid scans (6/11 vs. 0/17; p = 0.001) and recurrent urinary tract infections (33.3% vs. 8.1%; p = 0.009) were more frequent with Enterococcus spp.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In these infants, Enterococcus spp. in urine usually had a normal dipstick but was associated with more urinary tract abnormalities than E. coli. Enterococcal infections with abnormal dipsticks were associated with more renal scan abnormalities and recurrences; the significance of isolates with normal dipsticks remains uncertain.

articles.title: Cardiac toxicity and dysrhythmias in acute poisoning: a ten-year cohort study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Cardiac toxicity is frequently cited as an important cause of morbidity and mortality following acute drug overdose. The true incidence of direct drug related clinically significant cardiac complications and malignant dysrhythmias in more recent toxicology practice remains poorly defined. We aim to determine the frequency, nature, and outcomes of cardiac complications in patients presenting with acute poisoning.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained clinical toxicology database over a 10-year period. Patients with acute poisoning managed by a specialist toxicology service were included. Cardiac complications were defined as hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg) or a primary cardiac dysrhythmia considered temporally related to the poisoning. Sinus tachycardia was excluded. Demographics, exposures, treatments, and outcomes were extracted.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 9,743 poisoning presentations were included. Cardiac complications occurred in 473 patients (4.9%). Hypotension occurred in 368 patients (3.8%), primary dysrhythmias in 164 patients (1.7%), and both hypotension and dysrhythmia in 59 patients (0.6%). Most dysrhythmias were isolated bradycardia (139/164, 85%), commonly associated with clonidine (40%) and beta-blocker/calcium channel blocker poisoning (35%). Only 25 patients (0.3% of all poisoning presentations) developed primary dysrhythmias: atrial dysrhythmias (3), conduction abnormalities/delays (10), ectopic rhythms (5), asystole (1) or ventricular dysrhythmias (6; 0.06%). Malignant ventricular dysrhythmias occurred in six patients and were associated with sotalol, methadone, escitalopram, dothiepin, and nortriptyline poisoning. Twenty-one deaths occurred during the study period, but no death was attributable to a primary dysrhythmia temporally related to poisoning.Discussion: In this large cohort of almost 10,000 poisoning presentations, cardiac complications occurred in approximately one in twenty patients. However, almost 95% of these were either hypotension or isolated bradycardia. Only six patients (0.06%) had ventricular dysrhythmias. Our findings support previous studies demonstrating that clinically significant ventricular dysrhythmias are uncommon among unselected populations presenting with acute poisoning. We found that only a few individual drugs, such as sotalol, methadone, tricyclic antidepressants, and escitalopram, were associated with ventricular dysrhythmias, and that such events were rare overall.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Cardiac effects occur in approximately 5% of acute poisoning presentations but are predominantly hypotension or sinus bradycardia. Clinically significant ventricular and supraventricular dysrhythmias are uncommon, occurring in less than 0.3% of cases. Death directly attributable to a primary poisoning-related dysrhythmia is rare.

articles.title: Clinical and toxicological factors associated with pediatric intensive care unit admission in pediatric acute poisoning: a 10-year retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Acute poisoning is an important cause of emergency department visits among children and adolescents. Early identification of patients requiring escalation-of-care or pediatric intensive care unit-level monitoring remains clinically challenging. The purpose of this study is to evaluate clinical and toxicological factors associated with pediatric intensive care unit admission in pediatric acute poisoning.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study included 652 patients younger than 18 years managed for acute poisoning between 2015 and 2024 at a tertiary university hospital. Demographic, exposure-related, toxicological, clinical, and laboratory variables were analyzed. Pediatric intensive care unit admission was evaluated as an escalation-of-care and healthcare utilization outcome. Three multivariable logistic regression models were constructed, including models excluding variables closely related to admission decisions to reduce potential incorporation bias.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 652 patients, 99 (15.2%) were admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. Across the primary and sensitivity models, delayed presentation, psychiatric disorder history, and multiple-drug ingestion remained independently associated with admission. Lower Glasgow Coma Scale score and cardiovascular findings were associated with admission in models including clinical severity variables. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses demonstrated poor discriminatory performance of individual parameters, indicating that none were suitable as stand-alone triage tools. No deaths occurred, invasive mechanical ventilation was required in one patient, and advanced organ-support interventions were uncommon.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Pediatric intensive care unit admission appeared to reflect both observed clinical instability and anticipated toxicological risk rather than poisoning severity alone. The poor discriminatory performance of individual parameters suggests that admission decisions are multifactorial and should not rely on a single clinical or laboratory variable.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Delayed presentation, multiple-drug ingestion, psychiatric disorder history, and clinical severity indicators were associated with pediatric intensive care unit admission. These findings should be interpreted as observational evidence regarding escalation-of-care decisions rather than as a validated prediction model or triage tool in this single-center pediatric poisoning cohort.

articles.title: Diagnostic performance of xylazine test strips in urine from fentanyl-positive hospitalized patients.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Xylazine is an α-2-adrenergic agonist increasingly detected in the illicit drug supply, particularly in combination with fentanyl, yet no FDA-cleared rapid diagnostic assay exists for detection in biological specimens. Commercially available xylazine test strips, developed to evaluate drug samples, have been proposed for clinical use. We aim to evaluate the clinical screening performance of xylazine test strips when applied to urine specimens from hospitalized patients with fentanyl-positive routine hospital urine drug screening.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-center diagnostic accuracy study included 250 consecutive residual urine specimens from hospitalized patients with fentanyl-positive routine hospital urine drug screening. Fentanyl positivity was not confirmed by hospital liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Each specimen underwent testing with a commercially available xylazine test strips and liquid chromatography-mass spectometry for xylazine detection and quantification as the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, and exact 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Liquid chromatography-mass spectometry detected xylazine in 71 of 250 specimens (28.4%). Xylazine test strips identified 19 true positives, 139 true negatives, 40 false positives, and 52 false negatives. Sensitivity was 26.8% (95% CI 16.9-38.6%), and specificity was 77.7% (95% CI 70.8-83.5%). Positive and negative predictive values were 32.2% and 72.8%, respectively. The positive likelihood ratio was 1.2 and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.94. Most LC-MS-positive specimens (91.5%) had xylazine concentrations below the manufacturer-reported xylazine test strips detection threshold of 1,000 ng/mL.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: When applied to urine specimens from hospitalized patients with fentanyl-positive routine hospital urine drug screens, commercially available xylazine test strips demonstrated limited diagnostic utility, largely due to low sensitivity at clinically observed concentration ranges. Xylazine test strips results should not be used in isolation to guide clinical decision-making until validated point-of-care assays designed for biological specimens become available.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Commercially available xylazine test strips demonstrate poor clinical screening performance when applied to urine specimens from hospitalized patients with fentanyl-positive routine hospital urine drug screens.

articles.title: Beyond safe storage: closing product-safety gaps in childhood ingestion injuries in Japan.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Unintentional ingestion of medicines and button batteries by young children is developmentally predictable. Japan has relied mainly on caregiver warnings, and it is unclear how far prevention has been built into products.

abstract.label: MEDICINES AND CHILD-RESISTANT PACKAGING
abstract.text: Japan has no general legal requirement for child-resistant medicine packaging. Such packaging could add protection when safe storage fails.

abstract.label: BUTTON BATTERIES AND PRODUCT CLASSIFICATION
abstract.text: Serious ingestions continue, while mandatory toy standards leave gaps in protection across household products.

abstract.label: SURVEILLANCE
abstract.text: National hospital-based surveillance of household product ingestions was narrowed in 2019, limiting assessment of national burden and policy effects.

abstract.label: REGULATION IN OTHER COUNTRIES
abstract.text: Australia and the United States have introduced button battery safety requirements that extend beyond toys.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Japan could require child-resistant packaging for medicines that are toxic in small doses, require secure battery compartments across household products, extend packaging and warning standards to online sales, and rebuild surveillance. Poison centres could help guide surveillance and prioritise medicines for packaging requirements.

articles.title: The secretory life of pets: bites from western hognose snakes reported to the California Poison Control System.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The western hognose snake (Heterodon nasicus) is a popular pet reptile. While sometimes classified as nonvenomous, it produces mildly toxic saliva from a low-pressure secretory organ in the temporal region (Duvernoy's gland), causing local reactions following snakebites. We aim to review cases from a statewide poison control system to characterize clinical effects and outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This is a 10-year retrospective review of calls about western hognose snakebite to the California Poison Control System, using product-substance codes and a free-text keyword search. Demographic, clinical, and bite-circumstance data were summarized and analyzed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: There were 35 cases from January 2016 to March 2026, ranging from 11 to 82 years (median 22; IQR 18-29 years), of whom 69% were female and 46% were aged 21 years or younger. A large majority (89%) were bitten by their own pets; one bite occurred at a reptile exposition. All bites affected the hands, typically during feeding, handling, or enclosure cleaning. Local swelling occurred in 91% of cases, with extension to the wrist or forearm in 43%. Skin changes (ecchymosis, erythema or blistering) were noted in 26%, and 6% developed nausea and vomiting. Vital signs and labs, checked in 23% and 11% of cases respectively, were unremarkable. Management typically included wound care, tetanus vaccination update, and anticipatory guidance for infectious complications. Two patients required hospitalization for two or more days for treatment of presumed cellulitis. In one case with extensive edema, rattlesnake antivenom was administered due to doubts about the reported bite history; in the second case, antivenom was recommended for similar reasons, but withheld after photographic identification confirmed the pet snake.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The western hognose snakebite can cause cytotoxic edema, and prolonged bites may pose a higher risk of severe injury. Clinical care should focus on pain control, wound care, and anticipatory guidance for post-bite infection and hypersensitivity reactions due to the components of snake saliva, which may require specific treatment with antibiotics or anti-inflammatory medications. Rattlesnake antivenom has no role in managing this type of snakebite.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Western hognose envenomation can lead to mild to moderate soft tissue injuries, which require supportive and symptomatic care and, rarely, hospital admission. Many bites occurred in pet owner adolescents, who may benefit from preventive safety education.

articles.title: Beyond Clinician Well-Being: Nurse Practitioner Burnout and Job Satisfaction Linked to Higher Risk of Emergency Department Use and Hospitalization for Persons With Dementia.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Most care for persons with dementia is provided in primary care practices, yet high rates of burnout and job dissatisfaction may challenge the delivery of high-quality care. The complexity of dementia care may further contribute to clinician strain. Nurse practitioners increasingly deliver primary care to persons with dementia, yet little is known about whether their job outcomes (satisfaction and burnout) impact acute care utilization (emergency department visits and hospitalizations) for persons with dementia.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study examined the association between primary care nurse practitioner job outcomes and acute care utilization among persons with dementia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a national cross-sectional study linking survey data from 847 primary care nurse practitioners to Medicare claims for 74,157 persons with dementia. Burnout and job satisfaction were measured using single items. Risk Ratios [RR], calculated from multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with time as a constant, estimated associations between nurse practitioner job outcomes and acute care utilization.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Most nurse practitioners (92%) reported job satisfaction; 30% reported some burnout, and 8% reported high burnout. Job satisfaction was associated with lower risk of emergency department visits (RR=0.91; 95% CI: 0.85-0.97) and hospitalizations (RR=0.92; 95% CI: 0.86-0.99). High burnout was associated with a higher risk of emergency department visits (RR=1.09; 95% CI: 1.01-1.17) and hospitalizations (RR=1.08; 95% CI: 1.00-1.17).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Nurse practitioner burnout and job satisfaction were independently associated with acute care utilization among persons with dementia. Workforce well-being may be an important factor in delivering high-quality, dementia-capable primary care.

articles.title: Pediatric Musculoskeletal Infections: Who Needs a Tap or MRI? From Kocher to PEMCRC.

abstract.text: Bacterial musculoskeletal infections (MSKIs), including septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and pyomyositis, are challenging diagnoses to make in pediatric emergency medicine because their presentation frequently overlaps with more common conditions, including transient synovitis, Lyme arthritis, reactive arthritis, and other inflammatory arthritides. While delayed diagnosis may result in significant morbidity, over-testing may expose children to invasive procedures, advanced imaging, sedation, hospitalization, and unnecessary antimicrobial therapy. Pediatric emergency clinicians must therefore balance the competing risks of missed infection and excessive diagnostic evaluation and treatment. Numerous tools exist to aid clinicians, including blood biomarkers-white blood cell (WBC) count, absolute neutrophil count (ANC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT). However, blood biomarkers have limited diagnostic accuracy when used in isolation. To address this limitation, clinical prediction tools that combine laboratory values with clinical features to stratify risk have been developed. In this review, we summarize the data for clinically available biomarkers and clinical prediction tools for the evaluation of pediatric bacterial MSKIs and discuss their practical application, limitations, and integration into clinical decision-making in the emergency department (ED). Ultimately, we provide a framework to help pediatric emergency clinicians identify children who require advanced testing and interventions while avoiding unnecessary evaluation and treatment in low-risk patients.

articles.title: Complex arrhythmias in the absence of severe valvulitis: a paediatric case of acute rheumatic fever.

abstract.text: A 15-year-old boy was admitted to the emergency department with arthralgia of the knee. He was diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever based on clinical examination, electrocardiography, echocardiography, and elevated inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and anti-streptolysin O titre. First-degree and second-degree Mobitz type 1 atrioventricular blocks, moderate frequency uniform ventricular premature beats, as well as non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, were detected on 24-hour Holter electrocardiography monitoring.

articles.title: Comparing the paths of Hedgehog release in artificial and natural settings.

abstract.text: The Hedgehog (Hh) family is a central model for signaling gradient formation despite its members undergoing dual N- and C-terminal lipidation during biogenesis. This process strongly binds Hh proteins to the plasma membrane of the cells that produce them, preventing their spontaneous solubilization. Therefore, lipidated Hh proteins require specific molecular mechanisms for their controlled release. Here, we synthesize the available in vivo data on Hh solubilization and dispersion, focusing on three proposed mechanisms centered on the Hh release enhancers Dispatched and Scube2. This approach aims to reconcile conflicting experimental findings on the mechanistic functions of these enhancers, to clarify previous conceptual inconsistencies, and to contribute to a unified understanding of the prerequisites for forming precise Hh gradients.

articles.title: Heat Stroke Cooling Devices for Prehospital Use: A Systematic Review.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Heat stroke and heat exhaustion (HS/HE) are life-threatening conditions requiring immediate intervention. Cooling devices play a critical role in emergency and prehospital care, yet their effectiveness and field readiness are inconsistently reported. This systematic review evaluates commercially available cooling devices for the treatment of HS/HE with an emphasis on device feasibility, performance, and suitability for prehospital and remote deployment.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in August/October 2025 across academic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Compendex, Engineering Village, and IEEE Xplore) and gray literature via Google Advanced Search. Academic records were screened using Rayyan, while gray literature was organized in Excel with the aid of a custom HTML scraper. Devices were included if they met the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) definition of a medical device, were designed for adult human use, and specifically addressed HS/HE. Parameters extracted included working principle, cooling rate, weight, dimensions, volume, power requirements, external resource demands, and reusability. Cooling performance was benchmarked using thresholds reported by McDermott, et al, and portability was assessed using the MIL-STD-1472H single-person carriage limit of ≤16kg.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 18 devices were identified and evaluated. Only three met the ideal cooling rate threshold (≥0.155°C/minute), and two others achieved acceptable performance (0.078-0.154°C/minute). Approximately 61% of devices did not report cooling rate data. Five devices met field portability criteria (≤16kg), though most were limited by reliance on water, power, or disposable components. Only one device demonstrated feasibility for remote use; this device, however, lacked full reusability.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: No device meets the combined criteria of effectiveness, portability, field readiness, and reusability for HS/HE treatment. Current FDA pathways do not require reporting of key performance metrics, highlighting a regulatory gap. There is a need for development of field-appropriate solutions and revised evaluation standards that prioritize cooling performance, resource independence, and usability in austere environments.

articles.title: Acute anisocoria during nebulized ipratropium therapy: the value of medication and device review.
Still's disease and malignancies: insights into the balance between inflammatory enhancement and immune control. Data from the International AIDA Network Still's Disease Registry.
authors: From the International AIDA (AutoInflammatory Diseases Alliance) Network, from the Autoinflammatory Diseases Working Group of the Italian Society of Rheumatology (SIR)

abstract.text: Still's disease is an autoinflammatory condition marked by excessive activation of the innate immune system, resulting in intense and persistent systemic inflammation if left untreated. Chronic inflammation is recognized as both an initiator and promoter of carcinogenesis, although growing evidence suggests it may act against cancer development. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the cancer risk in patients with Still's disease. Data were obtained from the international Autoinflammatory Diseases Alliance (AIDA) Network registry for Still's disease. Statistical analysis included a machine learning-based approach to evaluate associations between independent variables and malignancy. A total of 626 patients with Still's disease were included, of whom 14 (2.2%) developed 15 malignant neoplasms. Patients with malignancy history exhibited higher age at disease onset and diagnosis, as well as longer duration of fever during flares. Machine learning-based analysis, including Elastic Net and Firth's penalized likelihood logistic regression, identified an association between cancer development and fever duration (relative risk = 1.002, 95% confidence interval 1.000-1.004, p = 0.01). Despite being a severe systemic inflammatory condition, Still's disease appears to be associated with a relatively modest prevalence of cancer. However, uncontrolled systemic inflammation, as reflected by prolonged fever duration, may contribute to carcinogenesis in these patients.

articles.title: Timing of the Adrenaline Administration in Witnessed Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Retrospective, National Cohort Study in Japan, Using a 2014-2020 Dataset.
articles.journal_full: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: We evaluated the association between the timing of initial adrenaline administration and outcomes in witnessed pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA).

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: A multicenter, retrospective cohort study addressing resuscitation time bias by performing a risk-set matching analysis using time-dependent propensity scores.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: Analysis of data from the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine OHCA (JAAM-OHCA) registry, which is a nationwide, multicenter, prospective collection of prehospital and in-hospital data involving Japanese patients with OHCA.

abstract.label: PATIENTS
abstract.text: Pediatric patients (< 18 yr) with witnessed OHCA who received adrenaline, during the period June 2014 to December 2020.

abstract.label: INTERVENTIONS
abstract.text: None.

abstract.label: MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
abstract.text: We compared patients who received adrenaline in specific time intervals (1-10, 11-15, 16-20, 21-25, or 26-30 min) after first contact with emergency medical services with those who still had not received adrenaline during the same time. The primary and secondary outcomes were survival and favorable neurologic outcome at one month, defined as a Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category score of 1-3. We identified a total of 259 OHCA patients who had received adrenaline at 1-10, 11-15, 16-20, 21-25, 26-30, and 31 minutes or later; at each respective time point, there were 15, 39, 62, 55, 37, and 51 patients. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs for 1-month survival at each time group compared with patients at risk were: 1-10 minutes, RR, 2.94 (95% CI, 0.38-22.81); 11-15 minutes, RR, 0.97 (95% CI, 0.30-3.12); 16-20 minutes, RR, 1.00 (95% CI, 0.29-3.48); 21-25 minutes, RR, 1.35 (95% CI, 0.54-3.40); and 26-30 minutes, RR, 1.71 (95% CI, 0.27-10.78). We failed to identify an association between time interval and greater or lesser probability of survival or neurologic outcome.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In the JAAM-OHCA registry, with pediatric data from 2014 to 2020, we failed to identify an association between earlier adrenaline administration and greater probability of 1-month survival or favorable neurologic outcomes.

articles.title: Defining the rural-urban faultline in prehospital trauma care: How dataset and metric choice reveal geography-dependent disparities.
Impact of pre-existing bleeding disorders on outcomes in patients with traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major global public health problem. This study aimed to evaluate the association between pre-existing bleeding disorders and clinical outcomes among patients with TBI. We hypothesized that pre-existing bleeding disorders would be associated with worse outcomes following TBI.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the 2021-2023 National Inpatient Sample (NIS) to evaluate the association between pre-existing bleeding disorders and clinical outcomes among patients aged 15 years or older hospitalized with TBI.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mortality was significantly higher in the bleeding disorder group (13.9% vs. 4.8%; p < 0.001), the median length of stay was longer (5 days vs. 3 days; p < 0.001), median hospitalization costs were substantially higher (US $20,582 vs. US $13,515; p < 0.001), and discharge home was less frequent (44.8% vs. 61.6%; p < 0.001). After adjustment for age, comorbidity burden, injury severity, and other clinically relevant covariates, pre-existing bleeding disorders remained independently associated with higher odds of in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR, 2.31; 95% CI, 1.99-2.69).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Pre-existing bleeding disorders were independently associated with higher odds of in-hospital mortality after TBI. Patients with these disorders also experienced worse clinical outcomes. Early recognition and appropriate hemostatic assessment may support individualized management in this vulnerable population.

articles.title: A Rare Case Report of Type II Kounis Syndrome With Literature Review: Acute Anterior ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction Following Bee Sting.

abstract.text: Kounis syndrome (KS), also known as allergic angina, is a rare but serious condition defined by acute coronary syndrome occurring alongside a hypersensitivity reaction. We report the case of a 42-year-old male smoker who developed Type II KS after a hymenoptera sting. The patient came to the emergency department with a sudden decreased level of consciousness and retrosternal chest pain. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads, and coronary angiography revealed total proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was performed successfully. Echocardiography documented a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% with regional wall motion abnormalities, indicating significant myocardial injury. The patient was discharged with a treatment plan that included valsartan, spironolactone, bisoprolol, ticagrelor, acetylsalicylic acid, and atorvastatin. This case highlights the diagnostic and treatment challenges of KS and stresses the need for early recognition and a team-based approach to achieve better clinical results.

articles.title: Nebulized Tranexamic Acid in Posttonsillectomy Hemorrhage: A Retrospective Study of a Standardized Treatment Algorithm.
articles.journal_full: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate efficacy of nebulized tranexamic acid (TXA) in reducing the need for surgery after posttonsillectomy hemorrhage (PTH).

abstract.label: STUDY DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective analysis of a treatment protocol for PTH with pre-protocol patients serving as historical comparisons.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: Tertiary children's hospital.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Patients <18 years of age who presented to the emergency department (ED) with PTH from August 2022 through August 2025 were included. Beginning March 1, 2024 patients presenting with PTH in stable condition received nebulized TXA. Bleeding severity was categorized into active bleeding, small clot involving <50% of the fossa, large clot involving ≥50% of the tonsillar fossa, or no bleeding. Those with active bleeding or persistent large clot after TXA underwent surgery. Those with small clots or no bleeding were observed for 3 hours or 1 hour before discharge, respectively.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 121 patients with PTH were evaluated. 80% of untreated patients required surgery versus 66% of the TXA group (P = .15). In patients with small clots, 88% of untreated patients required surgery versus 21% of patients in the TXA group (P = .003). No adverse events were reported with TXA use. We estimated 32 surgeries were avoided in the post-protocol period, with net cost savings of approximately $138,162.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Nebulized TXA reduced the need for surgery in PTH, particularly in patients presenting with clots encompassing <50% of the tonsillar fossa. Our algorithm provides a reasonable framework for PTH treatment and can safely reduce the need for surgery and limit resource utilization.

articles.title: Intra-Provincial Variation of Brief Substance Use Withdrawal Hospitalizations in Ontario, Canada: A Cross-Sectional Study: Variations intra-provinciales des hospitalisations de courte durée pour sevrage de substances en Ontario (Canada) : une étude transversale.
articles.journal_full: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie

abstract.text: ObjectiveIn Ontario, substance use disorders are the top reason for mental health and addictions-related hospitalizations, many of which are related to substance withdrawal. Our objective was to identify briefer withdrawal-related hospitalizations that are potentially manageable in medically supported community-based settings, assess the degree of intra-provincial variation for these types of admissions, and examine the health care utilization of these patients.MethodsWe conducted a population-based, cross-sectional study using linked health administrative data for Ontario residents hospitalized with alcohol- or opioid-use withdrawal between January 1, 2019 to December 31, 2021. Brief withdrawal admissions (BWAs) were defined as hospitalizations with a stay of 0-4 days and without intensive care. We calculated BWA rates per 100,000 person-years (PY), overall and for health regions within the province. Log-binomial regression models were used to examine differences in health care utilization in the year following a BWA compared with the year prior to admission.ResultsThere were 12,544 BWAs in Ontario during our study period (28.6 admissions per 100,000 PY) with a greater than 7-fold difference (p < 0.001) between the provincial health regions with the highest (North West region, 149.5 per 100,000 PY) and lowest (Central region, 20.8 per 100,000 PY) rate. In the year following a BWA, 30% of patients required hospital admission and 50% had an emergency department visit for substance use, which represented a significant increase of 63% (Relative Rate (RR) = 1.63; 95% Confidence Interval (95% CI) 1.55-1.71, P-value <0.001) and 11% (RR = 1.11; 95% CI 1.08-1.14, P-value <0.001), compared with the year prior to admission, respectively.ConclusionsUnderstanding the variation in BWAs, and the significant health care use following such events, is vital in supporting provincial efforts to improve withdrawal management. Future research should examine if providing more resources to community-based withdrawal services to manage BWAs results in improved patient outcomes and reduced acute care capacity/costs.

articles.title: Establishing a core outcome set for use in trials of severe acute paediatric asthma exacerbation (2-17 years): study protocol for an international co-design Delphi survey - a Paediatric Emergency Research Network study initiative.
authors: Pediatric Emergency Research Networks (PERN) asthma working group

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Asthma is one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood and a leading cause of emergency department (ED) presentations worldwide. However, for those experiencing a severe exacerbation, there is a limited evidence base to decide which treatment works best. A major contributor to this, is the considerable heterogeneity in outcome selection which limits comparison between trials. The development of a core outcome set (COS) may improve this, enhancing the quality, comparability and applicability of future research. This protocol describes the development of the first internationally derived COS for trials evaluating interventions in severe, acute asthma exacerbations.

abstract.label: METHODS AND ANALYSIS
abstract.text: A modified Delphi methodology will be used. An international steering committee comprising experts has been established through the Paediatric Emergency Research Network Asthma Working Group. For participants, this study will seek balanced representation across the six WHO regions and include clinicians who regularly manage children with severe acute asthma exacerbations and parents of children previously hospitalised with an asthma exacerbation. A target of 180 participants will be recruited, allowing for an anticipated 30% attrition rate between rounds and approximately 80 participants completing the final round. Three rounds of online surveys will be undertaken. Participants will rate the importance of outcomes identified through a systematic review and qualitative studies, with opportunities to suggest modifications and additional outcomes. Consensus after round 3 will be defined as either: (1) ≥70% of participants from both stakeholder groups scoring an outcome as critically important (7–9 on a 9-point Likert scale) and ≤15% scoring it as of limited importance (1–3) or (2) ≥90% of participants from either stakeholder group scoring the outcome as critically important.

abstract.label: ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
abstract.text: Ethical approval was granted by the Southern Adelaide Health Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC reference number 2025/HRE00375). Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations and stakeholder engagement activities. This study has been prospectively registered with the Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET), registration number 1016.

articles.title: Predictors of severe measles outcomes in hospitalized patients in Jerusalem, 2025.
articles.journal_full: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Measles is a vaccine-preventable disease. Defining risk factors for poor outcomes in hospitalized patients can improve future measles outbreak preparedness.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Data were collected on all confirmed measles cases that were evaluated at one of the emergency departments in the three main hospitals in Jerusalem from the first reported case of the current outbreak on 10 April 2025 to 31 December 2025. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were analysed using robust Poisson multivariable models to calculate incidence rate ratios (IRR) for hospitalization, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and death.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 786 individuals who visited the emergency department with confirmed measles, the rates of hospital admission (≥1 day), ICU, ECMO, and death were 83.4%, 6.4%, 0.8%, and 1.4%, respectively. Complete data were available for 567 patients, of whom 303 (53.4%) were male. The median age was 2.1 years (interquartile range, 1.2-3.8 years), and 474 (83.6%) were younger than 5 years. Most patients were unvaccinated (91.0%). Secondary infections were frequent, including lobar pneumonia (28.7%) and community-acquired bacteraemia (3.5%). Respiratory support and severe dehydration were associated with hospital admission (IRR: 1.4, 95% CI, 1.3-1.5; p <0.001 and 9.5, 4.8-18.4; p <0.001, respectively) and ICU admission (IRR: 1.3, 1.2-1.4; p <0.001 and 5.2, 2.1-12.4; p <0.001, respectively). Community-acquired bacteraemia was associated with death or ECMO (IRR: 44.5, 12.5-158.6; p <0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Despite high access to medical care in this urban setting, measles caused substantial morbidity and mortality. Respiratory compromise, severe dehydration, and bacteraemia identified patients at increased risk of severe outcomes.

articles.title: Food Allergy Impact on Military Excellence: Epidemiology and Operational Outcomes.
articles.journal_full: The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Food allergy (FA) commonly disqualifies applicants from United States military service, though military members diagnosed with FA during service often continue to serve. The impact of FA on military operations is unknown.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: We aim to investigate the impact of FA on military operations by examining epidemiologic trends, demographics, and severe outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We completed a retrospective study including active-duty service members with diagnostic codes for food anaphylaxis, food allergy, and food adverse reactions between 2017 and 2024. We collected epidemiologic data, demographics, and outcomes including medical encounters and evacuations.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: FA prevalence increased over time, peaking at 33,557 or approximately 2.4% of service members in 2024. FA prevalence was higher in women (4.5%), Black individuals (3.7%), individuals with either longer time in service or >2 deployments (3.9-4%). Prevalence was lower in Marines (1.2%), pilots/aircrew (1.9%), and combat/artillery/infantry (1.5%). In total over our 8-year study there were 4,275 emergency department (ED) visits, 143 hospitalizations, and 7 medical evacuations, averaging approximately 534 ED visits, 18 hospitalizations, and less than one medical evacuation annually.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This study examining FA in the military reveals that although prevalence has increased, FA-related hospitalizations and medical evacuations remain uncommon. Although military accession policy nominally disqualifies many individuals with FA from service, the prevalence of FA in service members has increased over time. Based on our results, FA-related severe outcomes such as hospitalizations and medical evacuations are rare and do not currently pose substantial risk to military operations, supporting possible revision to current accession policy.

articles.title: A mysterious danger for kidney disease exacerbations: short-term impacts of ultrafine particles on hospital visits.

abstract.text: Ultrafine particles (UFPs) are more toxic than fine particulate matter (PM2.5) but are generally ignored. Limited health research existed on UFPs, especially for kidney diseases. We investigated if UFPs could increase kidney-disease related hospital emergency department (ED) visits. Time-stratified case-crossover design was used for evaluating the short-term impacts of UFP. Daily exposure to UFPs was assessed by a previously validated chemical transport model. ED visits with principal diagnosis of kidney diseases, geocoded at street level, from 2013 to 2018, were obtained from New York State hospital discharge database covering 95% of all hospitals. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate the excess risks (%ER) for every inter-quartile range (IQR) change (ERIQR). Among 269,945 ED visits, increasing kidney-disease ED visits were associated with UFPs on individual lag 1 day and all cumulative lag days (lag 0-1 to lag 0-6). The ER of ED visits peaked on lag 0-3 days (ERIQR = 0.74, 95% confidence interval: 0.28, 1.20). Stronger associations were found among non-African American, older adults (>65 yrs), during days with high temperatures, low humidity, and fall/winter season. Our findings suggested the kidney toxicity of UFPs and suggest that routine measures should be taken to monitor UFP concentration and control its emission.

articles.title: Challenges in Infection Prevention and Control in Paramedicine: A Modified Nominal Group Technique Consensus Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are a major patient safety concern, yet infection prevention and control (IPC) in emergency ambulance services is challenging due to unpredictable environments, operational pressures, and equipment limitations. Evidence is limited regarding how ambulance fleet and equipment design influence IPC compliance. This study aimed to identify expert priorities for improving the availability and utility of IPC equipment and consumables in paramedicine.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A modified Nominal Group Technique was conducted with experts in infection prevention, paramedicine, clinical governance, education, and operations. Participants collectively generated ideas concerned with IPC in emergency ambulance services and subsequently ranked these through an anonymous survey to determine priority areas.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Ten experts participated. Human factors were ranked as the most influential determinant of IPC compliance, followed by education and training, physical environment, equipment and consumables, and contaminated equipment management. Key barriers included organizational culture, compliance fatigue, inconsistent education, uncontrolled environments, and fleet design limitations.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: IPC compliance in ambulance services is primarily shaped by behavioral, organizational, and environmental factors rather than equipment provision alone. Systems-based, co-designed interventions addressing human factors, education, organizational support, and equipment design are essential to improve IPC adherence and enhance patient and clinician safety.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted, electrocardiogram-derived, sequential rule-based decision tree for exclusion of acute coronary syndrome as the etiology of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a single-center retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: After out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), deciding which patients without ST-segment elevation warrant emergency coronary angiography is difficult, as standard electrocardiogram (ECG), troponin, and echocardiography are limited in the early post-arrest window. We aimed to develop a sequential rule-based decision tree to identify post-ROSC patients in whom acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is unlikely to be the arrest etiology.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this single-center retrospective study, adult patients with OHCA were divided into development (2020-2024; n = 329) and temporal validation (2025; n = 71) cohorts. Post-ROSC 12-lead ECGs were analyzed by a deep-learning platform generating ten digital biomarkers. Five candidate biomarkers were combined into a rhythm-stratified sequential decision tree under a zero false-negative constraint; its performance was compared with that of individual biomarkers and validated in the temporal cohort.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The tree classified 171/329 (52.0%) and 32/71 (45.1%) patients in the development and validation cohorts, respectively, as "ACS not likely," with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified at any node. Yield concentrated in the non-shockable subgroup, in which the model excluded 169/261 (64.8%) non-ACS cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC], 0.824), outperforming each individual biomarker. In the shockable subgroup, which carries a high pretest probability of ACS, 38/40 patients (95.0%) were retained as "ACS not excluded."

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A rhythm-stratified, rule-based decision tree combining AI-assisted ECG-derived biomarkers classified approximately half of post-OHCA patients as "ACS not likely" with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified, principally in the non-shockable subgroup. This transparent, bedside-deployable framework warrants prospective multicenter evaluation.

articles.title: Ventilation monitoring in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest care.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Adherence to American Heart Association (AHA) ventilation guidelines during cardiac arrest is challenging.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Prospective, Before/After quality assurance study determining adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by Milwaukee County Emergency Medical Services and Kenosha Fire in Wisconsin using (Before) end tidal carbon dioxide [ETCO2] to monitor ventilations - Real BVM Help® applied but blinded versus (After) Real BVM Help®.

abstract.label: PRIMARY ENDPOINTS
abstract.text: mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in-target for rate, tidal volume, and both rate and tidal volume. AHA 2020 guidelines were followed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: From 9/29/22-12/22/23, 278 patients were entered (148 Before/130 After). Average age: 62.3 ± 16.7 years; 185 (67%) male. Mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in Before/After Groups in-target for rate (47.7 ± 25.1% vs 74.4 ± 24.1% respectively, p < 0.0001), tidal volume (15.3 ± 15.4% vs 45.4 ± 23.8% respectively, p < 0.0001), and rate and tidal volume (7.5 ± 9.6% vs 39.0 ± 23.3% respectively, p < 0.0001) were significantly higher in the After Group.
