In the Before Group, using ETCO2 to monitor all ventilations (N = 22,037 ventilations), only 43.8% were in-target for rate, 13.5% in-target for tidal volume, and 6.8% in-target for rate and tidal volume with a lower-than-target tidal volume delivered in 58.2% of all ventilations.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Real BVM Help® was associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines. ETCO2 monitoring failed to approach both rate and tidal volume guideline adherence with a lower-than-target tidal volume being the most common parameter delivered out-of-target (58.2%). Ventilation rate and tidal volume monitoring with real-time feedback should be considered during treatment of cardiac arrest.

articles.title: Early identification of recurrent out-of-hospital cardiac arrest using clinical ECG features.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) after initial return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is associated with relatively poor outcomes. Early identification of rearrest might enable intervention to prevent rearrest. In this study, we sought to determine whether clinical ECG features can predict rearrest.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients who achieved ROSC between 2018 and 2024. We evaluated the association of ECG features (QRS width, standard deviation of Normal-to-Normal intervals, root mean square of successive NN interval differences, and percentage of NN intervals that differ by more than 50 ms) within individual 15-s segments throughout a 5-min window prior to rearrest as well as their temporal trends over the 5-min analytic window.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 1489 OHCA patients achieving ROSC, 1298 were analyzed; 528 (40.7%) experienced rearrest. Rearrest patients were older, less likely to receive bystander CPR (48.7% vs. 61.9%), and had lower survival (20.4% vs. 43.1%) and favorable neurologic outcomes (7.8% vs. 21.2%; all p < 0.001). We found lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher HR variability in those with rearrest. Identification was highest 1 min prior to rearrest (AUROC 0.74), declining beyond 3 min. Models using temporal trends achieved AUROC 0.67; strongest predictors were heart rate variability measures and QRS width.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Established ECG features achieved good prediction for rearrest with identification improving closer to time of rearrest. Future work leveraging novel features or more advanced artificial intelligence models may further improve prediction.

articles.title: Noninferiority of implementing a telephone follow-up based pathway after uncomplicated pediatric appendectomy: A retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: In-person postoperative follow-up after pediatric appendectomy imposes burdens without established clinical benefit over telemedicine follow-up. Telemedicine follow-up is safe after adult surgery and has high satisfaction after pediatric general surgery, but its safety after pediatric appendectomy has not been established. We evaluated whether implementation of a telephone-based follow-up pathway was noninferior to an in-person follow-up model for 30-day emergency department (ED) visits.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of patients <18 years undergoing appendectomy for uncomplicated acute appendicitis between 2020 and 2025 using a Pediatric Health Information System query with manual chart review. On November 1, 2022, a telephone-based follow-up pathway was implemented. Pre-vs. post-implementation cohorts were compared. The primary outcome was a related ED visit within 30 days. Noninferiority was prespecified at an absolute margin of 3 percentage points using a one-sided 97.5% confidence interval (CI).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1570 patients (738 pre-, 832 post-implementation), receipt of telephone follow-up increased from 10.3% (n = 76) to 65.7% (n = 547) (p < 0.001), and completion of any postoperative follow-up increased from 65.3% to 73.3% (p = 0.002). Thirty-day related ED visits occurred in 32 (4.3%) patients pre-implementation and 28 (3.4%) post-implementation. The adjusted absolute risk difference was -1.03 percentage points (one-sided 97.5% CI, -∞ to +0.85), below the prespecified 3-percentage-point noninferiority margin.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Implementation of a telephone-based follow-up pathway after uncomplicated pediatric appendectomy was noninferior for 30-day related ED visits, while improving overall follow-up completion and reducing the need for burdensome in-person visits.

articles.title: Chronic neurotoxicity of di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) at no observed adverse effects level (NOAEL)-range doses induces neurobehavioral disorders in adult zebrafish.

abstract.text: Di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP), as the most common member of phthalic acid esters (PAEs), is considered an endocrine-disrupting compound (EDC) and causes prominent developmental, reproductive toxicity, metabolic dysfunctions, and neurotoxicity. However, the potential neurotoxicity associated with chronic DEHP exposure at concentrations below the no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) in adult zebrafish remains poorly understood, largely due to a lack of experimental evidence from animal studies. Thus, to comprehensively characterize the potential neurological effects of DEHP, adult zebrafish were used as an animal model to evaluate neurotoxicity following 4 weeks of exposure to DEHP at concentrations within the NOAEL range (5, 50, and 200 mg/L). Behavioral assessments included the light-dark preference test, novel tank diving test, novel object exploration test, social interactions test, and conditioned place preference (CPP) test. After 4 weeks of chronic exposure to DEHP, zebrafish exhibited marked neurobehavioral alterations, including increased time spent and distance traveled in the dark zone and reduced exploratory behavior in unfamiliar environments (reduced top-zone exploration in the novel tank test and reduced novel-object zone exploration); DEHP exposure also disrupted social interactions and impaired learning and memory in zebrafish. The LC-MS/MS results revealed that changes in neuro-behavioral profiles were closely associated with neurotransmitter levels in the brain of zebrafish. The present study provides a valuable reference for drawing attention to the assessment of DEHP neurotoxicity below the NOAEL.

articles.title: Dynamic Early Postreperfusion Physiology Is Associated With Organ Recovery After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.
articles.journal_full: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)

abstract.text: Prognostication after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) predominantly relies on characteristics available before or at initiation of extracorporeal support. We investigated whether the early metabolic response to extracorporeal reperfusion provides complementary information on subsequent recovery. We retrospectively analyzed 91 patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with ECPR. Lactate was assessed before and 12 h after extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) initiation. Outcomes included in-hospital mortality, successful ECMO weaning, cerebral edema/hypoxic brain injury, and favorable neurological survival. Associations were adjusted for low-flow duration. Twelve hour lactate was lower in survivors than nonsurvivors (5.45 vs. 9.04 mmol/L; p = 0.002), whereas prereperfusion lactate did not differ. In paired measurements (n = 38), mortality discrimination increased from an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.47 before reperfusion to 0.80 at 12 h. Each 5 mmol/L higher 12 h lactate was associated with mortality (odds ratio [OR] = 2.73), lower odds of ECMO weaning (OR = 0.44), and cerebral edema/hypoxic injury (OR = 2.07) after low-flow adjustment. Early metabolic response after extracorporeal reperfusion was associated with survival and both circulatory and cerebral recovery. Dynamic post-reperfusion physiology may provide complementary information beyond static pre-reperfusion assessment.

articles.title: Integrating YOLOv8-based disaster detection with deep reinforcement learning for closed-loop UAV emergency response scheduling: A simulation study.

abstract.text: Aerial perception and dispatch scheduling in unmanned aerial vehicle emergency response are commonly arranged as a one-directional pipeline, and the contribution of closing the loop between them has not been measured under controlled conditions. This study evaluates a framework in which a YOLOv8 scene classifier gates task discovery, a Disaster Situation State Matrix aggregates spatially indexed detection outputs under exponential temporal decay, and a proximal policy optimization scheduler acts on that matrix. Evaluation used a 32 × 32 grid testbed with four vehicles, ten training seeds per configuration, and one hundred frozen evaluation scenarios per seed, with a complete two-by-two ablation separating policy access to the state matrix from the rate at which the matrix is refreshed. Runtime perception updating raised task completion from 0.4971 to 0.5859 relative to an initial-snapshot policy, a gain of 8.87 percentage points (95% CI 7.26 to 10.32, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0078). Policy access to the state matrix carried a main effect of 36.42 percentage points (95% CI 34.83 to 37.79) and refresh rate a main effect of 1.81 percentage points (95% CI 0.90 to 2.82), with no evidence of interaction. Under a shared six-action interface and identical perception constraints, the proposed scheduler exceeded a greedy heuristic by 3.44 percentage points (95% CI 2.03 to 4.91, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0078). Replacing confusion-matrix sampling with replayed YOLOv8 predictions on held-out images reduced completion by 1.28 percentage points, and temporally persistent detection errors extended the longest uninterrupted error run to seventy-one steps. Structural exposure of the state matrix to the scheduling policy, rather than refresh frequency alone, accounts for the observed performance of the framework.

articles.title: Dynamic assessment of renal resistive index using point-of-care ultrasonography for early detection of sepsis-induced acute kidney injury: A multicenter clinical trial protocol.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication of sepsis, significantly increasing both mortality risk and healthcare costs. Early prediction and diagnosis of sepsis-associated AKI (SA-AKI) remain challenging due to the delayed detection of existing renal injury markers. Although research suggests that the Renal Resistive Index (RRI) shows promise for earlier prediction of AKI, large-scale, multicenter clinical studies to support this are currently lacking.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This multicenter, open-label, prospective observational cohort study enrolled 238 patients who were diagnosed with sepsis according to the Sepsis 3.0 criteria. The Renal Resistive Index (RRI) was measured using bedside ultrasound within 2 hours of diagnosis and subsequently every 8 hours during their individualized standard treatment. Concurrently, blood samples were collected to quantify creatinine and cystatin C, and urine samples were obtained to detect kidney injury markers, including TIMP-2/IGFBP-7. The primary endpoint is to determine the threshold and accuracy of the Renal Resistive Index in predicting sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI). Secondary endpoints include examining the dynamic trend of the RRI, assessing the RRI's predictive value for 28-day mortality in sepsis, and evaluating the correlation between the RRI and creatinine, cystatin C, and urinary TIMP-2/IGFBP-7 levels.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This study assesses the accuracy and feasibility of using bedside ultrasonography to monitor the Renal Resistive Index (RRI) for the early detection of sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI). Early identification of SA-AKI is crucial for improving clinical outcomes in sepsis, making this approach highly relevant for timely intervention.

abstract.label: ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
abstract.text: This study received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of the initiator's institution. Study results will be initially reported to the collaborating investigators. Following review and consensus by the Trial Steering Committee, the research report will be drafted by the initiating investigator and disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at scientific conferences.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400082420), Registered on March 28, 2024.

articles.title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound in Diagnosis of Breast Cancer-Related Lymphedema: A Multimodal Database and Deep Learning Approach.

abstract.text: Breast Cancer-Related Lymphedema (BCRL) is a common complication after breast cancer treatment, leading to chronic arm swelling and reduced quality of life. Early detection remains challenging due to limitations in current assessment methods and a shortage of expert clinicians. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) imaging offers a cost-effective, non-invasive tool for BCRL evaluation; however, the visual disparity between affected and unaffected arms can be subtle. To address this, we introduce a multimodal dataset containing B-mode images, radio-frequency (RF) data, perometry-based arm volume measurements, the number of dissected lymph nodes, the time elapsed since surgery, and body mass index (BMI) from 57 subjects. Additionally, the dataset includes an assessment of the severity of BCRL by an expert clinician (A.T.). We also propose a deep learning-based framework for automated BCRL diagnosis using multimodal data. Our method first employs a Siamese-based architecture to extract and compare features from bilateral arm images, addressing subject-specific variability. We further improve the method by incorporating clinical tabular data and investigating the effect of multimodal fusion and supervised contrastive learning on the model's performance. To our knowledge, this is the first automated deep learning approach for BCRL diagnosis. Using three-fold cross-validation, the proposed Multimodal model achieved an AUC of 91.0%, an accuracy of 87.0%, and an F1 score of 83.5%. It outperformed the two other variants, Unimodal-A and Unimodal-B, in BCRL classification across most metrics. The source code and trained model will be released at http://code.sonography.ai.

articles.title: User-Centered Evaluation of an AR Virtual Triage Tag: Responder Perceptions and Performance with Virtual and 'Real' Patient Actors.
articles.journal_full: IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics

abstract.text: Rural emergency responders, serving ∼49 million people, are under-experienced and under-trained to handle mass casualty incidents (MCIs). Our prior work has proposed AR tools to facilitate novice emergency responders in MCI triage, concluding with an introductory lab study of the AR tool's usability with actual emergency responders. Given the high risk and consequential nature of MCI triage, 1) sterile, controlled lab settings are not sufficient in isolation to evaluate the actual scalability of these AR tools, and simultaneously, 2) it is impossible to jump straight to actual field evaluation without further proof of concept. Thus, this work offers additional AR tool evaluation with emergency responders through two contextually embedded simulations-one with virtual patients and one with 'real' patient actors situated in a physical space. This paper describes the two simulations created via a partnership with a national training facility for MCI triage, Disaster City at Texas A&M Engineering's Extension Service (TEEX). This paper discusses the AR tool's usability in progressively embedded real context via subjective semi-structured interviews and objective performance measures, and finally explores the effectiveness of the simulations themselves for evaluative purposes.

articles.title: Portable ultra-low field MRI in neurocritical care and intensive care units: A systematic review of diagnostic performance and feasibility.

abstract.text: To synthesise evidence on the diagnostic performance, safety, feasibility and clinical impact of ultra-low-field portable magnetic resonance imaging (pMRI) in adult neurocritical care and intensive care unit (ICU) populations. PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched from inception to 6 February 2026 and supplemented by grey literature and citation searching. We included original English-language studies of adult ICU, neurocritical care or emergency department patients undergoing pMRI at ≤ 0.1 T. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias in diagnostic comparisons was assessed with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework, and feasibility and safety outcomes were appraised narratively. Because of heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. The review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261302014). Eleven studies published between 2020 and 2024 were included, comprising 694 patient participants and 715 patient examinations, plus 40 healthy controls. Cohorts overlapped substantially: six studies came wholly and one partly from a single institution, and one ECMO study was a subset of another. The number of unique patients is therefore estimated at 281 to 677. In the multicentre ECMO study, adverse events occurred in 3 of 50 patients (6%). One was serious: an intra-aortic balloon pump malfunction attributed to electrocardiographic artefact. No adverse events were reported in the other seven independent cohorts that reported safety outcomes, and two studies did not report safety outcomes. For ischaemic stroke, pMRI detected infarction in 45 of 50 patients (90%). By sequence, sensitivity was 100% for FLAIR, 98% for T2-weighted imaging and 86% for diffusion-weighted imaging. Visual DWI-FLAIR mismatch identified patients scanned within 4.5 h with 60% sensitivity, 82% specificity and a 93% negative predictive value. Sensitivity for intracerebral haemorrhage was 80.4% (specificity 96.6%) on initial blinded evaluation. It was 92.1% (specificity 99.3%) in a later cohort in which raters had clinical context and images used deep-learning reconstruction, with lower sensitivity for infratentorial haemorrhage (75.0%). Only one subdural haemorrhage and no extradural haemorrhages were reported. Midline-shift detection showed 93% sensitivity, 96% specificity and a kappa of 0.87. pMRI detected hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in 12 of 12 affected post-cardiac-arrest patients. In ECMO patients, pMRI detected 8 of 8 ischaemic events, compared with 4 of 8 on head CT, but only 1 of 2 haemorrhages. Up to 28% of examinations were nondiagnostic, mainly because of motion. Ultra-low-field pMRI is a feasible bedside neuroimaging adjunct with a low but non-zero adverse-event rate. It is of particular value for ischaemic injury, midline shift and serial monitoring. Lower and variable sensitivity for haemorrhage, the nonspecificity of FLAIR hyperintensity, overlapping single-institution cohorts and small samples mean that larger multicentre validation studies are needed.

articles.title: Toward multimodal physiological assessment of clinical performance in simulation-based medical education: a machine learning approach.
articles.journal: Adv Health Sci Educ Theory Pract
articles.journal_full: Advances in health sciences education : theory and practice

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Assessment of learner performance in simulation-based medical education commonly relies on faculty observation. Learners' physiological responses may provide complementary information about responses to clinical task demands, but their relationship with observed performance is complex and context dependent. Whether multimodal physiological patterns can reliably distinguish faculty-assigned performance categories across simulation events and learner populations remains unclear.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective observational study developed machine-learning models using physiological data alone to classify learner performance according to faculty-assigned novice versus competent categories during high-fidelity simulation. Data were collected from 152 learners (74 Emergency Medicine residents, 70 Anesthesiology residents, 8 Emergency Medical Services students) across 470 simulation scenarios. A multimodal assessment platform synchronized physiological signals (electrodermal activity, heart rate, skin temperature) from Empatica E4 wristbands with faculty evaluations. A genetic algorithm was employed for feature selection, and neural network models were evaluated using multiple leave-N-out strategies to assess generalizability across learners.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The neural network achieved 84-85% balanced accuracy across thresholds 0.45-0.70, with sensitivity 93.3-95.4% and specificity 72.9-76.2%. Despite class imbalance (80.6% competent, 19.4% novice), performance remained robust, with Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.687-0.706 and precision-recall area-under-the-curve (PR-AUC) values of 0.969-0.970 across thresholds.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Multimodal physiological features enabled classification of faculty-assigned performance categories with strong discrimination in internal validation. These findings support the potential of temporally resolved, physiology-informed analytics to complement faculty assessment and facilitate targeted review of simulation events. Further work is needed to strengthen rating-label validity and temporal alignment and to evaluate model transparency, fairness, and generalizability across institutions, simulation contexts, and learner populations.

articles.title: Primary healthcare use prior to hospital consultations for spinal disorders among Danish children and adolescents: A descriptive nationwide registry-based study.

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Hospital-based spine-related diagnoses in children are often preceded by substantial healthcare use, but patterns and determinants remain poorly understood. This study aimed to describe pre-hospital primary healthcare use according to parental spine-related hospital diagnoses, the child's comorbidity burden, and household income. We conducted a nationwide, registry-based cohort study including all Danish children aged 2-17 years with a first hospital-based spine-related diagnosis between 2009 and 2022 (n = 46,497). Healthcare services with general practitioners (GP), chiropractors, physiotherapists, and office-based specialist providers in the two years prior to diagnosis were quantified. Primary healthcare use was described across age groups, parental spine-related hospital diagnoses, the child's comorbidity burden, and income tertiles. In the two years before diagnosis, children had a median of 9 reimbursed GP services (IQR [5-17]), 0 chiropractor services [0-0], 0 physiotherapy services [0-0], and 0 office-based specialist services [0-1]. GP use was common, whereas use of non-GP providers was highly skewed, with most children having no or few reimbursed services and a smaller subgroup having repeated service use. Descriptive patterns of healthcare use varied according to parental spine-related hospital diagnoses and comorbidity burden. Healthcare use showed no clear descriptive gradient across household income groups.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Patterns of primary healthcare use varied according to parental spine-related hospital diagnoses and comorbidity burden. No clear overall income gradient was observed, although patterns varied by provider type. These findings describe heterogeneous pre-hospital primary healthcare use in this population.

abstract.label: WHAT IS KNOWN
abstract.text: • Spinal pain is common in children and is associated with substantial burden, including school absence and later risk of chronic pain. • Hospital-based spinal diagnoses in children are increasingly non-specific and often represent conditions that could be managed in primary care.

abstract.label: WHAT IS NEW
abstract.text: • Higher primary healthcare use was observed among children with greater comorbidity burden and among those with parental spine-related hospital diagnoses. • Differences in total primary healthcare use across household income groups were small, with no clear income gradient.

articles.title: 24-hour risk updating for major ICU complications after severe trauma: a prospective cohort study.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Conventional trauma prognostic models rely primarily on admission data and cannot account for subsequent physiological response to treatment. We evaluated whether routinely collected physiological information available at 24 h provides incremental prognostic information for major intensive care unit (ICU) complications in severely injured patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective cohort of adults with severe trauma (Injury Severity Score [ISS] ≥ 15) admitted to the ICU between January 2024 and April 2025. The primary outcome was a composite of major respiratory, hemodynamic, renal, or septic complications during the ICU course. TRISS was compared with an admission ridge model incorporating ISS, Glasgow Coma Scale, hemoglobin, lactate, and international normalized ratio, and a 24-h updated ridge model additionally incorporating 24-h lactate and change in creatinine. Performance was internally validated with 1,000 bootstrap resamples.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 109 patients, median ISS was 29 (IQR 20-38), and 73 (67.0%) developed major ICU complications. Optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.788 for TRISS, 0.873 for the admission model, and 0.887 for the 24-h updated model; Brier scores were 0.178, 0.140, and 0.131. Compared with the admission model, the 24-h updated model improved performance (ΔAUC 0.016, 95% bootstrap interval 0.004-0.030; ΔBrier - 0.010, - 0.017 to - 0.005). Twenty-four-hour lactate and creatinine change were the strongest contributors to the update.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In severely injured ICU patients, incorporating physiological evolution during the first 24 h refined admission-based prognostic assessment. Lactate and creatinine trajectories provided incremental information for major ICU complications during the ICU course. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Anxiety and Adult ADHD Symptoms Among Occupational Injury Cases Presenting to the Emergency Department: A Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Work-related injuries have economic and psychosocial consequences. Emerging evidence suggests neurocognitive and affective factors, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms and anxiety, may contribute to occupational injury risk; however, data integrating these factors in emergency department (ED) settings remain limited. This study aimed to compare ADHD and anxiety symptom burden between adults with occupational injuries and age- and sex-matched non-injured controls and to evaluate symptom associations with occupational injury.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Adults presenting to a tertiary ED in Türkiye with occupational injuries and age- and sex-matched non-injured controls were assessed using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). Sociodemographic, occupational, hazard, injury, and clinical variables were recorded. Logistic regression evaluated factors independently associated with occupational injury, and correlations with sleep duration were analyzed.

abstract.label: FINDINGS
abstract.text: A total of 609 participants were included (292 injured; 317 controls). Injured workers showed higher ASRS and BAI scores than controls (p < .05). ASRS and BAI scores demonstrated gradients across occupational hazard class, trauma mechanism, and clinical outcomes, including hospitalization and impairment. Prior injury history was more frequent among injured workers. In multivariable analysis, occupational hazard class, ASRS scores, and BAI scores remained independently associated with occupational injury. Sleep duration showed moderate negative correlations with ASRS and BAI scores.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS/APPLICATION TO PRACTICE
abstract.text: Adult ADHD and anxiety symptoms were associated with occupational injury in ED presentations. Screening for neurocognitive and affective vulnerabilities, together with fatigue and sleep management strategies, may enhance occupational injury prevention efforts. Further longitudinal studies are warranted.

articles.title: Predictors of Lower Back Musculoskeletal Disability Among Emergency Department Healthcare Professionals: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs), particularly lower back (LB) pain are highly prevalent in emergency department (ED) healthcare professionals with significant health-related impacts due to the high and unexpected workload.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to identify the predictors of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals in Jordan, including physical, psychological, and ergonomic occupational factors.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A multicenter convenience sample of ED healthcare professionals was recruited from Jordanian ED departments. Data collection included demographics, ergonomics-related factors and a group of validated outcome measures: the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21). A stepwise multivariable linear regression model was used to identify predictors of LB disability.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The study included 447 participants, of whom 57% were male (n = 255) and had a mean age of 35.1 ± 7.0 years. Predictors of the ODI (R2 = .31) included depression (B = 0.456, p < .001), taking sick leave in the past 12 months (β = 6.8, p < .001), safe handling and posturing practices (B = -5.584, p < .001), age (B = 0.32, p < .001) and presence of musculoskeletal injury in the past 12 months (B = 4.6, p = .022).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This study highlights the burden of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals. LB disability was significantly associated with depression, recent Musculoskeletal injury, Musculoskeletal-related sick leave and older age, with safe handling and posture practices showing a protective effect. Comprehensive interventions to integrate ergonomic improvements, mental health support, workload optimization, and exercise programs.

articles.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
articles.journal_full: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

abstract.label: RATIONALE
abstract.text: Substantial uncertainty exists regarding how healthcare system factors, especially care setting types, affect the uptake and implementation of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy screening in practice. Evidence suggests that the care environment may influence diagnostic processes.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To assess the effectiveness of maternity and non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus or diabetes in pregnancy.

abstract.label: SEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) up to April 2026, and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) up to December 2025. We also searched CENTRAL to identify ongoing trials.

abstract.label: ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA
abstract.text: We included RCTs and planned to include cluster-RCTs and NRSIs, but we did not find any. Eligible participants were pregnant women being screened for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes in pregnancy. We defined maternity healthcare settings as those specialising in care for pregnant, birthing, and postpartum individuals, with appropriate screening protocols, and non-maternity healthcare settings as general medical environments lacking a focus on pregnancy and women's care. We considered any screening format (e.g. risk-factor-based screening) and any diagnostic test (e.g. one- and two-step oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)).

abstract.label: OUTCOMES
abstract.text: Critical health service outcomes were compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines, diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy, maternal emergency department visits during pregnancy, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisation, length of neonatal hospitalisation, and care accessibility. Critical maternal outcomes included hypertensive disorders, maternal death, intensive care admissions, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance, including progression to diabetes, within 15 years after birth. Critical child-related outcomes encompassed perinatal death, neonatal intensive care admissions, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, large-for-gestational-age, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Further critical and important outcomes not included in the summary of findings tables can be found in the full text.

abstract.label: RISK OF BIAS
abstract.text: We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We had planned to use ROBINS-I version 2 to assess bias in the NRSIs if we had identified any.

abstract.label: SYNTHESIS METHODS
abstract.text: We used standard Cochrane methodology. We planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible (inverse-variance or Mantel-Haenszel approaches; fixed-effect model). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome.

abstract.label: INCLUDED STUDIES
abstract.text: We included one RCT with 781 participants: 390 were randomised to screening in a maternity healthcare setting and 391 were randomised to screening in a non-maternity healthcare setting. Except for screening compliance, trialists evaluated all outcomes using a per-protocol analysis instead of by original randomised groups. This approach created substantial disparities in sample sizes between settings and largely nullified the methodological protections typically provided by a randomised design. The trial evaluated screening for GDM only. We did not identify any ongoing studies or studies awaiting classification.

abstract.label: SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS
abstract.text: Health service outcomes Screening in a maternity healthcare setting may increase compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines (risk ratio (RR) 1.69, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 1.87; 781 participants) and may improve care accessibility, assessed as time to access antenatal diabetes care, measured in days (mean difference (MD) -4.70, 95% CI -6.03 to -3.37; 690 participants), both with low-certainty evidence. We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.01; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and length of neonatal hospitalisation (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.65; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No direct evidence was available on screening for diabetes in pregnancy as distinct from GDM. No data were reported on maternal emergency department visits, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisations, and costs. Maternal outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on pre-eclampsia (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.75; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The following outcomes were not reported: eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, maternal death, admission to intensive care, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance. Child-related outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on: stillbirth or foetal death (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), admission to neonatal intensive care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.71), preterm birth (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.71), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.59), large-for-gestational-age (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.04), shoulder dystocia (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.70), and birth trauma (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), all with 690 participants each and very low-certainty evidence. An effect estimate for neonatal death was not estimable (maternity setting: 0/475; non-maternity setting: 0/215).

abstract.label: AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: There is insufficient evidence to determine whether screening for gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy in maternity healthcare settings compared with non-maternity healthcare settings improves health service, maternal, or child-related outcomes. Low-certainty evidence from a single study indicates that screening in maternity healthcare settings may result in a reduction in time to access antenatal diabetes care and may increase compliance. The effects on other outcomes remain unknown. Conducting studies using intention-to-treat analyses could bridge existing research gaps, enhancing effect estimates and certainty.

abstract.label: FUNDING
abstract.text: This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP).

abstract.label: REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Protocol available via PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251108692.

articles.title: Establishing Welfare Evacuation Shelters for Children With Medical Complexity: A Prefecture-Wide Policy Shift Driven by Simulation in Tottori, Japan.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Children with medical complexity (CMC) are highly vulnerable during disasters, yet few Japanese welfare evacuation shelters accept them, leading to hospital-dependent planning. We aimed to assess the key issues hindering the establishment of welfare evacuation shelters for CMC.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In Tottori Prefecture (2020-2024), the government, municipalities, a university hospital, and device partners used facility assessments, staff education, and tabletop/field simulations (weekday earthquake with power outage and ventilator-dependent 5-year-old model) to identify gaps and iteratively revise manuals.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Key issues included space underestimation, difficult mobility, power insecurity, unreliable verbal information, unclear deterioration pathways, and undefined public health nurse (PHN) roles. Revisions established PHN-led reception/triage, standardized information collection, specified power sourcing, and set escalation/transport flows. A section on "Persons Requiring Medical Care" was added to prefectural policies, and the disaster medical guidance was updated, shifting preparedness from hospital-centered to shelter-based welfare.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This simulation-driven intersectoral model appears scalable; however, it was performed in a single prefecture with limited follow-up, impairing generalizability.

articles.title: Cardiac tamponade due to a displaced rib fracture: a case report.

abstract.text: Pericardial effusion causing cardiac tamponade is uncommon following blunt traumatic injury. We report the case of a 78-year-old woman who, following a road traffic collision, developed cardiac tamponade secondary to a displaced rib fracture. This case also demonstrates the value of repeated extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma (eFAST). Close monitoring of patients who are initially hemodynamically stable, in the context of their mechanism of injury, is essential in trauma care to reduce the morbidity and mortality that can occur without prompt management.

articles.title: [A survey on the required roles of dietitians in providing nutritional and dietary support during natural disasters].
articles.journal_full: [Nihon koshu eisei zasshi] Japanese journal of public health

abstract.text: Objectives When large-scale natural disasters occur, the Japan Dietetic Association-Disaster Assistance Team (JDA-DAT) dispatches dietitians to disaster-affected areas, where they collaborate with the affected local governments to provide nutrition and dietary support. Recognizing local government needs may result in more effective support. Therefore, this study aimed to identify the types of tasks that local government officials expect from JDA-DAT as aid providers. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of a more comprehensive disaster support system.Methods A nationwide survey was conducted targeting officials in the nutrition-related and disaster management departments of local governments nationwide. The survey investigated the priority of tasks expected of the JDA-DAT in disaster-affected areas and the types of tasks the recipients would like the JDA-DAT to undertake outside the disaster area (backup support). The priorities of tasks expected of the JDA-DAT in disaster-affected areas were classified as follows: ratings of 4 and 5 were considered high priority, 3 as medium priority, and 1 and 2 as low priority.Results The tasks in disaster-affected areas expected of the JDA-DAT, ranked in order of highest priority, were as follows: "tailored nutritional counseling for individuals necessitating special consideration who require nutrition and dietary support", "identification of residents requiring nutrition and dietary support (nutritional assessment) at evacuation shelters", "assessment of meal conditions at evacuation shelters and proposals for provided meals based on nutrient adequacy or deficiency (e.g., menu planning)", "management of stockpiled food and relief supplies (special dietary products): sorting special dietary products from general food items", and "support for coordination of provided meals (soup kitchens and boxed meal distribution): hygiene guidance". The items with high priority were similar in prefectural government offices and ordinance-designated cities/special wards, whereas some items were assigned high priority in municipalities (cities, towns, and villages).Conclusions The local government officials anticipate a wide range of support activities from the JDA-DAT. In particular, identifying individuals requiring special consideration and providing individualized support have received high priority. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the priority of requested support varies according to the type of municipality, underscoring the significance of supporters in understanding the roles of different local governments when engaging in disaster support activities.

articles.title: Segmental phase angle as predictor of activities of daily living and muscle health in patients with osteoporotic fracture A retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: This study aimed to determine whether the segmental phase angle is associated with clinical outcomes such as activities of daily living (ADL), muscle strength, and skeletal muscle mass in patients with osteoporotic fractures.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a retrospective cohort study of patients with osteoporotic fractures admitted to convalescent rehabilitation wards. The primary outcome was a Functional Independence Measure motor (FIM-motor) score at discharge, and secondary outcomes were handgrip strength and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI) at discharge. Multivariate analysis was used to adjust for confounders and to examine the association between segmental phase angle and outcome.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 115 subjects (97 women, age 81.0 ± 10.0 years) were included in the study. The median baseline phase angle was 3.6°. Multiple regression analysis adjusted for confounders showed that arm phase angle was independently positively associated with handgrip strength (β=0.250, P < 0.001) and SMI (β=0.215, P < 0.001) at discharge. Leg phase angle was independently positively associated with FIM-motor score (β=0.077, P = 0.045), handgrip strength (β=0.174, P < 0.001), and SMI (β=0.154, P < 0.001) at discharge.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The leg phase angle was associated with ADL, muscle strength, and skeletal muscle mass in patients with osteoporotic fractures at discharge. Segmental phase angle may be a useful indicator for considering intervention methods in patients with osteoporotic fractures.

articles.title: Age-adjusted and probability-adjusted D-dimer thresholds for the diagnosis of acute DVT: a narrative review.

abstract.text: In patients presenting to emergency departments with symptoms of lower-limb deep vein thrombosis (DVT), systematically ordering a compression ultrasonography (CUS) in all to rule out DVT contributes to crowding and low-yield testing. Contemporary diagnostic strategies aim at improving efficiency by avoiding the need for a CUS, while maintaining safety, as assessed by low short-term venous thromboembolism (VTE) rates among patients with a negative diagnostic work-up. This narrative review summarizes recent evidence, mainly from prospective management studies, supporting refined D-dimer-based pathways for first-episode DVT, and emerging data in patients with suspected recurrent DVT. In ADJUST-DVT, an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold (age×10 μg/L for ≥50 years) applied to outpatients with a non-high/unlikely pretest probability increased the proportion of patients ruled out without ultrasound by 7% overall as compared with the conventional 500 μg/L cutoff, with the largest gains in those ≥75 years. No failures were identified in patients with a D-dimer level 500 μg/L or greater but below the age-adjusted cutoff (0%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0%-2.3%). In the 4D study, a clinical probability-adjusted D-dimer strategy (low Wells with D-dimer <1000 μg/L; moderate Wells with <500 μg/L) achieved a 0.6% 3-month VTE rate while reducing ultrasound use by 47%. In patients with a suspected recurrent ipsilateral DVT, D-dimer levels are often higher than in patients without previous DVT and are therefore less useful to exclude the disease. In this situation, a negative D-dimer test may also be associated with a higher failure rate. Indeed, in the PREDICTORS study, a higher-than-expected prevalence of recurrent VTE at presentation in patients with a non-high pretest probability and a negative D-dimer was reported. While CUS is also frequently non-diagnostic due to residual thrombi, the THEIA Study showed that magnetic resonance direct thrombus imaging (MRDTI) can safely guide management as a single test. Together, these studies support practical, outcome-validated approaches that improve diagnostic efficiency and may facilitate implementation in real-world workflows, while highlighting the need for accurate pretest assessment and continued prospective validation of simplified algorithms.

articles.title: Defensive medicine and advanced imaging overuse in emergency departments: A focused review of imaging stewardship and overcrowding.

abstract.text: Emergency departments (EDs) are encountering a significant increase in patient volumes, compounded by greater reliance on advanced radiological imaging modalities. This trend is most evident for computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, with expanding use of emergency ultrasonography in selected pathways. These modalities are essential for time-sensitive diagnosis, triage, and risk stratification. Under diagnostic uncertainty, time pressure, crowding, and medico-legal concern, imaging may exceed evidence-based thresholds. Imaging overuse, also described as overutilization, has been associated with radiology bottlenecks, longer ED turnaround times, higher healthcare costs, and worse overcrowding. It may also expose patients to radiation, contrast-related risks, incidental findings, downstream testing, overdiagnosis, and avoidable financial burden. Excessive imaging demand further increases the workload of radiologists and emergency physicians and may contribute to reporting delays, cognitive fatigue, and burnout. This focused narrative review synthesizes the clinical, behavioral, and system-level drivers of overuse of advanced imaging in EDs, and proposes a conceptual reciprocal-pressure framework linking crowding, diagnostic uncertainty, defensive ordering, and radiology bottlenecks. It also discusses mitigation strategies, including clinical decision rules, computerized clinical decision support, Choosing Wisely initiatives, artificial intelligence-supported tools, shared decision-making, audit and feedback, and multidisciplinary imaging stewardship. The evidence supporting these strategies is heterogeneous, and their reported effects are not equivalent. The aim is to support safer, more efficient, and patient-centered diagnostic workflows in emergency care.

articles.title: Union rate and time to union following platelet-rich plasma therapy in fracture nonunion: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Fracture nonunion remains a challenging clinical problem associated with prolonged disability and repeated surgical interventions. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been proposed as a biological adjunct to enhance bone healing; however, clinical evidence remains inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of PRP in the management of fracture nonunion.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO Registration: CRD420261366849). PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies evaluating PRP in fracture nonunion and reporting union rate or time to union were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to compare PRP with control interventions. Risk ratios (RR) were calculated for union rates and standardized mean differences (SMD) for time to union. Additional single-arm analyses were performed to estimate pooled outcomes in PRP-treated cohorts.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-one studies comprising 877 patients were included. Two comparative studies (n = 119) demonstrated a higher likelihood of union with PRP (RR 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-1.36, p < 0.05) without significant heterogeneity. Six studies (n = 250) showed no significant difference in time to union between PRP and control groups (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.48-0.05), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 85%). In PRP-only analyses, the pooled union rate was 0.86 (95% CI 0.76-0.94; I² = 61%) across seven studies (n = 150), and the pooled mean time to union was 6.08 months (95% CI 4.26-7.90; I² = 100%) across eight studies (n = 187).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: PRP was associated with higher union rates in the limited comparative evidence, although no statistically significant difference in time to union was demonstrated. Heterogeneity in PRP protocols, methodological limitations, and the small comparative evidence base limit the certainty of these findings. PRP may have a potential role as a biological adjunct in fracture nonunion management, but further well-designed randomized controlled trials are required before definitive clinical recommendations can be made.

articles.title: Impact of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Pediatric Burn Injuries: A Cross-Sectional Study at a Canadian Tertiary Pediatric Hospital.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Provincial Health Orders led to many families spending more time at home. This study aimed to describe changes in the incidence, mechanisms, and severity of burn injuries for children seen at a provincial pediatric burn center during the COVID-19 pandemic.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Patients presenting to the Emergency Department with acute burns from 2019 to 2020 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients were grouped by time of presentation: prior to the COVID-19 pandemic (March 11, 2019 to December 31, 2019), or during the COVID-19 pandemic (March 11, 2020 to December 31, 2020). Groups were compared by demographics, burn characteristics, management, and outcomes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Fewer patients with burns presented to the ED during the COVID-19 pandemic (n = 117) versus prior (n = 132); however, during the pandemic, the proportion of all ED visits that were burn related was significantly higher (p = .003). There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups for injury time of day, mechanism, anatomical location, and burn depth. Burn management and time to healing were comparable, although 11% more patients had plastic surgery follow-up during the pandemic (p = .041).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The epidemiology of pediatric burn injuries did not significantly change during the COVID-19 pandemic, and access to care remained consistent. The results of this study may have implications for hospital resource allocation planning in the event of similar provincial health orders.

articles.title: May the POCUS Be With You! A Call to Radiologists and Sonographers. A Narrative Review.
articles.journal_full: Australasian journal of ultrasound in medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Clinicians across many specialties now perform point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) as a question-driven bedside examination. Emergency physicians, intensivists, cardiologists (focused cardiac ultrasound), anaesthetists, respiratory physicians, gastroenterologists and gynaecologists all perform bedside scans. A comprehensive, protocol-driven study with a multi-organ survey, Doppler interrogation and structured report remains the work of radiologists and sonographers. Confusion at this interface breeds friction among professionals.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This narrative review synthesises the POCUS literature with position statements from the ASUM, ACEM, ACEP, ASE, SRU/ACR, ANZCA, CICM, RANZCOG, RACS, RANZCR, EFSUMB, EuSEM and WFUMB. Three axes define POCUS: setting, completeness and operator credentials. POCUS is a spectrum. Depending on the operator's skill, qualification and available time, a clinician scan can answer a focused question in seconds or approach a comprehensive examination. We compared the Australasian and United States regulatory environments, where United States reimbursement drives stronger governance, and addressed quality assurance, false-positive and false-negative risk, image archiving, the sonographer-clinician relationship and POCUS practice across the specialties that scan at the bedside.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: POCUS and comprehensive departmental ultrasound complement each other. Clinician-performed ultrasonography has become a genuine multispecialty movement. The overdue step is to invite radiologists and sonographers, the workforce that anchors comprehensive ultrasound, into this movement. Now is the time for interdisciplinary teaching and knowledge sharing: shared image archives, joint credentialing, combined audits, reciprocal teaching, joint research and shared simulations across every specialty that performs bedside scans.

articles.title: Factors associated with the use of UK emergency services in children and young people with intellectual developmental disabilities.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Children and young people (CYP) with intellectual developmental disabilities (IDD) experience substantial health needs and higher healthcare utilisation compared with the general paediatric population. However, factors affecting the emergency healthcare use among children with IDD of genetic aetiology remain poorly understood. This study aimed to examine demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, genetic, and clinical factors of emergency service use among CYP with IDD in England.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study used linked administrative healthcare data from Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) emergency service records obtained from National Health Service (NHS) England. Participants were CYP aged between 4 and 15.5 years with confirmed pathogenic genetic variants associated with IDD identified via NHS medical genetic clinics. The outcome was the yearly emergency service use rate, calculated as the total number of lifetime emergency visits divided by age (years). Independent variables included demographic and socioeconomic factors, genetic characteristics, region of residence, adaptive functioning, behavioural and emotional adjustment, prosocial behaviour, general health status, and system-specific medical conditions. Primary caregivers completed questionnaires and provided information regarding the child's medical history and demographic information.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The average emergency attendance rate in this cohort was 0.73 visits per annum, which was much higher than that among children in the same age range from the general population. Emergency services were used more by younger IDD children with poorer adaptive functioning, more externalising and less prosocial behaviour, as well as those with complex multisystem conditions. Frequent attendance was associated with high rates of medical comorbidities especially seizures and respiratory problems. Regional differences were found with relatively higher usage in London and the North East of England. Attendance rates were not influenced by sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, genetic variant type or inheritance status.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This novel study demonstrated emergency healthcare utilisation among CYP with IDD of known genetic aetiology in England was primarily associated with clinical complexity, functional impairment, and younger age rather than socioeconomic or genetic factors. Their vulnerability to multisystem morbidity as well as regional disparities highlight the need for improved coordinated care and targeted service planning to reduce emergency healthcare dependence among children with disabilities.

articles.title: Patients experiencing homelessness in an urban emergency department: experience from a tertiary center in Tel Aviv.

abstract.text: People experiencing homelessness represent a distinct emergency department (ED) population, often lacking regular medical follow-up and experiencing delays in necessary care. ED visits commonly relate to unmet basic needs, chronic medical conditions, psychiatric illness, or substance-related complications. In many healthcare systems, unhoused populations are described as "super users" of emergency services. However, data on homelessness and ED utilization in Israel are limited. We conducted a historical cohort study at the Emergency Department of Tel Aviv Medical Center. ED visits between January 7, 2022 and May 31, 2023 involving patients documented as unhoused were identified using systematic free-text keyword searches. The demographics, presenting complaints, investigations, interventions, and dispositions were extracted. A longitudinal database (2018-2023) was constructed for each individual, capturing chronic illness, psychiatric diagnoses, substance use, repeat ED visits, hospitalizations, and outpatient utilization. Analyses were descriptive. Of 214 identified ED visits 149 persons experiencing homelessness were included. Most patients were men (84%), with a median age of 43 years, and 92% were living on the street. Available records suggested prolonged homelessness, though documentation was incomplete. High rates of chronic disease, infectious conditions, psychiatric disorders, and substance or alcohol use were observed. Most individuals presented once or only a few times; however, a small subgroup demonstrated frequent ED utilization, including some with more than 30 visits over 5 years. Common presentations included psychiatric complaints, trauma, substance-related conditions, and nonspecific pain. Only 1% of visits resulted in hospitalization. In this urban ED, homelessness was not uniformly associated with frequent emergency care use; rather, high utilization was concentrated in a small subset of patients. The substantial burden of psychiatric illness, substance use, chronic disease, and infection highlights complex medical and social needs. ED encounters represent opportunities for targeted interventions, harm-reduction strategies, and improved linkage to community and municipal services.

articles.title: Inflammation and thrombosis: from pathophysiology to future treatments.

abstract.text: Inflammation and coagulation are tightly interconnected host-defense systems that, when dysregulated, promote pathological thrombosis. This narrative review examines mechanisms, clinical settings, and therapeutic implications of thromboinflammation (TI) across venous, arterial, and microvascular thrombosis, with particular attention to the differences in clinical translation among vascular territories. Endothelial activation, tissue factor expression, platelet-leukocyte interactions, neutrophil extracellular traps, complement activation, inflammasome signalling, and impaired fibrinolysis converge to generate a procoagulant phenotype. These mechanisms modify Virchow's triad and contribute to venous, arterial, and microvascular thrombosis, although their relative importance varies across vascular territories. Clinically, TI is relevant in inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatologic and other immune-mediated disorders, sepsis, coronavirus disease 2019, clonal haematopoiesis, complement-mediated diseases, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. TI offers a unifying framework for mechanistic risk assessment and therapeutic development. In atherothrombosis, randomised trials have demonstrated that selective modulation of inflammatory pathways, particularly the NLRP3-interleukin-1β-interleukin-6 axis and colchicine-sensitive pathways, can reduce recurrent cardiovascular events. By contrast, the role of inflammation-targeted therapies for primary or secondary prevention of VTE remains uncertain. Future studies should identify disease-specific biomarkers and test targeted anti-inflammatory or immunothrombotic strategies, alone or alongside anticoagulation, to prevent thrombosis without compromising haemostasis effectively.

articles.title: Performance of pulmonary embolism diagnostic strategies in patients undergoing computed tomography pulmonary angiography.

abstract.text: Clinical probability scores and D-dimer-based diagnostic strategies are intended for early evaluation of suspected pulmonary embolism (PE), but their performance after clinician-driven referral for computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) remains uncertain. We prospectively evaluated PE diagnostic strategies among consecutive emergency department patients aged ≥13 years who underwent CTPA for suspected PE. Following the decision to order CTPA, the modified Wells and simplified revised Geneva scores were calculated, and the YEARS and PEGeD strategies were applied. Clinically significant PE, defined as segmental or more proximal embolism, was the primary outcome; any PE, including isolated subsegmental embolism, was the secondary outcome. Among 408 patients, clinically significant PE was confirmed in 144 (35.3%) and any PE in 154 (37.7%). The Wells score demonstrated better discrimination for clinically significant PE than the simplified revised Geneva score (area under the curve 0.725 [95%CI: 0.671-0.779] vs 0.656 [95%CI: 0.598-0.714]; P = 0.0003). Clinically significant PE was present in 21.6% and 24.4% of patients classified as PE unlikely by the Wells and simplified revised Geneva two-level classifications, respectively. Among 398 patients with D-dimer results, YEARS and PEGeD each demonstrated 96.5% sensitivity but identified only 13.8% and 13.6% of patients, respectively, as potentially eligible for imaging avoidance. Diagnostic performance showed a similar pattern for any PE. In this CTPA-selected cohort, the Wells score demonstrated better discrimination than the simplified revised Geneva score, but both two-level classifications yielded substantial counterfactual missed-PE rates. YEARS and PEGeD maintained high sensitivity but offered limited theoretical imaging-sparing potential.

articles.title: Preoperative Predictors of Prolonged Hospital Stay after Appendectomy in Children: A Prospective Cohort Study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To identify preoperative predictive factors of prolonged hospital stay following appendectomy in children.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A prospective cohort study was carried out in a tertiary pediatric surgical referral center in Tunisia between January 2022 and December 2025. All consecutive children younger than 14 y who underwent appendectomy during the study period were eligible for inclusion.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: During the study period, 653 pediatric patients underwent appendectomy, including 132 patients (20.2%) with prolonged hospital stay. The mean age was 9.5 ± 2.7 y, and 436 patients (66.8%) were male. Six variables emerged as independent predictive factors of prolonged hospital stay following appendectomy. These included age less than 6 y, duration of symptoms greater than 48 h, pre-hospital antibiotic use, Sun's Pediatric Comorbidity Index ≥3, Alvarado score ≥7, and CRP >90 mg/L. Among these predictors, elevated CRP demonstrated the strongest association with prolonged hospital stay.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Several simple and readily available preoperative factors were independently associated with prolonged hospital stay following appendectomy in children. Early recognition of these factors may support improved perioperative planning, optimized resource allocation, and more accurate communication with caregivers.

articles.title: Syndesmotic screw fixation is associated with higher overall treatment costs when compared with suture button stabilisation in a single UK major trauma centre.
articles.journal_full: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Ankle fractures frequently involve syndesmotic disruption, requiring stable fixation to restore joint function. Syndesmotic screw fixation remains widely used but carries significant drawbacks, including implant breakage, stiffness, and frequent need for removal. Suture button stabilisation offers clinical and economic advantages by preserving physiological motion and reducing reoperation rates. This study evaluates these costs under normal, unselected clinical practice, where implant choice and removal decisions were made independently by treating surgeons without protocol influence.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study compares treatment costs of syndesmosis screw fixation and suture button stabilisation for syndesmotic injuries in a single UK Major Trauma Centre. 75 patients aged 16-60 years, with length stable or length stabilised ankle fractures with syndesmotic injuries, between October 2020 to October 2023 were included.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The two cohorts were demographically similar and operative times were comparable (p = 0.170). Complications and reoperations were significantly higher with screw fixation (p < 0.001), with 56.8% undergoing removal, adding £31,460 in costs over three years. Overall, screw fixation cost £687 more per case than suture button stabilisation. Screw fixation became more costly when the hardware removal rate exceeded 8%. This dropped further to 2% when costs of additional follow up visits were also included.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Despite a higher initial implant cost, suture button stabilisation demonstrated fewer complications and no hardware removals. In contrast, 56.8% of screw fixation cases underwent implant removal, leading to screw fixation costing £687 more per case on average, highlighting the superior clinical and economic value of suture button stabilisation in this pragmatic study.

articles.title: [Life-threatening hemorrhage after tonsillotomy in a child : A structured recommendation for action in the prehospital setting].

abstract.text: One week after an uncomplicated ENT-surgery in a 7-year-old boy, a sudden and massive hemorrhage from the oropharyngeal area occurs. The arriving emergency medicals find an apathetic child with active bleeding and recognise quickly the need for immediate action. Based on this case report, the measures taken and an overview of surgical procedures involving the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils in children, a guideline for prehospital care is proposed to enable structured action in such a potentially life-threatening situation.

articles.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder is associated with higher rates of healthcare utilization but similar clinical outcomes after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
articles.journal_full: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is increasingly recognized as a factor that may impact surgical recovery. Currently, its effect on outcomes following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) remains unclear. This study investigates whether a preoperative diagnosis of PTSD is associated with increased postoperative healthcare utilization.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective, multi-institutional cohort study was performed using a large electronic medical record database. Patients undergoing primary, single-level ACDF were identified and stratified by the presence of PTSD diagnosis before surgery. Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 ratio using over 300 demographic and clinical variables. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days, 90 days, and two years postoperatively.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 3774 patients were included after matching, with equal distribution between cohorts. Patients with PTSD had increased opioid utilization at both 30 days (OR: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.2-1.7; P<0.001) and 90 days (OR: 1.5, 95% CI: 1.2-1.8; P < 0.001), as well as higher rates of emergency department visits at 90 days (OR: 1.2, 95% CI: 1.0-1.5; P = 0.020). No significant differences were observed in long-term complications, including adjacent segment disease or reoperation rates at two years.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Preoperative PTSD diagnosis is associated with increased short-term healthcare utilization following ACDF but does not seem to impact long-term surgical outcomes. These findings support the need for targeted perioperative management strategies in this patient population.

articles.title: Preventing re-fractures in Western Sydney: three-year outcomes of an Australian fracture liaison service utilising a novel automated fracture-finding Tool.
articles.journal_full: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Fragility fractures impose a major burden on health systems, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged regions. Western Sydney, home to some of Australia's most disadvantaged groups, faces unique challenges in osteoporosis care. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a hospital-based Fracture Liaison Service (FLS) in reducing refracture rates amongst the most vulnerable.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Fragility fractures are an important predictor of future fractures. Secondary fracture prevention brings significant benefits for patients, clinicians and healthcare systems. Fracture liaison services (FLS) are established models of care to prevent secondary fractures. However not all FLSs are equal, with differences in models of care and target population.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Westmead Hospital, a major tertiary centre in Western Sydney, established a FLS in 2019. This study compares one and three-year refracture rates between patients managed by the FLS and a control group - patients approached by FLS but lost to follow-up, non-attenders or those who declined treatment. Fracture cases were identified using an automated ICD-10/SNOMED-based fracture finding tool. Baseline variables included age, sex, index fracture site, and Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included 406 patients who presented to the Westmead Emergency Department with a minimal-trauma fracture between 2019 and 2022. Of these, 279 were managed by the FLS and 127 served as controls. Baseline characteristics were similar across groups, with the exception that FLS participants were more likely to have sustained a fracture within the preceding three years (10.0% vs 1.6%, p < 0.005). At three years, refracture rates were significantly lower in FLS patients (10.4% vs 23.6%, p < 0.001), with no difference at one year (4.3% vs 5.5%, p = 0.61). FLS participation was associated with a ~ 70% reduction in refracture risk between 1 and 3 years after index fracture (HR 0.309, p < 0.0005).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: FLS attendance was associated with a significant reduction in refractures, with less than half the risk at three years, despite the higher prior incidence of fractures. No benefit was seen at one year, indicating that FLS evaluation may require a longer latency period to establish anti-fracture efficacy.

articles.title: Rapid Offload to Avoid Delays to Mitigate Ambulance Patient Offload Time.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Ambulance patient offload time, the interval from emergency medical service arrival to completion of transfer of care to emergency department personnel, is associated with delayed treatment, prolonged emergency medical service turnaround, and operational and financial strain. In California, ambulance patient offload time has received legislative attention through Assembly Bill 40, enacted to reduce ambulance offload delays, expedite care, and improve emergency medical service community response. This quality improvement project evaluated whether a dedicated ambulance receiving area, named Ambi ROAD (Rapid Offload to Avoid Delays) supported by a dedicated nurse and standardized staff workflow training, was associated with reduced ambulance patient offload time at a high-volume emergency department.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using a retrospective pre-post observational design, monthly data from the 12 months before implementation were compared with those from the 12 months after implementation. The intervention was refined through multiple Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles. Monthly 90th percentile ambulance patient offload time values and ambulance arrival volumes were obtained from the 2 local emergency medical service agencies that served the site. Monthly ED census was also evaluated to assess utilization trends.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mean monthly 90th percentile ambulance patient offload time decreased from 80.00 to 30.58 minutes for Sacramento County ambulance arrivals (t = 8.64, P < .001, d = 3.53) and from 81.58 to 33.67 minutes for Sierra-Sacramento Valley ambulance arrivals (t = 9.38, P < .001, d = 3.83). Ambulance traffic increased from 654.50 to 764.58 per month for Sacramento County (P < .001) and from 759.83 to 801.92 per month for Sierra-Sacramento Valley (P = .022). The emergency department census did not change significantly (P = .442).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: A dedicated ambulance receiving area, a dedicated offload nurse, and standardized workflow training were associated with substantial reductions in ambulance patient offload time despite an increased ambulance volume. This approach may help emergency departments move toward regulatory targets, or similar aims, and support more timely initiation of patient care and faster emergency medical service turnaround.

articles.title: Pediatric Emergency Department Bootcamp: A Quality Improvement Initiative Creating Competence and Confidence in New Graduate Nurses.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: After the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic and 2022 pediatric tripledemic, a Midwestern children's hospital pediatric emergency department experienced critical nursing workforce challenges. This led to increased turnover with the rate of 1 campus peaking at nearly 50%. A specialty-focused supplemental orientation program was developed to build competence and confidence and reduce turnover.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An 11-week supplemental orientation program (pediatric emergency department bootcamp) was implemented with weekly 4-hour sessions: 2 hours of didactic instruction, 1 hour of skills practice, and 1 hour of simulation. The scaffolded curriculum progressed from foundational pediatric assessment to body system-specific content and high-risk scenarios. Retention, turnover, and orientation extensions were compared pre- and post-intervention. Surveys measured participant confidence and competence. Quality metrics and qualitative data were reviewed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Post-implementation, the first-year registered nurse turnover rates for both campuses decreased from 38.53% to 0.00%. Overall registered nurse turnover decreased from 20.62% to 3.14%. Among the 29 nurses who completed the pediatric emergency department bootcamp, 83% have reached or are on track to reach their 2-year anniversary in the department. Cost avoidance exceeded $1.7 million. Survey results revealed improved confidence and competence, though these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the loss of survey data.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The pediatric emergency department bootcamp reveals that a structured, multimodal supplemental orientation program can meaningfully improve new graduate readiness and reduce costly turnover in high-acuity pediatric settings. Despite limitations, including small cohort sizes and survey data loss, turnover reduction was consistent across 2 campuses. With leadership support, protected scheduling, and simulation infrastructure, this model is adaptable to other specialty nursing units facing similar workforce challenges.

articles.title: Leveraging Primary Care Resources Through Quality Improvement to Increase Follow-up After Mental Health Emergency Department Visits.
