We mapped the published evidence on POCUS-based ETT placement confirmation in transport, organized around six axes: clinical indication, transport modality, operator training, impact on management, technical barriers, and patient-oriented outcomes. Scoping review per the Joanna Briggs Institute 2020 framework, reported per PRISMA-ScR. Nine sources searched January 1st, 2015-May 12th, 2026: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Europe PMC, Consensus.app, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, and forward-citation tracking. Dual independent screening and charting were performed in Covidence with built-in conflict adjudication. From 2447 unique records, 51 met final inclusion. One primary study evaluated diagnostic performance in adult patients in an out-of-hospital setting. The remaining 50 records comprised contextual primary studies and secondary evidence, including cadaver and simulation studies, training evaluations, feasibility implementations, and reviews. Distribution by modality was skewed toward ground emergency medical services (EMS); rotor-wing helicopter EMS (HEMS) evidence was predominantly training-based; fixed-wing evidence was essentially absent. Operator profiles in transport-relevant studies were predominantly paramedic, flight medic, or flight nurse, mismatched against the physician-dominant pooled in-hospital meta-analytic estimates. No included study measured patient-oriented outcomes. Evidence supporting POCUS-based ETT confirmation in pre-hospital and critical care transport remains limited. Most studies addressed training, simulation, feasibility, or implementation rather than diagnostic performance in transported patients, and none demonstrated an effect on patient-oriented outcomes. Transport-specific prospective studies are needed before hospital-derived diagnostic-accuracy estimates can be generalized to transport practice.

articles.title: Auditing Report Order in Emergency Teleradiology Using Routine Event Logs.
articles.journal_full: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine

abstract.text: This study aims to describe recorded report-order inversions in emergency teleradiology and assess their interpretation when assignment and active interpretation times are unavailable. We reconstructed computed tomography (CT) transmissions from July 2025 through June 2026, requiring a unique exact linkage and stable priorities. An inversion occurred when a later examination received its first recorded report before an earlier examination still unresolved at the same provider. Eligible head-abdomen pairs were analyzed using dependence-preserving intervals, an empirical conditional reference and secondary models incorporating retrieved imaging workload proxies. Among 8170 examinations, 6,051 had the standard ED urgent category. Later head CT inverted 1060/1761 earlier-abdomen pairs (60.2%; 95% confidence interval, 57.5-62.7%); later abdominal CT inverted 154/1038 earlier-head pairs (14.8%; 12.3-17.5%). Observed-minus-reference differences were - 4.5 percentage points (- 7.3 to - 1.6) and - 11.4 (- 14.2 to - 8.8). Counts were usable for 3474/3565 target examinations and 2665 pairs. Report-order asymmetry did not demonstrate preferential dispatch. Observed inversion proportions were below the empirical conditional reference probabilities. This does not establish protective scheduling. Routine exports support a descriptive audit; additional workflow events are necessary to identify mechanisms or compare dispatch policies.

articles.title: Are the Mental Health Concerns of Youth Presenting to an Emergency Department More Scute or Severe than Those Waiting for Outpatient Care?

abstract.text: BackgroundMental health patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) are potentially more unwell than those waiting for mental health services on outpatient waitlists. They often receive prioritized mental health follow up care, yet this practice may be unjustified if they do not have greater severity and acuity of mental illness.ObjectiveAdolescent mental health patients from an outpatient waitlist sample are compared to those who attended the ED to seek help but were not admitted to hospital.MethodAdolescents completed intake questionnaires at time of outpatient (regular or post ED) intake visit at a pediatric hospital in Canada. Statistical comparisons between the groups were completed on multiple measures of demographic and clinical features.ResultsThe ED group reported more substance use, higher psychiatric symptom severity scores for ODD, ADHD, and MDD, more recent self-harm, suicidal ideations and suicide attempts and lower general functioning. They also reported more ethnic diversity.ConclusionThe greatest differences were seen on measures of suicide risk acuity and substance use, which suggests outpatient interventions immanently focussed on these targets for ED attenders. Considering the high amount of suicide risk, despite lower acuity, in the outpatient wait list sample, future studies should investigate how to most equitably service these two populations.

articles.title: [The South African Flag Sign (SAFS) is a deadly diagnosis not to miss. About eleven cases].

abstract.text: Between 2025 and 2026, our emergency medical service managed 850 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI); eleven (1.3%) of them presented the SAFS on electrocardiogram. This pattern is a rare electrocardiographic finding typically associated with the first diagonal (D1) branch occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery 1. It was first described by S. Sclarovsky in 1994, who reported a special form of anterior wall myocardial infarction characterized by ST-segment elevation (STE) in non-contiguous leads DI, aVL, and V2 with reciprocal changes in DIII and aVF 2. In 2016, Littman coined the term 'South African flag sign' to denote a visual mnemonic device or aid for this ECG pattern, with the objective of facilitating earlier detection of 'high lateral' myocardial infarction (MI) 3. We report eleven cases that exhibited this pattern to highlight the electrical aspect and especially its severity.

articles.title: New developments in locking plate osteosynthesis - A narrative review.

abstract.text: Plate osteosynthesis has evolved significantly, progressing from the first plates with externally protruding screws to anatomically precontoured systems designed for minimally invasive application. In this narrative review, we provide a brief recap of the history of locked plating and highlight the most relevant developments of the last two decades. These include anatomical innovations and mechanobiologically optimized plates, as well as emerging systems capable of monitoring the fracture healing progress.

articles.title: The use of PMMA bone cement in trauma surgery: A narrative review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement has been used for decades in orthopaedic surgery, primarily for fixation of endoprostheses. In trauma surgery, its role is more heterogeneous and often underappreciated.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This narrative review summarizes the material properties, biological behavior, and clinical applications of PMMA in trauma surgery, including prosthesis fixation, screw augmentation, and its use as a temporary spacer. Finally, the use of PMMA used as a permanent spacer, including technical tips is described.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: PMMA provides high compressive strength, minimal shrinkage, and reliable handling characteristics. Cement augmentation improves implant anchorage in osteoporotic bone. As a spacer, PMMA plays a key role in staged reconstruction. Finally, in selected patients and as a salvage procedure, PMMA may function as a permanent load-sharing implant when combined with stable internal fixation.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: PMMA remains a versatile, inexpensive, and widely available tool in trauma surgery beyond its classical role in arthroplasty.

articles.title: Surface topography and nanostructural modifications for the prevention of bacterial infections.

abstract.text: Implant-associated infections represent severe complications in orthopaedics and trauma surgery, largely driven by early bacterial adhesion and subsequent biofilm formation on device surfaces. The increasing incidence of multidrug-resistant pathogens further complicates management and underscores the urgent need for preventive, antibiotic-free strategies. Surface functionalization of implantable metals has emerged as a key approach to inhibit bacterial colonization at the implant-tissue interface while minimizing systemic toxicity and selective pressure for resistance. This review provides a comprehensive and clinically oriented overview of two major surface-based strategies: micro/nano-scale surface patterning (non-releasing approaches) and nanostructured antibacterial metallic coatings (releasing or contact-killing systems). Surface patterning modifies topography, wettability, and surface charge to reduce bacterial adhesion or induce mechanical disruption of bacterial membranes. Although highly promising in vitro and not reliant on the release of antimicrobial agents, hence not inserting compounds with potential toxicity, current evidence indicates that patterned surfaces alone often provide limited and transient protection in vivo, where protein adsorption and complex microbial communities may mask topographical effects. In contrast, nanostructured antibacterial metallic coatings offer broad-spectrum antibacterial and antibiofilm activity through ion release and/or contact-mediated mechanisms. Advances in plasma-assisted deposition technologies, including magnetron sputtering, pulsed laser deposition, and ionized jet deposition, enable precise control over coating thickness, morphology, and ion-release kinetics, thereby enhancing antibacterial efficacy while preserving biocompatibility and osteogenic potential. Recent in vivo data support the durability and safety of thin nanostructured coatings, highlighting their translational potential. Although not-yet clinically available, due to challenges in clinical translation of biomedical devices, these strategies can build a new generation of antibacterial device, with efficacy targeted to the microbial community and to tackling biofilm. Comparative observations suggest that while surface patterning represents a valuable complementary strategy, nanostructured metallic thin films currently provide more robust and clinically relevant antimicrobial performance. Future research should prioritize standardized antibiofilm testing models, validation in complex in vivo settings, combination strategies integrating patterning and coatings, and the rational tuning of multi-metal systems to address heterogeneous microbial communities.

articles.title: Cerclage wiring: Innovations and applications.

abstract.text: Immediate full weight-bearing of osteosynthesis constructs is gaining increasing importance in modern trauma surgery. Many geriatric patients cannot reliably adhere to partial weight-bearing instructions, and younger patients may benefit from accelerated rehabilitation enabled by early full weight-bearing. In this context, an older technique of minimally invasive cerclage fixation of the tibia is receiving renewed attention. The surgical technique has been adapted to contemporary cerclage systems and biomechanically evaluated for the first time. Several studies using synthetic and cadaveric bone models have demonstrated that modern cable cerclages, particularly in spiral fractures, are capable of significantly increasing the stiffness of both locking plate and intramedullary nail osteosyntheses, provided that anatomical reduction is achieved through the cerclage. From a biomechanical standpoint, the additive cerclage thus enables immediate postoperative full weight-bearing. Early clinical studies suggest, that minimally invasive tibial cerclage can be applied without an increased complication rate and is associated with faster rehabilitation and higher patient satisfaction in the early postoperative phase. Although evidence is limited, the principle of additive cerclage appears to be transferable to humeral shaft spiral fractures.

articles.title: Overview and new developments in intramedullary and cephalomedullary nailing.

abstract.text: The primary objectives of osteosynthetic fracture stabilization are accurate fracture reduction, restoration of the anatomical axis and rotational alignment, and the provision of adequate biomechanical and biological conditions to support bone healing. In fractures of long tubular bones, these goals can be optimally achieved by intramedullary nailing, which provides long-segment internal splinting along the anatomical axis of the bone combined with locking screws to ensure axial and rotational stability. In addition, intramedullary nailing is a tissue-preserving technique, as nail insertion is performed remote from the fracture site, thereby minimizing soft tissue trauma within the fracture zone. The indications for intramedullary nailing include epiphyseal and diaphyseal fractures of long bones, selected metaphyseal fractures that can be stabilized using anatomically contoured nails, as well as reconstructive procedures such as the treatment of nonunions, corrective osteotomies, and arthrodeses of the lower extremity. A major advantage of intramedullary nailing is the high primary stability of the implant, which generally allows early functional rehabilitation. The resulting biomechanical benefits permit early full weight bearing and, in the treatment of fracture healing disorders, are associated with high rates of osseous union. Continuous improvements in implant design and instrumentation, together with the introduction of anatomically contoured reconstruction nails, are expected to further expand the indications and effectiveness of intramedullary nailing. This narrative review summarizes historical milestones, biomechanical principles, technical aspects, and recent implant developments in intramedullary nailing, with a particular focus on cephalomedullary nailing for unstable trochanteric and subtrochanteric femoral fractures. Special emphasis is placed on fracture reduction quality, implant selection, and screw positioning, as these factors remain the strongest determinants of fixation stability and clinical outcome.

articles.title: Review of a "Bone Glue Fixation" development.

abstract.text: The paper presents some of the background to the development of bone glues. Whilst there have been many attempts over the last 100 years to find a safe and effective biomimetic adhesive biomaterial it is only recently that promising and feasible candidates have been developed. In particular a formulation based on a combination of an amino acid, phosphoserine (PSer), together with calcium salts and water, has demonstrated the potential to meet clinically defined requirements for a bone adhesive (Osstic®). This bone glue has achieved first in human use after having demonstrated consistent preclinical performance.

articles.title: Alternate non-metallic implants in fracture care - A review.

abstract.text: The use of implants in the treatment of fractures evolved over the last decades. Until today, most implant designs are based on metallic alloys such as Titanium or stainless steel. However, the global ageing population with increasing numbers of fragility and pathological fractures challenges current implant designs regarding stress shielding, fragile soft tissue and advanced demands like reduced imaging artefacts for radiotherapy planning. Therefore, alternative non-metallic implants that more closely resemble the mechanical properties of bone or provide additional stability as intramedullary augmentation have become available. This narrative-review summarizes the current available (2026) technology, biomechanical properties, clinical applications, outcomes and complications of CFR-PEEK implants and photodynamic bone stabilization implants in fracture management. In total n = 100 publications were taken into consideration for this narrative-review. Non-metallic-implants for fracture care are still a niche product in the treatment of fractures. However, with the ageing population and the increasing number of impaired bone quality and stability, these methods could help reduce stress shielding and force distribution comparable to physiological bone (CFR-PEEK implants) or allow additional augmentation (photodynamic bone stabilization) in reduced bone quality.

articles.title: Innovation in external fixation: Emerging hardware, software and automation technologies.

abstract.text: External fixation remains a cornerstone of contemporary orthopaedic trauma and limb reconstruction surgery. While the biological principles for bone healing and regeneration established by Ilizarov continue to underpin modern practice, significant technological innovation has occurred over the past two decades. These developments have focused on improving construct stability, enhancing deformity correction accuracy, reducing technical complexity and improving the patient experience. Advances in hardware design have expanded fixation options and increased the adaptability of circular frames in complex trauma and reconstructive settings. Parallel developments in software have transformed deformity analysis, preoperative planning and correction execution through improved registration systems, virtual frame construction and cloud-based treatment platforms. More recently, remote patient support systems and automated strut technologies have sought to reduce the treatment burden associated with prolonged frame use. This review examines contemporary innovations in external fixation, focusing on developments in hardware, software, patient engagement technologies and automation. The available evidence is critically appraised and future directions explored. While many innovations demonstrate clear theoretical and practical advantages, robust clinical evidence remains limited for several emerging technologies. Nevertheless, the convergence of advanced engineering, digital health technologies and artificial intelligence is likely to fundamentally reshape the future of external fixation.

articles.title: Modernizing preoperative planning in orthopaedic trauma surgery.

abstract.text: Preoperative planning in orthopaedic trauma remains largely experience-driven despite advances in imaging and predictive modeling. Although three-dimensional (3D) reconstructions improve fracture visualization, they do not routinely predict biomechanical stability across competing fixation strategies. Automated segmentation and finite element analysis (FEA) offer the potential to transition trauma planning from primarily anatomic to a method by which constructs may be optimized. This narrative review summarizes the current state of 3D planning and segmentation, describes the principles and established applications of FEA, delineates the workflow of finite element modeling in clinical practice, and integrates representative clinical cases to illustrate how plate positioning and screw configuration affect construct stability and works alongside the surgeon to help inform decisions. Broader implications for hospital systems, patients, and industry are discussed, along with future integration into navigation, robotics, and intraoperative 3D imaging workflows.

articles.title: Patient-specific instrument with 3D printing technology in orthopaedic trauma: A narrative review.

abstract.text: 3D printing technology has been increasingly used in orthopaedic surgery. Current literature has demonstrated the benefits of applying 3D printing in orthopaedic trauma with the use of patient-specific instruments (PSI) including surgical guides and implants on selected bone fracture regions. This narrative review outlines the development of PSI including the navigation templates and implants using 3D printing technology. A comprehensive summary was presented for the application and effectiveness of PSI for fracture treatment in the upper extremities, pelvic region and lower extremities surgeries, particularly in regards to operative time, surgical accuracy and functional outcomes. 3D-printed patient-specific navigation guide had been used in reduction and fixation surgeries such as for navigating Kirschner wires (K-wire) insertion and screw placement in different bone fracture regions. PSI significantly increased surgical accuracy of K-wire insertion and screw placements, with significant reduction in operative time. For functional outcomes, 3D-printed navigation guide was comparable to conventional surgery. There are increasing studies exploring the clinical feasibility of patient-specific metal implant using 3D printing technology with advantage of high accuracy in fracture surgeries. Future studies to investigate the clinical efficacy of the patient-specific metal implants are warranted.

articles.title: Generation Z and engagement in orthopaedic trauma: A multigenerational qualitative study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Healthcare systems face increasing demand due to population ageing and workforce shortages. At the same time, Generation Z is entering surgical training. Their work values may differ from those of previous generations, potentially affecting engagement in demanding specialties such as orthopaedic trauma surgery. This study explores multigenerational perspectives on professional identity, work intensity, academic engagement, and work-life integration within orthopaedic trauma.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Prior to the 2024 Leadership Forum of the Osteosynthesis and Trauma Care Foundation (OTCF), a standardized questionnaire consisting of declarative statements rated on a five-point Likert scale was distributed to orthopaedic trauma residents and senior consultants from international chapters. During the Forum, a moderated multigenerational discussion was conducted. The session was recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic qualitative analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eight residents and fifteen consultants from Europe, North America, South America, Africa, and Asia participated. Across generations, intensive training was considered essential for achieving surgical mastery. However, younger participants emphasized work-life boundaries, institutional recognition of non-clinical work, and psychological safety. Senior surgeons more frequently described their profession as central to their identity and viewed unpaid academic engagement as intrinsic to surgical responsibility.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Generation Z trainees demonstrate strong commitment to orthopaedic trauma but differ from senior surgeons in expectations regarding professional identity, uncompensated academic work, and work-life integration. Recognition of evolving professional values is critical for workforce sustainability and intergenerational collaboration in trauma surgery.

articles.title: Tight rope fixation in fracture management.

abstract.text: The use of tightrope fixation using metal buttons linked by suture material was first reported in 2005 when their use was suggested as an alternative to syndesmosis screws in ankle fractures associated with a diastasis. These implants are now used widely as a component of fixation in ankle fractures with a diastasis. The published results of their use in these injuries have shown that they are an effective method of treating diastasis of the ankle tibio-fibular syndesmosis with some evidence to suggest that they have a lower rate of malunion, fewer implant related complications, a reduced need for implant removal and in some trials better functional outcomes than screw fixation. Variations of these devices have also been used for fixation of lateral third clavicular fractures and acromioclavicular dislocations. Their use alone or in combination with plate fixation has been shown to be an effective method of fixation of lateral third clavicle fractures with a low rate of malunion and implant related problems. They have also shown to be an effective method of treatment for acromioclavicular dislocation, although there is still debate about the role of surgical treatment for these injuries. There are miscellaneous reports of their use for other fractures and dislocations in other anatomic locations notably for Lisfranc injuries in the foot. Better quality prospective clinical studies are still needed to define their exact role in fracture management.

articles.title: Adherent antimicrobial coatings for orthopaedic implants - A narrative review.

abstract.text: There is a broad consensus among orthopaedic and trauma surgeons, as well as infection specialists, that antibacterial coatings represent an important tool for both the prevention and management of fracture-related infections. Nonetheless, the choice of commercially available implants fitted with an antibacterial coating remains limited. Intramedullary nails with resorbable, antibiotic eluting coatings have been commercially available for over a decade. Although multiple case series have shown evidence of efficacy of antimicrobial orthopaedic implants, randomized controlled trials are still lacking and their uptake in everyday clinical practice has been slow. More recently, nails with galvanic noble metal coatings were introduced, with encouraging clinical results. The most widely used coatings with the longest clinical track record are silver coated joint replacement endoprostheses, which have been successfully employed in revision surgeries and in patients undergoing tumor-related procedures. Silver coated plates are on the verge of market introduction and will represent the first of their kind to be broadly available. Overall, adherent antibacterial coatings are showing beneficial outcomes in terms of safety and efficacy. Health-technology assessments show cost effectiveness, demonstrating that in higher risk patient populations, the additional cost of using a coated implant is significantly less than the cost of treating an infection. Regulatory hurdles remain high, especially in the USA, where, to be best of our knowledge, coated implants have not been approved yet. Driven by the clear clinical need, we anticipate a dynamic near future in this field, with progress moving toward establishing coated implants as the standard of care for appropriate patient populations and expanding the range of available coating solutions. Such developments will ultimately benefit patients, surgeons, and the overall healthcare system.

articles.title: Distal femur plate-nail constructs. Belt and suspenders?

abstract.text: Given the inherent complexity of distal femoral fractures and non-unions, management should be directed by an experienced orthopaedic trauma surgeon to ensure optimal reduction and stable fixation. This report describes the surgical technique of three cases managed with dual nail-plate fixation, supplemented by a review of contemporary literature regarding this hybrid construct. Evidence from meta-analyses suggests that combined fixation significantly minimizes total complications and reoperations compared to single-construct fixation in distal femur fractures. Notably, these clinical benefits are achieved without a significant increase in operative duration, blood loss, or hospital stay. However, the current literature is restricted to retrospective studies, underscoring the imperative for prospective randomized controlled trials to validate these clinical benefits.

articles.title: Past, present and future of distal radius corrective osteotomy: From 2D based reconstruction to 3D data-driven, patient specific care.

abstract.text: Corrective osteotomy for distal radius malunion has evolved from two-dimensional (2D) radiograph based planning and surgeon performed geometric analysis to advanced three-dimensional (3D) virtual surgical planning (VSP). Historically guided by predefined radiographic parameters, contemporary practice increasingly emphasizes symptom severity and patient-specific functional goals. CT-based 3D models, contralateral surface matching, and patient-specific guides and implants have improved the accuracy of deformity correction. However, greater anatomical precision does not automatically translate into superior functional outcomes. Future progress depends on standardized evaluation frameworks, multicenter data collection, and predictive models to determine the clinical value of virtual surgical planning (VSP) and patient-specific implants (PSI) in delivering individualized, cost-effective and function-oriented care across the entire treatment pathway.

articles.title: 3D printed scaffolds for reconstruction of segmental long bone defects: A mini narrative review.

abstract.text: Large segmental bone defects remain a major challenge in orthopedic reconstruction because successful healing requires both mechanical stability and coordinated biological regeneration. Although autologous bone grafting remains the clinical gold standard due to its osteogenic, osteoinductive, and osteoconductive properties, its application is limited by donor site morbidity, restricted graft availability, and increased operative burden. These limitations have stimulated the development of scaffold-based regenerative strategies aimed at restoring structural integrity while promoting bone regeneration. Recent advances in additive manufacturing have enabled the fabrication of patient-specific three-dimensional (3D) scaffolds with controlled architecture, porosity, and mechanical properties that approximate native bone structure. This mini-review summarizes recent developments in 3D-printed scaffolds for the reconstruction of long bone defects, with particular emphasis on differences between non-biodegradable metallic constructs and biodegradable polymeric, ceramic, and composite materials. Porous titanium scaffolds demonstrate high mechanical stability and early osteointegration, making them promising for extensive load-bearing defects, although concerns remain regarding long-term stress shielding and permanent implant retention. Biodegradable ceramics and polymer-based scaffolds offer improved biological integration and controlled degradation, but often require further optimization of mechanical stability and biological augmentation. Composite constructs combining polymers, ceramics, or bioactive metals aim to integrate structural support with enhanced osteogenic and angiogenic responses. Despite encouraging preclinical results and emerging early clinical applications, current evidence remains limited by small patient cohorts, heterogeneous scaffold designs, and insufficient long-term outcome data. Future studies should focus on standardized scaffold designs, comparative clinical trials, and long-term evaluation to clarify the optimal role of 3D-printed biomaterials in the treatment of large segmental bone defects.

articles.title: Mini-fragment applications for lower extremity long bone fractures: A narrative review.

abstract.text: Mini-fragment systems (2.0, 2.4 and 2.7 mm) have evolved from fixation of just hand and foot fractures to have become an indispensable component of complex fracture fixation all over the appendicular skeleton. Surgeons currently use mini-fragment fixation in provisional fixation capacities, as adjunctive fixation to larger fixation constructs and in isolation in select situations. The versatility and popularity of these implants is far reaching, even in the lower extremity long bones, where their usage may be somewhat non-intuitive. In this narrative review we delineate the rationale for the use of these implants. We then illustrate several applications for these implants throughout the lower extremities that have proven useful.

articles.title: Defining three coagulation-based phenotypes for OHCA patients undergoing ECPR: an unsupervised cluster analysis.
articles.journal: Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care
articles.journal_full: European heart journal. Acute cardiovascular care

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Coagulopathy is frequent in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), yet its prognostic significance and heterogeneity remain poorly characterised.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To characterize coagulopathy at ECPR initiation, identify coagulation phenotypes, evaluate their association with outcomes, and describe their temporal evolution.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: All consecutive refractory OHCAs treated with ECPR (2013-2024) were included. Phenotypes were identified by unsupervised K-means clustering on PT-INR, aPTT, platelets, antithrombin, fibrinogen, and D-dimer measured at ECPR initiation. Associations with survival, neurological outcomes, and complications were assessed by multivariable logistic regression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 406 ECPR patients, 360 had coagulation data for analysis (initial shockable rhythm 67%, low-flow 70 min [IQR 58-81]). Three phenotypes were identified: severe consumptive coagulopathy (phenotype 1, n=49, 13.6%), mild consumptive coagulopathy (phenotype 2, n=175, 48.6%), and preserved coagulation (phenotype 3, n=136, 37.8%). Phenotype 1 had no survivors, compared with survival of 8.6% and 33.1% in phenotypes 2 and 3, respectively; favourable neurological outcome was achieved in 0%, 5.1%, and 17.6%. Phenotype severity correlated with ischaemic burden (lactate, arterial pH, end-tidal CO2, and low-flow duration). On multivariable analysis, phenotype 2 was associated with lower survival (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.55) and favourable neurological outcome (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12-0.81) versus phenotype 3. Bleeding incidence rates were 38, 12, and 2.5 events per 100 patient-days in phenotype 1, 2, and 3, respectively (all p < 0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Three distinct coagulation phenotypes at ECPR initiation were independently associated with survival and neurological outcome and appear to reflect ischaemic injury severity. These findings require validation in independent cohorts before clinical application.

articles.title: [Prevention in Emergency Medicine].

abstract.text: Emergency medical services and emergency departments face rising demand, population ageing and limited alternatives to hospital-based acute care. Prevention is therefore relevant across the emergency care pathway. This narrative review outlines primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary prevention in emergency medicine. Primary prevention includes health literacy, first-aid and resuscitation training, and targeted support for vulnerable groups. Secondary prevention focuses on early recognition, structured emergency call triage and referral to appropriate services. Tertiary prevention aims to prevent recurrent emergencies and avoidable hospital admissions through coordinated follow-up, planned home visits and case management. Quaternary prevention seeks to avoid overdiagnosis, overtreatment and non-beneficial transport through appropriate on-scene assessment, advance care planning and palliative care. Preventive approaches can improve care navigation, reduce avoidable emergency contacts and support patient-centred care. Their implementation requires clear legal responsibilities, sustainable funding and close collaboration between emergency medical services, primary care, nursing, hospitals and social services. Workforce health and training should be part of a preventive emergency care strategy.

articles.title: To probe or not to probe - Inappropriate urinary catheterization in the emergency department: Epidemiology, indications, and the potential impact of bladder ultrasound.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Indwelling urinary catheterization is a common invasive procedure performed in emergency departments (EDs), yet inappropriateness rates in this setting generally exceed those observed in medical and surgical wards, ranging from 26% to 72% in published series. Inappropriate catheterization contributes to a substantial burden of potentially preventable catheter-associated urinary tract infections and non-infectious complications.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: This narrative review examines the epidemiology of urinary catheter misuse in EDs, recalls the clinical indications defined by reference guidelines, and discusses the role of interventions and bladder ultrasound, performed with automated scanners or point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), in catheterization decision-making.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists and inclusion of key guidelines regardless of publication date.

abstract.label: FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Interventions combining education with decision-support tools have been associated with less inappropriate catheterization. Bladder ultrasound, while valuable for confirming functionally suspected retention, may promote volume-based catheterization decisions at the expense of functional clinical reasoning, a mechanism not yet formally evaluated in ED-specific studies and identified as a research priority.

articles.title: Optimizing US Prehospital Care of ST-Segment-Elevation Myocardial Infarction Because Time Is Life, Not Just Muscle.
National assessment of trauma care system capacity in Ecuador: Evaluating institutional resources and practitioner KAPS domains.

abstract.text: We evaluated Ecuador's trauma care system capacity by analyzing the discrepancy between hospital infrastructure and the individual dimensions of the Knowledge, Attitudes, Practices, and Safety (KAPS) framework among medical specialists. A nationwide, multicomponent cross-sectional study was conducted (2025-2026), comprising a complete structural audit of 49 eligible public hospitals (Levels II and III) and a KAPS survey of 215 trauma-facing specialists representing 36 institutions (73.5% institutional participation rate). Spatial workflow efficiency was assessed via Emergency Department-to-Computed Tomography (ED-CT) transit distances. Independent multivariable Poisson regression models evaluated each KAPS dimension separately, reporting adjusted Incidence Rate Ratios (IRR)accounting for institutional clustering and professional seniority. The institutional audit revealed significant operational constraints: 51.0% of hospitals lacked 24/7 radiological coverage, and 16.3% experienced CT scanner downtime. Spatial ED-to-CT distances were significantly greater in Level III tertiary centers, reaching up to 300 meters (p = 0.006). Among specialists (N = 215 across 36 hospitals), ecological associations with provincial trauma volume yielded wide confidence intervals spanning the null value across domains (Knowledge: rho = 0.113, 95% CI: -0.39-0.61; Reported Practice: rho = -0.160, 95% CI: -0.66-0.34), reflecting low statistical precision from macro-level aggregation. Dimension-specific multivariable models revealed marked inter-specialty divergence: Emergency Physicians exhibited lower Knowledge (aIRR = 0.61; 95% CI: 0.50-0.74), but higher rate ratios in Reported Practices (aIRR = 1.48; 95% CI: 1.34-1.65), Attitudes (aIRR = 1.12; 95% CI: 1.09-1.16), and Safety (aIRR = 1.18; 95% CI: 1.12-1.25) relative to General Surgery. Ecuador's trauma network exhibits a measurable discrepancy between nominal infrastructure and operational availability. System capacity is constrained by physical architectural barriers and a divergence between practitioners' subjective perceptions and objective decision-making skills. Strategic priorities must include a unified National Trauma Registry, integrated teleradiology, and continuous scenario-based training.

articles.title: Barriers and facilitators of evidence-informed health policymaking in Nepal: A scoping review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Evidence-informed health policymaking (EIPM) is essential for strengthening health systems and achieving equitable health outcomes. Despite policy commitments in Nepal, the translation of research evidence into policy and practice remains limited. This scoping review synthesizes the barriers and facilitators influencing EIPM across health policy domains in Nepal.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 that examined barriers and facilitators of EIPM in Nepal were identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Global Health. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and conducted descriptive and thematic analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 2,139 records identified, 26 studies met the inclusion criteria. The studies covered maternal and neonatal health, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), nutrition, emergency care, health systems governance, climate-health, public health regulation, and COVID-19 ethics. Barriers were grouped into five themes: systemic and governance challenges; capacity and resource constraints; evidence-related issues; contextual and cultural factors; and operational gaps. Common barriers included political interference, fragmented coordination, workforce shortages, inadequate funding, donor-driven agendas, poor dissemination of research, and limited implementation guidance. Facilitators clustered into four themes: institutional and structural enablers, political and leadership commitment, capacity building and stakeholder engagement, and global and donor support. Sector-specific differences were observed, with socio-cultural barriers more prominent in maternal and neonatal health, governance and coordination challenges particularly evident in NCD policies, and technical capacity and data limitations more pronounced in climate-health policy.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Nepal's EIPM landscape reflects strong commitment but uneven institutionalization. Strengthening governance, institutional capacity, evidence systems, and coordination across federal, provincial, and local institutions is essential to improve the translation of research into policy and practice. Institutionalizing EIPM requires not only producing evidence but also creating systems that routinely generate, translate, and use evidence for decision-making.

articles.title: Depression and antidepressant use are associated with prolonged recovery and increased opioid dependence following ulnar nerve transposition.

abstract.text: Depression is common among patients with cubital tunnel syndrome and may adversely influence surgical recovery. This study evaluates the impact of depression and antidepressant use on postoperative complications following ulnar nerve transposition (UNT). A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX Research Network. Adults undergoing primary UNT between 2005 and 2025 were identified and stratified by depression status. Three 1:1 propensity-matched analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of (1) depression status, (2) antidepressant use among depressed patients, and (3) specific antidepressant subclasses. Matching controlled for demographics and comorbidities. Outcomes included 90-day medical and postoperative complications and 1 year pain-related outcomes and opioid dependence. After matching, 11,821 patients were included in each cohort. Depression was associated with significantly higher 90-day medical morbidity, including infection (RR 1.39, P = 0.0008), acute postoperative pain (RR 1.28, P < 0.0001), emergency department utilization (RR 1.37, P < 0.0001), and increased need for PT evaluation (RR 1.21, P < 0.0001) and orthopedic aftercare (RR 1.11, P = 0.001). At 1 year, depressed patients demonstrated higher rates of persistent elbow pain (RR 1.16, P < 0.0001) and nearly double the risk of opioid dependence or abuse (RR 1.88, P < 0.0001). Among patients with depression, preoperative antidepressant use was associated with higher 1-year opioid dependence (RR 1.66, P = 0.007) and persistent pain (RR 1.21, P = 0.001). SSRI use specifically was linked to increased long-term pain (RR 1.17, P = 0.001) and opioid dependence (RR 1.31, P = 0.023). TCA use was associated with higher 90 day ED visits (RR 1.20, P = 0.022), while atypical antidepressants were associated with increased acute postoperative pain (RR 1.42, P = 0.004). Depression was associated with adverse postoperative outcomes after UNT. Antidepressant use, particularly SSRIs, was associated with higher long-term pain and opioid-related risk; however, these associations may reflect underlying depression severity rather than a direct pharmacologic effect.

articles.title: "IMSS Multicenter Hip Fracture Registry Report: 2024".

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: The IMSS 2024 multicenter hip fracture (HF) registry showed an in-hospital mortality rate of 2.6% and an emergency department stay of 24 h (IQR 9-47); however, critical challenges persist, such as low surgical goal completion within 36 h (8.6%) and high post-discharge follow-up loss (70.6% at 30 days). Report of the Multicenter Hip Fracture Registry of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS): 2024.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hip fracture (HF) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality that entails high costs for the healthcare system. The number of cases will increase in the coming years.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To describe the standards of care for HF in multiple IMSS hospitals.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An observational, multicenter, longitudinal, and descriptive study was carried out. Twenty hospitals in Mexico were included. Data were recorded on hospital stay, epidemiological data, and management, with follow-up at 30 and 120 days after discharge. The data was analyzed using SPSS version 22.0.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1,095 subjects participated, with a median age of 79 years (IQR 74-85), predominantly women (n = 786; 71.8%) from the community (n = 1009; 92.1%), autonomous (Barthel 90 points IQR 75-100). The mean time to transfer to the emergency department was 88.2 ± 197 h. Pertrochanteric type HF was the most frequent (n = 573, 52.3%). Thromboprophylaxis was given in 84.8% (n = 929) and antibiotic prophylaxis in 50.7% (n = 555). The goal of 36 h for the surgical procedure was achieved in 8.6% of subjects (n = 94), with the most frequent cause of delay being delay in scheduling (n = 824, 75.3%). The mean time from emergency room to surgical procedure was 6.6 ± 6.3 days. Acute mortality was 2.6% (n = 28). Secondary prevention at discharge occurred in 65.3% (n = 715) of subjects. At 30 days, 754 subjects (70.6%) were lost to follow-up and were discharged with a mortality rate of 7.6% (n = 24), while at 120 days, 87 subjects (30.1%) who had been assessed at 30 days were lost, with a mortality rate of 7.4% (n = 15).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: There was a slight improvement in the standards of care in HF compared to last year; however, improvements are required in specific areas.

articles.title: Naxos disease: current insights from early clinical observations to genetics and precision medicine.

abstract.text: Naxos disease is the prototype of the Naxos disease cardiocutaneous spectrum, a group of inherited desmosomal disorders characterised by distinctive hair and skin abnormalities that precede the development of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). Since its original clinical description in 1986 and the subsequent identification of the first ACM-causing gene (JUP), Naxos disease has provided fundamental insights into the pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of inherited desmosomal cardiomyopathies. This review provides current insights into the evolving clinical spectrum, encompassing the characteristic cutaneous signature, early electrical abnormalities, progressive structural myocardial remodelling, inflammatory ("hot-phase") episodes, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure. We discuss the expanding genotype-phenotype relationships involving JUP, DSP and DSC2, highlighting how distinct genetic substrates influence ventricular involvement, disease severity and clinical outcomes while sharing common desmosomal mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on early clinical recognition, multimodality imaging, genetic diagnosis, risk stratification and lifelong multidisciplinary management. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of international collaborative registries, including NAXCARE, in generating prospective real-world evidence to refine genotype-informed surveillance, improve risk prediction and support precision medicine. Nearly four decades after its original description, Naxos disease has evolved from a rare inherited syndrome into the prototype of desmosomal cardiomyopathy, demonstrating how careful clinical observation can drive molecular discovery, precision medicine and improved patient care.

articles.title: Crisis Interventions for Children and Adolescents with Depression and Suicidality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

abstract.label: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
abstract.text: To review the evidence on crisis services for children and adolescents experiencing acute psychopathological crises, particularly severe depression, suicidal ideation, self-harm, and suicidal behaviour, and to examine their effectiveness in reducing symptoms, improving family functioning, and preventing hospitalisation.

abstract.label: RECENT FINDINGS
abstract.text: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO. Searches of PubMed, Web of Science, PsycInfo, and ClinicalTrials.gov identified 15 eligible studies evaluating 15 crisis interventions. Four interventions targeted suicidal ideation and self-harm through brief, structured approaches, demonstrating reductions in suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts, and emergency department visits. Seven family-focused interventions (evaluated in eight studies) improved communication, family cohesion, and reduced hospitalisation rates. Three interventions aimed to stabilise crises and facilitate linkage with community services, improving continuity of care and decreasing emergency service utilisation. One residential intervention (evaluated in two studies) showed mixed findings, with some behavioural improvements but limited effects on internalising symptoms. Current evidence suggests that crisis services might be a promising alternative to hospitalisation for children and adolescents experiencing acute mental health crises. These interventions provide intensive support within the young person's natural environment, promote family involvement, and were associated with reductions in suicidal ideation, depressive symptoms, emergency visits, and hospital admissions. Despite promising findings, the evidence base remains limited, largely observational and heterogeneous, and causal conclusions cannot be drawn. Future research should directly compare different crisis service models and include long-term follow-up to determine the most effective approaches and their sustainability over time.

articles.title: Implementation of a procedural POCUS training programme for paediatric Surgeons in a resource-limited setting: a pilot feasibility study.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: In public hospitals in low and middle-income countries, imaging services are typically unavailable outside daytime hours, delaying ultrasound access in paediatric emergencies. Implementation models for procedural point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in resource limited paediatric surgical units remain scarce. We describe the implementation of a pragmatic POCUS training programme in a Bolivian paediatric surgical unit.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Retrospective report of a case series (March 2020 - March 2024) following PROCESS 2020 guidelines.

abstract.label: PRIMARY OUTCOME
abstract.text: operational feasibility, defined as the ability of the paediatric surgical team to perform ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction without concurrent sonographer presence.

abstract.label: SECONDARY OUTCOME
abstract.text: reduction success rate. Three paediatric surgeons and one surgical resident participated in approximately 24 supervised sessions over a two-month period.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-five patients underwent ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction; from the third case onward, hydrostatic reduction procedures were performed without concurrent sonographer presence, including during periods without scheduled imaging coverage; 20 (80.0%) [95% CI 59.3-93.2%] achieved successful reduction; five required surgical conversion. Five patients with ileo-ileal intussusception and intestinal compromise underwent surgery. No perforation or other serious adverse event was documented in the available clinical records.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A pragmatic supervised training programme enabled a Bolivian paediatric surgical team with no prior formal ultrasound training to perform ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction without concurrent sonographer presence, providing preliminary feasibility evidence for procedural POCUS in resource-constrained paediatric surgical care.

articles.title: Non-invasive ventilation for general paediatricians.

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Over the past two decades, non-invasive ventilation (NIV) has transitioned from being primarily used in specialist intensive care units to becoming a standard intervention in high dependency units, general paediatric units, emergency departments, and increasingly, patients' homes. Despite this expansion, many general paediatricians still perceive NIV as outside their primary expertise. With this review, we aim to address that gap and equip general paediatricians with the knowledge and confidence to appropriately initiate NIV, monitor its effectiveness, and recognise when escalation of care is required. We narratively reviewed the physiological rationale for non-invasive respiratory support (NRS), including high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and the two principal modalities of NIV-continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP)-and summarised disease-specific evidence from recent literature, including randomised trials, systematic reviews, and international consensus statements. This is a narrative rather than a systematic review: we searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Paediatric Respiratory Reviews for English-language publications from January 2018 to June 2026 using the terms "non-invasive ventilation", "high-flow nasal cannula", "CPAP", "BiPAP", and "children", supplemented by references already known to the authors, and selected articles for relevance and recency, prioritising randomised trials, systematic reviews, and consensus statements. HFNC is an oxygenation device rather than a ventilatory device, and its mechanism, clinical applications, and therapeutic goals differ from CPAP and BiPAP. We introduce the Indications, Contraindications, Equipment, Mode and settings, Assessment and monitoring, Next steps (ICEMAN) framework as a practical tool for structured and safe initiation of NIV in routine clinical practice, and apply it across bronchiolitis, acute severe asthma, pneumonia and hypoxaemic respiratory failure, neuromuscular disease, and obstructive sleep apnoea.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The essential requirements to initiate NIV outside the PICU are well-trained staff, appropriate monitoring, a reliable oxygen supply, and a clear plan for escalation to a higher level of care. Selection of patients for NIV outside the PICU requires careful attention to indication, contraindications, equipment, monitoring, and escalation pathway by using frameworks like ICEMAN.

abstract.label: WHAT IS KNOWN
abstract.text: • HFNC, CPAP, and BiPAP are established, physiologically distinct respiratory therapies now used well beyond the PICU.

abstract.label: WHAT IS NEW
abstract.text: • The ICEMAN framework, updated with PALICC-2 ARDS criteria, gives non-specialists a structured, teachable approach to safe NIV initiation.

articles.title: Chest tube fixation strength depends on suture caliber and fixation technique rather than tube diameter: a biomechanical cadaver study.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Chest tube dislodgement remains a relevant complication in emergency, trauma, and intensive care medicine. In a previous biomechanical study, the Modified Johannesburg technique using Mersilene USP 1 demonstrated superior fixation strength compared with other chest tube fixation techniques. The present study aimed to determine whether suture size, suture material, and chest tube diameter influence fixation strength.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A prospective interventional biomechanical cadaveric study was performed using fresh porcine thoracic wall specimens. A total of 320 load-to-failure tests were conducted under standardized laboratory conditions. Two fixation techniques, Modified Johannesburg and Purse String, were compared using two chest tube diameters (20/28 Ch) and four non-absorbable braided suture configurations: Mersilene USP 1, Mersilene USP 2 - 0, Silk USP 1, and Silk USP 2 - 0. Each experimental group consisted of 20 specimens. Specimens were tested in a uniaxial testing machine until construct failure. Force [N] and elongation [mm] at failure were measured. The experiments were videotaped, and the failure mechanism was analyzed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The Modified Johannesburg technique demonstrated significantly higher pull-out forces compared to the Purse String technique (125.0 vs. 66.4 N; p < 0.001), as did larger suture sizes (USP 1 vs. 2 - 0; p < 0.001) and Mersilene compared to Silk (114.6 vs. 76.9 N; p < 0.001). Chest tube size had only a very small and inconsistent effect on pull-out strength. The predominant failure mode was suture rupture (94.7%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Chest tube fixation strength is significantly influenced by fixation technique, suture size, and suture material. The effect of chest tube diameter on fixation strength appeared negligible. The Modified Johannesburg technique, size 1 sutures, and Mersilene material provided superior biomechanical stability. Since failure occurred predominantly by suture rupture, the suture appears to represent the weakest link of the fixation construct.

articles.title: Changes in patellar height following suprapatellar and infrapatellar tibial nailing: a retrospective comparative cohort study.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Patella baja has been described after infrapatellar tibial nailing and may contribute to postoperative knee morbidity; however, whether the nail insertion approach influences postoperative patellar height remains unclear. This study compared longitudinal changes in patellar height (PH) after suprapatellar and infrapatellar intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures. We hypothesized that the suprapatellar approach would better preserve patellar height.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective comparative cohort study included 114 tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing between 2016 and 2023, using a suprapatellar (n = 86) or infrapatellar (n = 28) approach. Patellar height was assessed using the Caton-Deschamps Index (CDI) on preoperative and final follow-up radiographs. The primary outcome was the longitudinal change in CDI (ΔCDI). Fracture union, complications, and reoperations were secondary outcomes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The mean reduction in CDI was greater following infrapatellar than suprapatellar nailing (ΔCDI - 0.116 ± 0.173 vs. -0.011 ± 0.107; p = 0.001). After adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration, this association remained significant (adjusted β=-0.055; 95% CI - 0.107 to - 0.004; p = 0.035), although sensitivity analyses showed attenuation after additional adjustment for sex. Fracture union rates were similar between approaches (93.0% vs. 92.9%; p = 0.987), with no statistically significant differences in complications or reoperations.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Infrapatellar tibial nailing was associated with a significant postoperative reduction in PH compared with the suprapatellar approach. This association persisted after adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration but was sensitive to additional adjustment for sex. These findings highlight a potential relationship between nail insertion approach and postoperative PH but do not establish an independent effect of surgical approach.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort study (Level III).

articles.title: Intraarticular calcaneal fractures: biomechanical analysis of two fixation constructs.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: The aim of this biomechanical study was to investigate the fixation stability of a small low-profile 2.7 mm variable-angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate supplemented with two additional independent cortex screws versus a traditional small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate in a standardized Sanders IIc fracture model.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Sixteen fracture models cocomposed of three polymer blocks (fragments) each and simulating Sanders IIc intra‑articular calcaneal fractures were assigned to two groups. Group 1 (control) received a small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate, while Group 2 received a small 2.7 mm variable‑angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate with two additional independent cortex screws. All constructs were instrumented using prefabricated pilot holes and standardized screw configurations. Biomechanical testing was conducted implementing a 3‑point-bending setup and progressively increasing cyclic loading to failure. Angular interfragmentary movements were quantified via motion tracking along with cycles to clinically relevant failure.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Initial stiffness (N/mm) in Group 1 (65.2 ± 34.7) was significantly lower versus Group 2 (232.5 ± 48.6), p = 0.020. Although angular interfragmentary movements around the anteroposterior axis were significantly greater in Group 1 versus Group 2 (p < 0.001), Group 1 demonstrated significantly smaller angular interfragmentary movements around the mediolateral axis for the central-to-posterior and anterior-to-posterior fragment pairs (p ≤ 0.004), while no significant difference between the groups was identified with regard to the central-to-anterior fragment pair (p ≥ 0.377). Cycles and loads (N) to clinically relevant failure in Group 1 (3635 ± 176 and 92.7 ± 3.5) were significantly lower versus Group 2 (17433 ± 628 and 368.7 ± 12.6), p < 0.001. Failure mode in Group 1 involved plate deformation, whereas Group 2 failed through breakage or bending of the independent cortex screws.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Biomechanically, fixation implementing a small low-profile 2.7 mm variable-angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate supplemented with two additional independent cortex screws demonstrated stability comparable to, and in certain respects superior to that achieved with a small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate in a standardized Sanders IIc fracture model. However, the findings of this laboratory study do not establish an isolated benefit of the 2.7 mm plate itself, nor do they demonstrate clinical superiority or support alterations to postoperative weight-bearing protocols.

articles.title: Changing Patterns of Transient Ischemic Attack Evaluation in US Emergency Departments.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: For US patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with transient ischemic attack (TIA), guidelines recommend resource-intensive multimodal evaluation to optimize secondary stroke prevention. These resources are not available in all EDs, and national patterns of ED TIA care are not well described.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To evaluate national trends in ED TIA care, including discharge practices, imaging use, and associated costs, and to assess patient- and hospital-level factors associated with these patterns.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This was a retrospective repeated cross-sectional study of ED visits using the 2013-2021 National Emergency Department Sample of the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project, a weighted, nationally representative annual sample of ED visits in the US. TIA and stroke encounters during the study period were identified among patients aged 18 years or older by a first-listed International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision or Tenth Revision code for TIA or stroke diagnosis. Analyses were performed from October 2024 to April 2026.

abstract.label: EXPOSURES
abstract.text: Calendar year.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: ED discharge; imaging use among discharged TIA encounters; and inflation-adjusted ED cost per discharged encounter.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included 2 151 408 (95% CI, 2 107 855-2 194 960) weighted ED visits for TIA (1 194 630 [55.5%] female; mean [SEM] age, 69.8 [0.05] years). Adjusted models found the predicted probability of discharge increased from 45% (95% CI, 43%-46%) in 2013 to 66% (95% CI, 64%-68%) in 2021 (P < .001 for trend). During this time, mean ED charges increased from $1746 (95% CI, $1662-$1830) to $2755 (95% CI, $2674-$2836) per encounter (P < .001 for trend). Imaging use among discharged TIA encounters increased substantially, including computed tomography angiography (predicted probability, 4% [95% CI, 3%-4%] in 2013 vs 45% [95% CI, 42%-47%] in 2021; P < .001 for trend) and magnetic resonance imaging (predicted probability, 17% [95% CI, 16%-19%] in 2013 vs 53% [95% CI, 50%-55%] in 2021; P < .001 for trend). Rate of discharge was higher in rural encounters than in urban encounters for all years studied, and the rate of magnetic resonance imaging use was lower.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: This cross-sectional study demonstrates a shift in TIA care over time that suggests increased use of the ED to expedite evaluation for TIA that previously occurred during a brief hospitalization. This approach has consequences in terms of cost and ED throughput and may not be as feasible in rural hospitals as it is in urban hospitals.

articles.title: Cognitive Bias in Emergency Radiology: Implications for Trauma Torso CT.

abstract.text: As the volume and complexity of trauma torso Computed Tomography (CT) scans continue to rise, the risk of diagnostic error in the emergency department (ED) remains a significant challenge. While perceptual misses are common, in the high acuity and time-pressured environment of the ED, many errors are driven by ingrained mental shortcuts that can lead to misinterpretation, ie, cognitive biases. This educational review presents 16 cases from a level 1 trauma and tertiary care institution, emphasizing diagnostic errors and near-misses encountered during the interpretation of emergency torso CT. Cases are organized by organ systems and highlight missed or misinterpreted findings involving the cardiothoracic, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and musculoskeletal systems. Each case illustrates a relevant cognitive bias, including framing bias, satisfaction of search, anchoring bias, premature closure, availability bias, zebra retreat bias, and blind spot bias. The pathophysiology of these commonly overlooked injuries will be reviewed with a focus on cognitive biases that lead to their omission and practical mitigation strategies to avoid them. This review emphasizes the importance of reviewing all available images independently with a systematic and consistent search pattern and only then integrating clinical information as a potential strategy to reduce cognitive biases. By recognizing these patterns of error and implementing mitigation strategies, radiologists may improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Illness in Children Presenting to the Emergency Department After International Travel: A 10-Year Retrospective Analysis From the University Hospital of Helsinki, Finland.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: We characterized infections after international travel and identified predictors of severe infection to refine management.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of children aged 0-18 years presenting to Helsinki University Hospital Emergency Department within 90 days of international travel between January 1, 2015, and January 26, 2025.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 921 patients (median age 5.1 years), 59.6% were travellers visiting friends and relatives (VFR), 31.7% outbound tourists, 7.3% migrants and 1.4% visitors to Finland. Sub-Saharan Africa was the most common travel destination (46.3%). The leading diagnoses were diarrhoea (36.0%), viral (22.6%) and respiratory infections (21.3%); 8.2% of infections were tropical and 15.3% potentially severe. Independent predictors of severe infection were migrant status, fever, travel from South-Central Asia, presentation > 5 days after return, and male sex. Malaria was diagnosed in 3.3% of patients, and only 22.4% of eligible travellers received adequate prophylaxis. Extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing organisms were frequent in Salmonella typhi infections and Escherichia coli pyelonephritis.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The main reason for paediatric travel was visiting friends and relatives. Migrants presented more frequently with potentially life-threatening infections. Only 22% of eligible travellers received adequate malaria chemoprophylaxis. Antimicrobial resistance represents a significant concern among paediatric travellers.

articles.title: Describing the patient trajectory for unplanned care in a region of Flanders, Belgium: A prospective observational study.
articles.journal_full: The European journal of general practice

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Demand for unplanned care in Belgium is high, placing pressure on both out-of-hours primary care facilities (OOHPCF) and emergency departments (ED). Understanding patient trajectories may help optimise care pathways and resource planning for planned and unplanned care.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe patient presentations and trajectories at OOHPCF and EDs in a region of Flanders, Belgium.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Data were collected in six EDs and three OOHPCF in the greater {redacted} region. All consultations were recorded during three randomly selected days in EDs and one full week in OOHPCF in 2024.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1,469 ED and 857 OOHPCF consultations were analysed. In EDs, trauma was the most common presentation (32%), followed by ear, nose and throat (ENT) and dermatology conditions (22%). In OOHPCF, trauma and orthopaedic problems accounted for 20% of consultations, followed by ENT (17%) and dermatology (14%). Most ED patients (71%) were discharged home. Self-referral accounted for 65% of ED visits; these patients were generally younger and presented with lower-acuity conditions. One in five patients had consulted another healthcare provider within the previous week. Pain and worry were the main drivers for attendance. Attending clinicians in both settings considered up to one-third of consultations manageable in planned care.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Rather than restricting access or apportioning blame to patients, our findings indicate the need to reassess measures throughout planned and unplanned care pathways for timely access to the most appropriate care setting while maintaining patient safety and equitable access to services.

articles.title: Family Resilience and Coping in Disasters, Pandemics, and Large-Scale Crises: A Systematic Review.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Disasters, large-scale crises, and prolonged adversities such as pandemics can place sustained psychosocial pressure on families and disrupt everyday family functioning. Although family resilience is increasingly used to explain why some families adapt better than others, the evidence base is dispersed across conceptual, empirical, and intervention-focused work.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and included peer-reviewed studies that examined family resilience or family coping in disaster, pandemic, or sustained adversity contexts. Study selection followed PRISMA 2020 principles. Data were extracted using a standardized form and synthesized using narrative and thematic approaches.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Forty-two studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Across contexts, family resilience was most often described as a dynamic, system-level process that involves shared meaning-making, organizational flexibility, and effective communication. Parenting practices repeatedly emerged as a key pathway linking family resilience to child adjustment. Resilience-oriented family interventions reported overall beneficial effects across disaster, pandemic, and serious illness contexts, with no evidence of harm.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Family resilience is a critical contributor to psychosocial adaptation during disasters and large-scale crises. Interventions that strengthen family-level processes-especially communication, coping skills, and supportive parenting-may offer a scalable approach to improve preparedness, response, and longer-term recovery.

articles.title: Breakout Session 9: Physical Environment.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: The physical environment of an alternate care facility (ACF) spans safety, security, infection prevention, emergency management, hazardous materials, and fire and life safety, and it proved inseparable from patient safety, staff wellbeing, and operational continuity. Symposium participants summarized operational lessons from establishing and sustaining ACFs across convention centers, hotels, tents, and other non-traditional spaces. Participants reported that effective sites integrated clinical staff into security and de-escalation rather than relying on law enforcement alone, controlled access through single monitored entrances, and managed both the internal care space and the external perimeter as part of patient care. Multidisciplinary walkthroughs were essential to identifying physical hazards before activation. Persistent challenges included the absence of smoke compartments in open and temporary structures, unverified ventilation and negative-pressure performance, unreliable power and connectivity, and environments lacking day-night differentiation that contributed to patient delirium. Recommended best practices include engineering environmental controls in advance, embedding infection prevention, wellness, and safety functions from activation, and protecting staff through dedicated respite and decompression space.

articles.title: Suicidal Behavior Before and After Hurricanes Irma and Maria in Puerto Rico: A Descriptive Analysis of Crisis Hotline (Línea PAS) Calls, 2015-2021.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Natural disasters can increase the risk of suicidal behavior, particularly in resource-limited settings. We characterized suicidal ideation and attempts before and after Hurricanes Irma and Maria (September 2017) in Puerto Rico using crisis-hotline surveillance data.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective descriptive analysis of suicide-related calls to Línea PAS, Puerto Rico's 24/7 government crisis hotline, from January 2015 through December 2021 (84 months). Monthly counts of suicidal-ideation and suicide-attempt calls were aggregated, stratified by sex and age group, and displayed as a time series with September 2017 as the index event, with exact Poisson and Wilson 95% confidence intervals.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Total suicide-related calls rose sharply about 2 months after landfall, peaking from November 2017 through January 2018 (maximum 4,548 calls in January 2018) before returning toward baseline by February 2018. Working-age adults (21-59 years) and women accounted for most calls. The surge coincided with prolonged power and telecommunications outages and with an independent rise in recorded suicide deaths.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: These descriptive, ecological findings are consistent with a substantial mental-health burden following catastrophic hurricanes and coincided temporally with prolonged infrastructure disruption; the design cannot establish causation. They support integrating crisis-hotline-based behavioral-health surveillance and rapid utility restoration into disaster preparedness for climate-vulnerable regions.

articles.title: Post-Disaster Recovery, Cancer Care, and Family Well-Being in Japan: A Structural Equation Modeling Study.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study examined how subjective disaster recovery and cancer-care satisfaction jointly shape family well-being in Japan, and when better cancer care accompanies higher well-being.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A quota-stratified web survey of 2,179 adults aged 20-69 was conducted across Japan (September 2019), with quotas by Fukushima residency and family cancer experience. Subjective recovery from any major disaster within 10 years (unexposed; recovered or in prospect; no prospect), household cancer experience, and Short FAMCARE satisfaction were modeled against latent well-being by structural equation modeling.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among non-cancer households (n = 1,324), unrecovered damage was associated with lower well-being (β = -0.08, 95% CI -0.13 to -0.03, P = 0.001), with no association in cancer-affected households (β = 0.00, P = 0.98). Among cancer-affected families (n = 855), high satisfaction was associated with higher well-being (β = 0.17, P < 0.001), more so in recovered than unrecovered households (contrast 0.149, 95% CI 0.031 to 0.268, P = 0.014). Resting on small subgroups, this interaction is exploratory.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Better cancer care did not offset incomplete disaster recovery; its association with higher well-being was confined to households with recovery achieved or in prospect. These cross-sectional findings are consistent with delivering reconstruction and cancer care together.

articles.title: Development of the Alternate Care Facility Symposium: Understanding National Experiences in Planning and Operations.
