abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Patient and caregiver satisfaction is a key indicator of health care quality and is particularly relevant in pediatric emergency care. Patient complaints represent an important source of information regarding organizational weaknesses and unmet expectations. The COVID-19 pandemic and recent changes in referral pathways have modified the functioning of these services. This study aimed to analyze patient complaints registered in the pediatric emergency department of a level II hospital between January 2020 and June 2025, characterizing temporal trends, main reasons for dissatisfaction, and patient profiles, and comparing findings with the pre-pandemic period.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective, observational, descriptive study based on the analysis of all complaints. Complaints were classified according to the Reader et al. taxonomy, evaluating demographic, clinical, and organizational variables as well as institutional response time. Data from January to June 2025 were available; annual estimates based on linear extrapolation were generated when required for descriptive comparisons.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 166 complaints were analyzed among 153,088 pediatric emergency department visits, corresponding to an overall complaint rate of 0.11%. After reaching their lowest values in 2020 and 2021, complaint rates fluctuated annually, with the highest observed complaint rate recorded during the first semester of 2025. Waiting time remained the main reason for dissatisfaction. An increase in complaints related to staff attitude, hospital logistics, institutional rules, and prior referral processes was observed during the post-pandemic period, including the period following implementation of the "Call Before, Save Lives" project. Most complaints were submitted by mothers and concerned children aged 1-9 years. Institutional response time varied over the study period, with the shortest response times observed during the first semester of 2025.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Patient complaints provide valuable information on persistent structural challenges and evolving patterns of dissatisfaction in pediatric emergency care, representing a useful tool for quality improvement initiatives.

articles.title: Bystanders and Close Ones in Unsuccessful Resuscitation: An Overlooked Population in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.

abstract.text: Bystanders, lay rescuers, and close ones involved in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest resuscitation attempts that end in death represent an often-overlooked population within emergency care. As community-centered resuscitation systems increasingly promote dispatcher-assisted cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), community first responder programs, and public CPR training, more individuals are becoming directly involved in resuscitation attempts, many of which are unsuccessful. Such experiences can be associated with emotional distress, intrusive memories, guilt, and post-traumatic stress symptoms. The impact may differ according to the person's relationship with the patient and their involvement in the resuscitation. This perspective paper discusses the psychological impact of unsuccessful resuscitation and considers the role of emergency nurses in providing support across dispatch, prehospital, and hospital settings. Approaches such as supportive follow-up contact and referral for psychological support, as distinct from formal psychological debriefing protocols, could help address some of these needs, although current evidence on their effectiveness remains preliminary. Greater recognition of people involved in unsuccessful resuscitation and their support needs may represent a further step in the development of community-centered resuscitation systems.

articles.title: Documentation-based fall categories, baseline functional status, and diagnosed multiregional injury after falls in older adults: A single-center retrospective study.
articles.journal_full: Journal of family medicine and primary care

abstract.label: CONTEXT
abstract.text: Older adults presenting to the emergency department (ED) after a fall show substantial heterogeneity in injury burden. However, the relationship between routinely documented fall information at presentation and broader injury distribution remains unclear.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: To examine whether documentation-based fall categories and baseline functional status information are associated with multiregional injury in older adults after falls.

abstract.label: SETTINGS AND DESIGN
abstract.text: Single-center, retrospective observational study conducted in a tertiary care ED from October 2022 to March 2024.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: Consecutive patients aged ≥65 years presenting after a fall were included. Falls were classified as A, dizziness/presyncope-associated; B, tripping/slipping/environmental; C, loss of balance during movement/transfer; and D, indeterminate/unclear. Baseline activities of daily living (ADL) were categorized as independent, dependent, or undocumented. The primary outcome was multiregional injury, defined as injuries involving ≥2 of seven body regions.

abstract.label: STATISTICAL ANALYSIS USED
abstract.text: Multivariable logistic regression and sensitivity analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1014 cases (median age, 82 years; 41.1% male), multiregional injury occurred in 38.6%. Category D was associated with lower odds of multiregional injury than category B (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.48-0.98). Undocumented baseline ADL (adjusted OR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.01-2.05) and ambulance transport (adjusted OR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.08-2.49) were associated with higher odds. Sensitivity analyses showed similar patterns.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Documentation-based fall categories, ambulance transport, and undocumented baseline functional status were associated with multiregional injury after falls in older adults. Nevertheless, these findings are exploratory, as documentation quality and diagnostic intensity may have influenced the outcomes.

articles.title: Life satisfaction and self-rated health in long-term survivors after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR): associations with functional outcome, cognition, anxiety, depression, fatigue, and physical activity.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The goal of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) is not only survival, but long-term satisfaction with life. Whether functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale; mRS), cognition, emotional symptoms, fatigue, and physical activity relate to life satisfaction in ECPR survivors remain unknown. We evaluated these aspects of health and their association with life satisfaction and self-rated health.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This cross-sectional follow-up included survivors ≥1 year after ECPR at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden (2010-2021). Primary outcomes were life satisfaction (World Values Survey) and self-rated health (EQ-5D-5L VAS). Secondary outcomes were mRS, Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Mental Fatigue Scale (MFS), and self-reported physical activity. Exploratory multivariable linear regression assessed associations with primary outcomes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 34 survivors, 26 (76.5%) participated; median follow-up was 5 [IQR 2-7] years; 96% had mRS 0-3. Median life satisfaction was 8 [6-9]/10 and self-rated health 81 [70-90]/100, similar to population reference values (7.55 and 80). Positive screen for cognitive impairment (MoCA < 26) was present in 56%, anxiety (HADS-A ≥ 8) 42%, depression (HADS-D ≥ 8) 15%, and fatigue (MFS ≥ 10.5) 50%. In exploratory multivariable analysis, moderate physical activity was associated with life satisfaction (B 0.36 per day/week; 95% CI 0.06-0.67; p = 0.023) and self-rated health (B 4.60; 0.71-8.50; p = 0.024).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Long-term ECPR survivors reported life satisfaction and self-rated health similar to population reference values. In exploratory multivariable analysis, moderate physical activity was the only variable associated with both. This supports assessing life satisfaction and physical activity in post-ECPR follow-up.

articles.title: Video laryngoscopy versus direct laryngoscopy for pediatric emergency tracheal intubation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation ILCOR Pediatric Life Support Task Force

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To compare video laryngoscopy with direct laryngoscopy for pediatric intubation during cardiac arrest and peri-arrest scenarios.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420251081694) searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane from inception to May 1, 2026. Two authors independently screened studies; data were extracted by one and independently verified by a second reviewer. Eligible studies compared video versus direct laryngoscopy in pediatric acute care; emergency department, intensive care, and prehospital settings. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and RoB2. Critical outcomes were survival to hospital discharge, first-pass intubation success, overall intubation success, and severe tracheal intubation-associated events. Additional data included study design, setting, age, operator type, and device. Meta-analyses used random-effects Mantel-Haenszel models reporting risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eighteen studies (17 observational, 1 RCT). First-pass success was higher with video laryngoscopy (72.2% vs 69.0%; RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.06-1.16; very low certainty). Severe adverse events were less frequent with video laryngoscopy (7.7% vs 11.8%; RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62-0.93; very low certainty). Overall success (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.01) and desaturation (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.01) were similar. No studies reported survival outcomes or data specific to cardiac arrest.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Among children undergoing emergency tracheal intubation, video laryngoscopy may be associated with improved first-pass success and fewer adverse events, although the certainty of evidence is very low and causal inferences are limited. No data were available for survival outcomes and cardiac arrest.

articles.title: Beyond Seizure Suppression: Caffeic Acid Phenethyl Ester and 10-Hydroxy-2-Decenoic Acid Improve Anxiety-like and Cognitive Behaviors in PTZ-Challenged Zebrafish.

abstract.text: Epilepsy is associated with recurrent seizures and behavioral and cognitive disturbances, highlighting the importance of assessing behavioral outcomes alongside seizure severity. Caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) has shown neuroprotective activity, whereas evidence for the neurobehavioral effects of 10-hydroxy-2-decenoic acid (10-HDA) remains limited. This study investigated their individual and combined dietary effects on seizure-like behavior and behavioral test performance in adult zebrafish (Danio rerio) challenged with pentylenetetrazol (PTZ). Fish received experimental diets for 8 weeks before exposure to 15 mM PTZ. A dietary valproic acid group was included as a comparator. Outcomes included behavioral seizure scores, the area under the seizure score-time curve (AUC), and performance in the novel tank diving and Y-maze tests. Compared with PTZ alone, CAPE, 10-HDA, and their combination reduced seizure scores and AUC values and increased upper-zone and novel-arm exploration (p < 0.05). The combined group spent more time in the novel arm than either single-compound group (p < 0.05), although its advantages varied across endpoints and pharmacological synergy was not established. Overall, dietary CAPE and 10-HDA were associated with lower behavioral seizure scores and improved test performance following acute PTZ challenge. Further studies are needed to distinguish these responses from independent effects on baseline behavior and the influence of seizure severity and motor function.

articles.title: Effect of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy in Reducing Intestinal Edema After Traumatic Liver Injury with Abdominal Packing: An Experimental Animal Study.

abstract.text: Background: Traumatic liver injury in severe trauma and temporary abdominal closure can lead to postoperative intestinal edema and inflammation. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) may mitigate these effects by modulating inflammatory pathways. This study investigated the effects of HBOT on mucosal preservation, with villus height and the villus-to-crypt (V/C) ratio as primary outcomes and mechanistic analyses of the NLRP3/caspase-1 pathway. Methods: Twenty male Sprague-Dawley rats (aged 7 weeks, weighing 260-300 g) were randomly assigned to HBOT (n = 10) or non-HBOT groups (n = 10) and underwent midline laparotomy (3-5 cm) with 50% left lateral lobe liver resection. After 4 min, the liver was packed with 2 × 2 cm aseptic gauze and the abdomen was temporarily sutured. After 24 h, the small intestine was isolated and flushed with phosphate-buffered saline. The primary outcomes were villus height and the V/C ratio, measured in the proximal jejunum. Secondary outcomes included villus width, crypt depth, villous surface area, and the Dvorak histological injury grade. Additional analyses included NLRP3, AIM2, pro-caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18 expression in bowel tissue (Western blot); plasma IL-1β and IL-18 (ELISA); and peripheral blood mononuclear cell catalase activity, cell viability (CCK-8), and LDH release. Results: The HBOT group demonstrated greater villus height compared with the non-HBOT group (347.68 ± 42.48 μm vs. 290.43 ± 43.47 μm; p = 0.008), corresponding to a 19.7% increase. The V/C ratio was significantly higher in the HBOT group (2.56 ± 0.31 vs. 2.12 ± 0.23; p = 0.002). Villus width was significantly reduced in the HBOT group (64.65 ± 4.24 μm vs. 73.93 ± 9.49 μm; p = 0.015). Pathological findings indicated that the HBOT group showed attenuated lamina propria edema and separation. In the intestinal tissue samples, NLRP3 expression was significantly lower in the HBOT group (0.09 [0.09, 0.12] vs. 1.00 [0.92, 1.06]; p < 0.001), and AIM2, IL-1β, IL-18, and cleaved caspase-1 followed similar trends. Conclusions: HBOT preserved intestinal villus structure after traumatic liver injury, as evidenced by greater villus height and a higher villus-to-crypt ratio. At the molecular level, HBOT suppressed NLRP3, AIM2, and cleaved caspase-1 protein expression in bowel tissue and reduced IL-1β and IL-18 protein levels. By limiting inflammasome activation and interstitial edema, HBOT may help preserve intestinal structural integrity after damage-control surgery.

articles.title: Incidence of traumatic injuries sustained following cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a single-centre retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Chest compressions form the basis of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in out of hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Recently, mechanical CPR (MCPR) devices have been introduced, particularly in the prehospital environment, avoiding the need for clinicians to perform conventional manual CPR (CCPR). At our institution, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is available for select OHCA patients in refractory arrest (ECPR). Given ECPR patients typically undergo prolonged chest compressions, there may be a higher likelihood of injury; however, evidence directly comparing ECPR and CCPR injury rates is lacking. This study aimed to investigate incidence and type of traumatic injuries following CPR and whether a difference between ECPR and CCPR patients exists.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 313 OHCA were identified between 2021-2024, with 136 meeting criteria. Mean CPR duration was 24 ± 16 min, and 37 patients (27%) received MCPR. Thirteen patients had ECPR with mean time from cardiac arrest to establishment of ECMO blood flow being 63 ± 18 min, of which 11 (85%) received MCPR. Injuries occurred in 58 patients (43%), with 23 (16.9%) sustaining clinically significant injuries. Rates of mortality were higher for the injured patients compared to the non-injured patients (41 [70%] vs 33 [43%] respectively, p = ≤0.05). On multiple variable logistic regression analysis CPR > 20 min, not ECPR or MCPR, was significantly associated with traumatic injury (OR 2.45, CI 1.15, 5.23, p = ≤0.05).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: CPR-related injuries are common. CPR >20 min, not ECPR or MCPR, is associated with higher rate of injury. CT imaging in this cohort could be considered to identify these injuries.

articles.title: Multimodal artificial intelligence assessment of simulated cardiac arrest performance: a pilot study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Assessment of simulated cardiac arrest performance is resource-intensive and subject to inter-rater variability. We evaluated whether a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) system could score video-recorded cardiac arrest megacode simulations with agreement comparable to expert raters.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Six scripted megacode simulations (three ventricular fibrillation, three pulseless electrical activity) representing exemplar, guideline-deviation and non-technical-deficiency performance were scored by two ACLS instructors using a validated team-leader checklist; consensus ratings served as the reference. Two operators analysed each video with Gemini 1.5 Pro at three temperature settings (504 item-level ratings). We calculated Cohen's kappa, Gwet's AC1, and sensitivity and specificity for identifying performed and omitted actions, and compared AI self-reported confidence between correct and incorrect ratings.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Expert inter-rater agreement was κ = 0.78 (95% CI 0.64-0.93). AI-expert agreement was κ = 0.62 (95% CI 0.49-0.75; range 0.40-0.86 across configurations) and AC1 = 0.77. The AI identified performed actions with high sensitivity (0.98, 95% CI 0.96-0.99) but detected omitted actions poorly (specificity 0.58, 95% CI 0.44-0.72), particularly omissions defined by timing or sequence. Temperature had no consistent effect. Incorrect ratings of actions as performed carried lower mean self-reported confidence than correct ones (93.6 vs 98.1), but 48% were made with maximal confidence.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A multimodal AI system reliably confirmed completed actions but frequently failed to detect omitted actions, yielding moderate overall agreement that was below expert-expert agreement. Current systems may support, but not replace, expert assessment of cardiac arrest simulation.

articles.title: Strategies for defibrillation during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest - protocol for a randomised clinical trial.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: There is a lack of evidence regarding which defibrillation strategy is the most effective during resuscitation. Anterior-posterior pad placement and double sequential defibrillation have been proposed as alternatives to standard anterior-lateral defibrillation for patients with refractory shockable rhythms, but evidence remains limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This trial will investigate whether there is a difference in 30-day survival when using anterior-posterior and double sequential defibrillation as compared to standard anterior-lateral defibrillation in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and a shockable rhythm.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This trial is an investigator-initiated, individually randomised, 3-group, clinical trial enrolling adult patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with at least one emergency medical services defibrillation attempt and if the last known rhythm is shockable and two manual defibrillators are available. Participants are randomised 1:1:1 to anterior-lateral defibrillation, anterior-posterior defibrillation, or double sequential defibrillation. The trial is planned to be conducted in Denmark, Finland, Belgium, and Ireland.The primary outcome is 30-day survival, with key secondary outcomes of 90-day survival and neurological status at 30 and 90-days assessed using the modified Rankin Scale. Additional outcomes include return of spontaneous circulation, hospital disposition, health-related quality of life, and longer-term survival and neurological outcomes.The planned sample size is 909 participants. Enrollment began in March 2025. 320 patients have been enrolled by September 2026. The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06781892).

articles.title: Blood Product Transfusion Patterns in One Lithuanian and Two Polish Academic Emergency Departments: A Retrospective Comparative Study.

abstract.text: Background and Objectives: Blood product transfusion is an important emergency intervention for patients with acute bleeding, severe symptomatic anemia, and selected hematological conditions. Patterns of ED transfusion may differ according to the local case mix, referral pathways, and blood bank processes. We compared transfusion-related characteristics and outcomes among patients treated in one Lithuanian and two Polish academic emergency departments. Materials and Methods: We performed a retrospective comparative study of adults (aged ≥18 years) in whom a blood product transfusion was initiated in the ED between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024 at one Lithuanian and two Polish academic hospitals. We compared patient characteristics, indication categories, shock index values, time to transfusion, blood product use, adjunctive therapies, laboratory values, ED disposition, hospital length of stay, and in-hospital mortality. Findings are reported as center-cohort comparisons and are not intended to represent national practice. Results: A total of 670 patients were included: 367 at the Lithuanian center and 303 across the two Polish centers. GI bleeding was significantly more common in the Lithuanian center cohort (48.8% vs. 22.8%; OR 3.22 [95% CI 2.30-4.53]; p < 0.001), whereas anemia and malignancy-related anemia were more frequent in the Polish center cohort (anemia: 34.7% vs. 18.3%, OR 0.42 [95% CI 0.29-0.6]; p < 0.001; cancer: 26.4% vs. 7.6%, OR 0.23 [95% CI 0.15-0.37]; p < 0.001). The median shock index was significantly higher in the Lithuanian center cohort than in the Polish center cohort (0.9; [IQR 0.7-1.2] vs. 0.7; IQR 0.6-0.9; 0.2 [95% CI 0.1-0.3]; p < 0.001), and pre-transfusion hemoglobin was lower (64.5 g/L [IQR 50-86] vs. 119 g/L [IQR 83-139]; p < 0.001). Uncrossmatched RBC units were more frequently administered in the Lithuanian center cohort (133 (36.9%) vs. 47 (15.6%); OR 3.18 [95% CI 2.18-4.64]; p < 0.001), as was fresh frozen plasma (71 (19.5%) vs. 3 (1%); OR 24.23 [95% CI 7.55-77.8]; p < 0.001). Conversely, platelet transfusions were more common in the Polish center cohort (17 (4.6%) vs. 45 (14.9%), OR 0.28 [95% CI 0.16-0.5]; p < 0.001). The median time from ED arrival to transfusion was longer in the Lithuanian center cohort than in the Polish center cohort (150 [IQR 75-256] vs. 117 [IQR 103-154], 23 [95% CI 9-39]; p = 0.002). Hospital admission was significantly more frequent in the Lithuanian cohort than in the Polish cohort (350 (95.4%) vs. 112 (37.0%); p < 0.001). Among admitted patients, the median hospital length of stay was significantly longer in the Lithuanian cohort compared with the Polish cohort (6 days [IQR 3-11] vs. 1 day [IQR 1-5]; 95% CI for the difference 3-4; p < 0.001). In-hospital mortality was 33.5% (n = 123) in the Lithuanian cohort and 13.9% (n = 42) in the Polish cohort (OR 3.13 [95% CI 2.12-4.63]; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Among transfused patients in the three participating academic EDs, the case mix, blood product use, transfusion timing, and unadjusted outcomes differed substantially. These center-specific findings may inform future prospective studies of how referral pathways, clinical populations, and local transfusion processes influence ED blood product utilization. They do not establish differences in national practice, transfusion appropriateness, or causal effects on clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Beyond the Image: Pitfalls, Cognitive Biases, and Safety Gaps in Non-Cardiac Neonatal Point-of-Care Ultrasound.

abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is now part of everyday work in neonatal intensive care, supporting diagnosis, procedures, and decisions in acutely unwell infants. Its spread has outpaced the development of training, credentialing, and quality assurance structures, and the neonatal literature rarely describes how and why the technique fails. In this perspective, we focus on non-cardiac neonatal POCUS (lung, cranial, and abdominal). We adapt existing frameworks into four error domains: indication, image acquisition, image interpretation, and clinical integration. We also separate errors that can occur in any ultrasound examination from those tied to the point-of-care setting, including confirmation, anchoring, and availability bias, time pressure, and fatigue. Using illustrative cases and comparative tables, we describe common look-alike findings, summarize thermal and mechanical bioeffects by organ, and discuss probe and gel hygiene in the neonatal unit. We then outline a stepwise pathway for training, supervision, credentialing, and quality assurance, and suggest practical safeguards: structured protocols and reports, simple debiasing habits, image archiving with periodic expert review, and close collaboration with radiology and cardiology. Seen in this way, investment in safety is part of the value of neonatal POCUS rather than an added cost.

articles.title: Predictors of Technical Difficulty in Emergency Department Ultrasound-Guided Nerve Blocks: A Multicenter NURVE Registry Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Ultrasound-guided nerve blocks (UGNBs) are increasingly used in emergency departments (EDs), but factors associated with technical difficulty remain poorly characterized.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To characterize the frequency of technical difficulty during ED UGNBs and explore patient-, provider-, and block-level factors associated with difficult procedures.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective analysis of the multicenter National Ultrasound-guided neRVE (NURVE) Registry, including UGNBs performed at 11 U.S. EDs from January 2022 through December 2023. This interval was selected to capture the complete initial two-year period of NURVE Registry data collection. Technical difficulty was defined by operator self-report using a standardized registry question. Mixed-effects logistic regression with institution as a random intercept was used to evaluate factors associated with technical difficulty.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1725 UGNBs included in the analysis, 82 (4.8%) were reported as technically difficult. In unadjusted analyses, technical difficulty was more common among patients with obesity and differed by block group. In mixed-effects regression, body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m² was independently associated with increased odds of technical difficulty compared with BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m² (odds ratio [OR] 2.94, 95% confidence intervals [CI] 1.58-5.47). Compared with fascia iliaca/femoral region blocks, truncal plane blocks (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05-0.87), distal upper-extremity blocks (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.94), and distal lower-extremity blocks (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.10-0.99) were associated with lower odds of technical difficulty. Provider role and prior procedural experience were not significantly associated with difficulty in unadjusted analyses.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Technical difficulty during ED UGNBs was uncommon. Obesity was the most consistent predictor of procedural difficulty, while block-group associations were more modest and influenced by site-level factors. These findings may help inform procedural planning and UGNB training initiatives.

articles.title: Emergency Department Pediatric Early Warning System for Identifying Resuscitation-Defined Critical Illness in Children: A Prospective Diagnostic Classification Study in Vietnam.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Early recognition of children with severe physiological illness is essential in emergency care. The Emergency Department Pediatric Early Warning System score (ED-PEWS) has not been evaluated in Vietnam. We assessed how well ED-PEWS recorded at presentation identifies children who meet criteria for resuscitation-defined critical illness in a high-acuity pediatric emergency setting.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective observational diagnostic classification study was conducted from August to October 2022 in the emergency and resuscitation department of a national tertiary children's hospital in Vietnam. Children aged 1 month to 15 years were enrolled according to a prespecified shift-based schedule. The outcome was resuscitation-defined critical illness within 24 h (cardiac arrest or bradycardia with poor perfusion requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation). Because the timing of scoring relative to interventions and outcome was not recorded, the analysis was interpreted as concurrent classification rather than prediction.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 805 children (median age 19 months; 65.3% male), 156 (19.4%) met the outcome criteria. The median ED-PEWS was 32 (interquartile range, 24-43) in children with the outcome and 10 (8-12) in those without (p < 0.001). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.952 (95% CI, 0.926-0.977). At the exploratory Youden-derived threshold of ED-PEWS ≥ 16, there were 143 true positives, 49 false positives, 13 false negatives, and 600 true negatives; sensitivity was 91.7% (95% CI, 86.2-95.5), specificity 92.4% (90.1-94.4), and negative predictive value 97.9% (96.4-98.9).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this selected high-acuity cohort, ED-PEWS showed strong concurrent discrimination for resuscitation-defined critical illness. Because the score and the outcome share physiological components and the threshold was derived and evaluated in the same dataset, these findings are exploratory and require multicenter external validation and comparison with existing triage systems.

articles.title: Incidence and Outcomes of Endotracheal Intubation in Patients Presenting With Acute Poisoning to the Emergency Department of a Tertiary Care Center in India: A Prospective Observational Study.

abstract.text: Objectives Endotracheal intubation is a critical airway intervention in severe acute poisoning, but its indications, timing, and outcomes are inconsistently described, and there are limited prospective data from Indian emergency departments (EDs). The primary objective of this prospective observational study was to determine the incidence of endotracheal intubation in adults (≥18 years) presenting with acute poisoning to the ED of AIIMS Rishikesh, Rishikesh, India. The secondary objectives were to (i) identify the clinical indications prompting intubation, (ii) enumerate indications stratified by poison type, (iii) record the timing and duration of intubation among intubated patients, and (iv) compare mortality between intubated and non-intubated patients. Methods A prospective observational study was conducted over 15 months (October 2024-December 2025) in the ED of AIIMS Rishikesh. Adult patients (≥18 years) presenting with acute poisoning were enrolled using consecutive sampling. Based on past departmental records, a sample size of 120 patients was estimated. Participants were followed for 28 days through hospital records or telephonic follow-up after discharge. Results This study included predominantly young adults with a slight male predominance (51.7%; 62/120), and the majority of poisoning cases were suicidal in nature. Pesticides, particularly organophosphorus (OP) compounds, were the most common poisoning agents, followed by household corrosives. Endotracheal intubation was required in 15.8% (19/120) of patients, with threatened airway due to a reduced Glasgow Coma Scale being the most common indication, followed by respiratory distress and excessive secretions. OP poisoning frequently required intubation due to multiple indications, while paraquat poisoning often required delayed intubation because of progressive respiratory failure. The overall mortality was 9.2% (11/120), with significantly higher mortality among intubated patients. Most deaths were attributed to OP compounds and paraquat poisoning. Male patients had higher rates of intubation and mortality. Conclusion This study found that 15.8% of adults with acute poisoning presenting to emergency required endotracheal intubation, with significantly higher mortality among intubated patients. OP compounds and paraquat were the leading causes of intubation and death. Most intubations were performed at presentation, emphasizing the importance of early airway assessment in the emergency while maintaining close monitoring for delayed respiratory deterioration, especially in paraquat poisoning.

articles.title: Diagnostic Performance of Corrected Carotid Flow Time for Assessing Fluid Responsiveness in Patients With Septic or Hypovolemic Shock: A Prospective Diagnostic Accuracy Study.

abstract.text: Background Predicting fluid responsiveness in patients with hemodynamic instability remains challenging. Corrected carotid flow time (CFTc) is a non-invasive bedside Doppler measure proposed to identify fluid responsiveness, but its reported performance is inconsistent. We evaluated baseline CFTc as a predictor of fluid responsiveness and assessed whether the post-bolus percentage change in CFTc corresponded with the echocardiographic change in stroke volume. Materials and methods This prospective diagnostic accuracy study included 80 adult patients presenting with new-onset shock of presumed septic and/or hypovolemic origin. All received a clinically indicated first bolus of 10 mL/kg Ringer's lactate. Stroke volume (SV) measured by transthoracic echocardiography and CFTc by carotid Doppler were obtained at baseline (T1) and 20 minutes after the bolus (T2). Responders were defined by a ≥15% rise in SV. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic performance of CFTc and its percentage change. Results An infective focus was identified in 61 patients (76.2%), with no source documented in 19 patients (23.8%). Thirty-two patients (40.0%) were responders. A baseline CFTc cut-off of ≤324.03 ms predicted responders with 71.9% sensitivity and 47.9% specificity (AUROC 0.563, 95% CI 0.435-0.691; p = 0.343). The percentage change in CFTc showed poor discrimination for fluid responsiveness (AUROC 0.568, 95% CI 0.436-0.700; p = 0.305) and corresponded weakly with the percentage change in SV (Spearman rho = 0.141; p = 0.213). Non-responders experienced recurrent hypotension more often and required earlier initiation of vasopressors. Conclusion In adults with new-onset shock, baseline CFTc did not usefully discriminate echocardiography-defined fluid responders, and the post-fluid change in CFTc showed weak correspondence with the change in stroke volume. CFTc should not be relied on alone to guide fluid resuscitation in this population.

articles.title: Reported Life-Threatening Polymorphic Ventricular Arrhythmia With Torsade-Like Morphology in a Patient With Gordon Syndrome and Hyperkalaemia.

abstract.text: Gordon's syndrome (pseudohypoaldosteronism type II) is a rare, inherited tubulopathy characterised by salt-sensitive hypertension, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis despite preserved renal function. Pathogenic variants affecting the with-no-lysine (K) signalling pathway include WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3. We report the case of a 37-year-old woman with genetically confirmed CUL3-related Gordon's syndrome who developed hyperkalaemia after a three-week interruption of bendroflumethiazide. During pre-hospital assessment, ambulance clinicians documented a self-terminating rhythm that they identified as torsade de pointes. The original recording cannot be retrieved; consequently, the rhythm classification, preceding QT interval, and possible alternative rhythm or artefact could not be independently assessed. Point-of-care venous blood gas potassium was 4.8 mmol/L, whereas formal laboratory potassium was 6.1 mmol/L. The sampling and processing information available did not establish the cause of this discrepancy. Subsequent echocardiography, computed tomography coronary angiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, and additional electrical assessment did not identify a definitive alternative substrate, although an intermittent electrical disorder could not be excluded. Following treatment of hyperkalaemia and multidisciplinary cardiology and electrophysiology review, an extravascular implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. Bendroflumethiazide was resumed, with subsequent improvement in potassium control. This case highlights the importance of uninterrupted thiazide therapy in Gordon's syndrome, assessment of discordant potassium measurements, and careful interpretation of a reported serious rhythm event when its original tracing is unavailable. The temporal association with hyperkalaemia does not establish that it caused torsade de pointes.

articles.title: Pediatric Transverse Myelitis: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Transverse myelitis (TM) is a rare inflammatory demyelinating disorder affecting the spinal cord. Although uncommon in children, approximately 20% of cases occur in the pediatric population. Children tend to have a better prognosis than adults. The etiology of TM is broad and includes, but is not limited to, viral and bacterial infections, association with other neurological disorders, and post-vaccination events. This case report describes a 16-year-old male patient who developed acute neurological deficits and urinary retention over several days. The patient was initially evaluated in the emergency department of a county hospital and was subsequently transferred to a tertiary pediatric hospital for further management. An extensive workup, including laboratory studies and imaging, revealed findings concerning for TM. The patient's symptoms did not resolve following a course of steroids. Therefore, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was added on the recommendation of the pediatric neuroimmunology team, resulting in resolution of his symptoms. He was eventually discharged home with full recovery of function and mobility. This case highlights a neurological presentation that can mimic other disorders and requires an extensive diagnostic workup for definitive diagnosis. Awareness of TM is important for early recognition and treatment, particularly in the emergency department, given the potential for rapid progression and significant morbidity.

articles.title: Catastrophic High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism With Recurrent Cardiac Arrest Successfully Treated With Rescue Mechanical Thrombectomy After Systemic Thrombolysis.

abstract.text: High-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) complicated by cardiac arrest carries an extremely high mortality, and the optimal rescue strategy after an inadequate response to systemic thrombolysis remains uncertain. We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with previous deep-vein thrombosis who was admitted after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and subsequently experienced three additional episodes of cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral central PE with severe right ventricular dilation and interventricular septal shift. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase was administered. Despite thrombolysis and vasopressor/inotropic support, persistent cardiogenic-obstructive shock, electrical instability, and severe right ventricular pressure overload remained. Approximately 4 h after thrombolysis, rescue mechanical aspiration thrombectomy was performed using the Indigo® Aspiration System with Lightning Flash™ (Penumbra, Inc., Alameda, CA, USA). Ultrasound-guided right common femoral venous access was obtained with an 18 F sheath, and aspiration was performed in both pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary artery pressure decreased from 34 mmHg before aspiration to 25 mmHg at the end of the procedure. The patient subsequently achieved progressive hemodynamic stabilization. After prolonged mechanical ventilation and tracheostomy, neurological recovery was favorable. At discharge, echocardiography showed normal biventricular systolic function. This case illustrates that prompt escalation to rescue mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in selected patients with high-risk PE when shock, electrical instability, and right ventricular overload persist despite systemic thrombolysis.

articles.title: Gastric residual volume in patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists: A comparative gastric ultrasound pilot study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release, promote satiety, and may slow gastric emptying. Introduced in 2005 for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity, these agents have prompted interest in assessing delayed gastric emptying as a potential biomarker to predict treatment response and to guide decisions regarding long-term therapy. Point-of-care gastric ultrasound (POCUS) offers a bedside method to assess gastric contents.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To compare gastric residual volume (GRV) on gastric ultrasound among patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs and nonusers and those with prior weight loss surgeries.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this comparative cross-sectional pilot study, gastric POCUS was done on patients with obesity who took GLP-1 RAs and other patients with obesity with no history of taking GLP-1 RAs prior to surgery in the supine and lateral decubitus positions. Antral cross-sectional area and GRV were measured using validated mathematical models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Patients receiving GLP-1 RAs demonstrated higher estimated GRV compared with nonusers. A higher proportion of GLP-1 RA users met ultrasound criteria for a full stomach.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Among patients with obesity, GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with enlargement of the gastric antrum, increased gastric volume, and greater residual gastric contents, leading to an elevated estimated risk of aspiration. This increased risk is primarily determined by gastric ultrasound findings rather than patient characteristics, comorbidities, or duration of treatment. Gastric ultrasound may support individualized perioperative decision-making regarding aspiration precautions.

articles.title: A comparative study between hyperbaric prilocaine 2% versus hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% for intrathecal anesthesia in cesarean section.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Bupivacaine has a variable block duration, while prilocaine provides a shorter, more predictable block but is less used in obstetrics. The goal is to compare the onset and duration of block induced by hyperbaric prilocaine 2% and hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% in intrathecal anesthesia for women undergoing elective cesarean sections (CS).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A prospective randomized and double-blind clinical trial included 144 individuals with uncomplicated pregnancies belonging to the American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status I or II. Patients were divided into two equal groups randomly: prilocaine group (Group A): received 60 mg hyperbaric prilocaine 2% (3 ml) intrathecally, and bupivacaine group (Group B): received 12.5 mg hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% (2.5 ml) intrathecally and 0.5 ml of normal saline. As 60 mg hyperbaric prilocaine 2% is equipotent to 12.5 mg of hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5%. Onset time and duration of sensory and motor block recorded.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mean arterial blood pressure was higher in Group A than in Group B at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min (P < 0.001), with no differences at baseline or 25-45 min. Intraoperative heart rate was substantially higher in Group B at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min, with comparable values at other time points. Visual analog scale (VAS) scores were higher in Group A at 1 h (P < 0.001) but substantially lower at 2 and 3 h (P < 0.001); VAS scores at 4 h were similar between groups.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Hyperbaric prilocaine 2% provides faster onset, shorter sensory and motor block duration, more stable hemodynamics and less maternal hypotension than hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% in CS, with similar neonatal outcomes and side effects.

articles.title: Improving Medication Management During SNF-to-Home Transitions.

abstract.text: Background: This case report focuses on an evolving approach to integrate pharmacists into the skilled nursing facility (SNF) discharge process to ensure appropriate medication use and improve post-discharge outcomes. This report describes the perspectives of 2 residents who were successfully enrolled in a larger pilot pharmacist-led service aimed at improving the discharge process from two University of Pittsburgh Medical Center's-affiliated SNFs to home using Rx Partners, LTC's At-Home medication management services. This was conducted over a 3-month period at two SNFs. Discussion & Conclusion: Thirty-nine residents were introduced to the service, 20 of whom were women, and 27 of whom were White, with a mean age of 74.1 years and an average SNF length of stay of 36 days. Two residents (5%) were ultimately enrolled. The primary outcome studied was resident-reported satisfaction with medication management 30 days after discharge. Secondary outcomes included completion of pharmacist-led education on high-risk medications, enrollment and continuation of pharmacy services, and medication-related rehospitalization or emergency department use within 30 days. Both residents enrolled reported excellent ratings across all domains of care on the satisfaction survey at the 30-day follow-up. One of the 2 residents had a 30-day rehospitalization not related to medication use. Despite design limitations, this pilot study reinforces the potential advantages of a medication discharge service before broader implementation to address a critical gap in care for older adults from a long-term care facility.

articles.title: Ambient Temperature and Heart Failure Hospitalizations in Older Adults in the US.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: The U-shaped association between ambient temperature and cardiovascular mortality is well established. However, limited knowledge exists about the association between ambient temperature and heart failure (HF) hospitalizations, particularly among older adults in the US. Understanding this association is essential to informing climate adaptation strategies and health policies.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To assess the association between daily ambient temperature exposure and HF hospitalization among Medicare beneficiaries both nationally and by climate region.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This time-stratified case-crossover study included older adults (aged ≥65 years) hospitalized for HF between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2022, based on Medicare claims data. Cases were defined as emergency department visits leading to HF hospitalization with up to 4 controls, or nonevent days, matched for the same patient on day of week, month, and year. The data analysis was performed between June 2025 and August 2026.

abstract.label: EXPOSURE
abstract.text: Daily mean ambient temperature derived from the Parameter-Elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model linked through residential zip code.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: The association between mean temperature exposure and HF hospitalization was estimated nationally and by 9 climate regions (Central, East North Central, Northeast, Northwest, South, Southeast, Southwest, West, West North Central) using conditional logit for distributed lag nonlinear models (reference, 75 °F). A 14-day lag was used for mean temperatures less than 75 °F and 0-day lag for mean temperatures greater than 75 °F.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1 517 756 HF hospitalizations from 996 312 patients (mean [SD] age, 78.0 [8.2] years, 60.3% female) were identified. Colder ambient temperatures were associated with increased HF hospitalizations nationally. At the regional fifth percentile temperature compared with 75 °F, the largest associations were observed in the West North Central (n = 17 286 [1.1%]; odds ratio [OR], 1.62; 95% CI, 1.25-2.11), West (n = 107 911 [7.1%]; OR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.28-1.53), Southwest (n = 30 536 [2.0%]; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.11-1.62), and Northwest (n = 33 353 [2.2%]; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.08-1.65) regions. Temperatures greater than 75 °F were not associated with increased HF hospitalization.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: This study found that among Medicare beneficiaries, colder ambient temperatures were associated with increased HF hospitalizations, whereas warmer temperatures were not. The U-shaped temperature-cardiovascular risk association described for cardiovascular mortality and other cardiovascular outcomes did not apply for HF hospitalizations among older adults in the US. These findings suggest that ongoing region-specific surveillance of heat- and cold-related HF hospitalization risk will be essential, particularly in areas with limited adaptive capacity.

articles.title: Effects of Piracetam and Hyperbaric Oxygen on Histopathological and Circulating Biochemical Responses Following Sciatic Nerve Crush Injury in Rats.

abstract.text: Background and Objectives: Peripheral nerve injury initiates a series of degenerative, inflammatory, and reparative responses. Piracetam and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) have been proposed as potential therapeutic interventions; however, their effects during the early phase following sciatic nerve injury require further investigation. This study evaluated early histopathological and circulating biochemical responses to piracetam and HBO in a rat model of sciatic nerve injury. Materials and Methods: Forty male Wistar Albino rats were randomly allocated to four groups following experimental sciatic nerve injury: an untreated injury control group (Group K), a hyperbaric oxygen therapy group (Group HBO), an intraperitoneal piracetam group (Group P), and a combined hyperbaric oxygen plus piracetam group (Group HBO + P). After 14 days, the rats were euthanised, and sciatic nerve tissues and blood samples were collected for histopathological and biochemical analyses. Results: No statistically significant differences were observed among the four groups with respect to axonal continuity, capillary formation, or myelin sheath regeneration. Fibroblast density was increased in Group P compared with Group K (p = 0.025), while no significant differences were detected among the remaining groups. Inflammatory cell counts were higher in Group P than in Group K (p = 0.037) and elevated in Group HBO + P compared with Group K (p = 0.014). Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF-1α) expression was highest in Group K. Additionally, neuron-specific enolase levels were significantly increased in Group P compared with Group K (p = 0.006). Conclusions: Under the conditions of this 14-day experimental study, piracetam and HBO were associated with differences in selected circulating biochemical parameters but did not produce statistically significant improvements in the assessed histopathological indices. The findings were interpreted as early responses to treatment, and longer follow-up studies are needed to determine whether these changes translate into sustained axonal regeneration or functional recovery.

articles.title: The Shapla Chattar atrocity (2013) in Bangladesh: A case of state-perpetrated human rights violations.
articles.journal_full: Torture : quarterly journal on rehabilitation of torture victims and prevention of torture

abstract.text: Background The 2013 Shapla Chattar event in Dhaka remains one of the most underreported state-perpetrated atrocities in South Asia; a peaceful protest was violently dispersed by state forces, resulting in mass casualties. For over a decade, media suppression, political repression, and the authoritarian climate silenced public discourse and academic inquiry. Following the regime's collapse in August 2024, new evidence has emerged, warranting a fresh investigation from a human rights perspective. Methods This study was conducted based on secondary sources, including fact-finding reports from human rights organization including Odhikar and Human Rights Watch, government data, and media archives. It evaluates the Shapla incident within the framework of international human rights law and the criteria for crimes against humanity. Results An estimated 93 to over 300 individuals were killed during the 5-6 May 2013 Shapla Chattar operation. Approximately 7,500 security personnel were deployed, and over 150,000 rounds of live ammunition were used. The demographic analysis of the 61 confirmed death cases shows that 80% of victims came from non-madrasa backgrounds. The use of excessive force, media blackout, and suppression of civil society point to a state-orchestrated assault. The Shapla atrocity satisfies all key criteria for crimes against humanity: it was widespread, systematic, targeted civilians, and was conducted with full knowledge of its consequences. Conclusion This study assessed the Shapla Chattar atrocity as a case of state-sanctioned violence, qualifying as a crime against humanity. It underscores the urgent need for judicial accountability and transparent investigation through the reformed International Crimes Tribunal.

articles.title: The Unusual Outbreak of Sepsis in a Cancer Hospital Caused by Intrinsically Contaminated Heparin Injection Vials.
articles.journal_full: Asian Pacific journal of cancer prevention : APJCP

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The outbreaks in oncology settings result in dreaded complications, especially in cancer patients who are already immunocompromised. Here, we describe the identification and response to an unusual hospital-acquired outbreak of bloodstream infections (BSIs) in cancer patients due to intrinsic contamination of a heparin injection vial with New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase (blaNDM)-positive Klebsiella pneumoniae.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An increased cluster of sepsis cases in cancer patients with chemoports was noted in the medical oncology department of a cancer center in North India in July 2024. These case clusters were identified by reviewing microbiological reports, and blood cultures were tested by automated identification and susceptibility testing, the Carba-R test, and molecular testing. Outbreak investigations were performed; causality assessment was also done. The clinical and demographic details of the case patients, along with other relevant histories, were collected from electronic medical records. Environmental samples were collected from high-touch surfaces, intravenous medications, saline, and heparin.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A cluster of 10 sepsis cases with culture-confirmed bloodstream infections (BSIs) was identified in the medical oncology department. Out of the 10 patients, 5 (50%) were admitted to the ward after visiting the central venous access device (CVAD) clinic, and 5 (50%) presented to the emergency department after recent chemotherapy. All cases had Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from blood cultures, which alerted the oncology team to a possible outbreak. All isolates were multidrug-resistant strains sensitive to ceftazidime-avibactam and tigecycline. The multidrug resistance gene detected in all isolates was blaNDM. The heparin injection vial was found to be the primary cause and single source of the outbreak. All isolates from heparin and patients' clinical samples were confirmed by molecular typing using Enterobacterial Repetitive Intergenic Consensus Polymerase Chain Reaction (ERIC-PCR). Interestingly, the contamination was found to be intrinsic to a new batch of heparin manufactured by the company.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This study highlights the importance of an infection surveillance system as part of pharmacovigilance, which helped detect the source of infection within a few days of the outbreak alert. Implementing standardized healthcare-associated infection (HAI) surveillance in a low-resource setting detected an ongoing heparin-associated outbreak. The outbreak investigation and the use of a multimodal approach reduced incident cases and informed changes in infection prevention and control (IPC) practices. The regulatory authorities (CDSCO and the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission) were also notified, which helped them enforce strict quality control and regulatory oversight in drug manufacturing.

articles.title: CT-Referenced Diagnostic Performance and Complementary Error Patterns of Artificial Intelligence Versus a Single Emergency Physician in Chest Radiograph Interpretation: A Retrospective Paired Diagnostic Accuracy Study.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support chest radiograph interpretation, but its clinical value depends not only on stand-alone accuracy but also on whether its errors differ from those of clinicians. We evaluated CT-referenced, target-specific diagnostic performance and complementary error patterns of a commercial chest radiograph AI system and a single emergency physician. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center, paired diagnostic accuracy study, 920 consecutive adults who underwent posteroanterior chest radiography and thoracic computed tomography (CT) within 4 h during the same emergency department encounter were included. A commercial AI system (hChestXR version 1) and a single blinded emergency physician independently assessed eight prespecified thoracic findings using CT as the reference standard. Paired differences were estimated with 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples and tested with exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Exact-target complementarity and simulated same-target OR/AND rules were secondary exploratory analyses. Results: Across 7360 patient-target assessments, including 1232 CT-positive findings, AI had significantly greater Holm-adjusted sensitivity for pneumothorax (90.8% vs. 50.8%), nodule/mass (63.3% vs. 32.7%), and rib fracture (77.2% vs. 46.5%). AI-only detections were most frequent for pneumothorax (47.7%), nodule/mass (44.9%), and rib fracture (43.6%), whereas physician-only detections were most frequent for atelectasis (24.8%), pulmonary edema (21.0%), and lung opacity (19.7%). In exploratory pooled analyses, sensitivity was 73.0% for AI and 62.0% for the physician. Exploratory simulated same-target OR/AND analyses demonstrated a sensitivity-specificity trade-off across pooled patient-target assessments but did not represent observed AI-assisted clinical performance. Conclusions: The AI system and the single emergency-physician reader in the study showed target-dependent, partly non-overlapping error patterns in this CT-selected emergency cohort. The findings support prospective multireader evaluation of AI as a second-reader tool but do not establish benefit from real-time AI-assisted interpretation.

articles.title: Association of Initial Peripheral Venous pO2 With 48-Hour Clinical Deterioration in Emergency Department Patients Undergoing Venous Blood Gas Testing.
articles.journal_full: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Peripheral venous pO2 is routinely reported with venous blood gas (VBG) results despite uncertainty regarding its prognostic significance. We evaluated whether initial peripheral venous pO2 was associated with 48-h clinical deterioration and provided prognostic information beyond age and lactate.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted an ambispective observational cohort study of adults undergoing VBG testing at a single urban academic emergency department, with prospective enrollment and index-data collection and retrospective ascertainment of 48-h outcomes. The primary outcome was a composite of ICU admission, death, vasopressor use, or positive-pressure ventilation within 48 h. The primary analysis modeled venous pO2 continuously and used multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age and lactate. Incremental performance was evaluated exploratorily by comparing an age-and-lactate model with a model additionally containing venous pO2.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 973 patients, 103 (10.6%) experienced the composite outcome. Median venous pO2 was 33 mmHg (IQR 25-44). Venous pO2 was not associated with clinical deterioration after adjustment for age and lactate (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.054 per 10-mmHg increase; 95% CI 0.957-1.161; p = 0.289). The AUROC was 0.649 for the age-and-lactate model and 0.654 after adding venous pO2 (ΔAUROC 0.005; DeLong p = 0.390).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this single-center cohort of adult ED patients undergoing VBG testing, no association was observed between peripheral venous pO2 and 48-h clinical deterioration. Adding venous pO2 did not improve apparent prognostic performance beyond age and lactate. We cannot exclude smaller associations or potential utility in selected disease-specific populations. Confirmation in larger multicenter cohorts using consecutive enrollment and external validation is needed.

articles.title: Case 355.

abstract.text: An 8-year-old girl presented to the pediatrician with headaches that she had been experiencing for the last 2-3 years but that had become intolerable in the previous 8 days. The headaches were described by the patient as not having any lateralization and mainly involving the frontal and occipital regions. The headaches were rated by the patient as being an eight out of 10 in terms of pain, which prevented her from sleeping. Analgesic therapy proved to be ineffective. The patient had no photophobia or phonophobia but had increased fatigue alongside developing nausea without vomiting. The patient did not have any dysphagia, ataxia, vertigo, or elocution issues. Previous MRI performed in a provincial hospital showed a mass in the posterior fossa that was displacing the brainstem. However, being unable to get an appointment to see a neurosurgeon in a timely manner, the patient presented to the emergency department of our university hospital due to worsening symptoms. In order to exclude an intracranial origin of the symptoms, brain MRI with contrast enhancement was performed (Figure).

articles.title: Case 351: Thalamic Dementia Secondary to Dural Arteriovenous Fistula.

abstract.text: A 76-year-old man with a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and dilated cardiomyopathy developed new symptoms of confusion, repeated falls, and urinary incontinence over the course of 3-4 months, which worsened over a 2-week period, leading to presentation at the emergency room. His partner reported that before this, he had no memory or movement disorders, but now he was experiencing memory lapses, such as forgetting his mother's recent death, and functional cognitive problems, including an inability to remember how to perform tasks that were previously simple for him, such as dosing his insulin with meals. At presentation, the patient was awake and alert, oriented to his name and location but not to the date. Full neurologic examinations, including of the motor and sensory systems and cranial nerves, were normal. There were no signs of meningism, no fever or leukocytosis, and no history of recent travel. Serum electrolyte panel and thiamine levels were normal, and he had no history of alcohol or drug abuse. Initial evaluation included noncontrast CT of the head, the results of which prompted multiphasic CT angiography of the head including parenchymal phase imaging and admission for observation and monitoring with serial noncontrast CT of the head. The patient's symptoms worsened during his hospital stay. He also developed facial twitching, increased drowsiness, and seizure episodes. He was therefore evaluated with noncontrast MRI of the brain and then digital subtraction angiography with external carotid artery and internal carotid artery contrast agent injections.

articles.title: Glaucoma management in adults: an update.

abstract.text: Glaucoma is a group of progressive optic neuropathies that cause optic nerve damage and visual field defects. It is typically asymptomatic until irreversible vision loss has occurred. Early detection relies on regular comprehensive eye examinations, with targeted case finding particularly important for people at increased risk. Lowering intraocular pressure is the only proven strategy to slow disease progression, and treatment should be individualised. Topical prostaglandin analogues (eye drops) are commonly used as first-line medical therapy, with once-daily dosing associated with improved adherence. Topical beta blockers may be added if the target intraocular pressure is not achieved or disease progression occurs. Patient adherence, eye drop technique and adverse effects should be reviewed regularly. Selective laser trabeculoplasty (a laser treatment that helps fluid drain out of the eye, thereby lowering intraocular pressure) is an effective first-line alternative to eye drops. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist or emergency department is required for a suspected acute angle-closure attack. Symptoms include severe eye pain, headache, blurred vision, halos around lights, nausea and vomiting.

articles.title: Normal on the Inside: A Case of Recurrent Abdominal Pain, Equivocal CT Appendicitis, and Histologically Normal Appendix in an Adolescent With Chronic Cannabis Use.

abstract.text: Cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS) and cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) are diagnoses of exclusion, and both can anchor clinical thinking in ways that delay recognition of organic pathology. We describe an 18-year-old male patient who attended the emergency department repeatedly between December 2025 and June 2026 with severe abdominal pain and vomiting, against a background of chronic cannabis use. Working diagnoses of CHS and CVS were recorded across multiple admissions. During his March 2026 admission, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis (CTAP) showed a mildly thickened appendix with small-volume pelvic free fluid, reported as mild acute appendicitis. Conservative management was commenced but failed to resolve symptoms. Laparoscopic appendicectomy was performed. Intraoperatively, the appendix appeared mildly dilated and injected. Histopathological analysis returned a normal appendix vermiformis with no inflammation, dysplasia, or malignancy. The patient was discharged with resolution of his acute symptoms but re-presented within weeks with identical complaints. At the time of writing, oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and familial Mediterranean fever testing are pending. Faecal calprotectin was 159 microg/g. When CT findings, operative appearances, and histology point in different directions, the underlying diagnosis is not resolved by surgery; it has to be reconsidered from the beginning.

articles.title: Pilot Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Simulation-Based Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Teaching for Final-Year Medical Students.

abstract.text: Background Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is increasingly used within emergency and acute care, yet undergraduate exposure to focused bedside echocardiography remains variable. Simulation may provide an opportunity for students to develop practical ultrasound skills while integrating findings into clinical assessment and decision-making. This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of a simulation-based bedside echocardiography teaching programme for final-year medical students and explored differences in confidence and knowledge between pre- and post-session respondents. Methodology A mixed-methods educational evaluation was undertaken with final-year medical students during their Preparation for Practice placement at a UK teaching hospital. The two-hour programme combined teaching on ultrasound principles and standard echocardiographic views with supervised image acquisition and simulation-based peri-arrest scenarios involving cardiac arrest, massive pulmonary embolism and pericardial tamponade. Thirty students were invited and 10 attended. Anonymous questionnaires assessed self-reported confidence and knowledge immediately before and after the session, and a five-question multiple-choice quiz objectively assessed knowledge. We also collected qualitative free-text feedback post-session. Confidence reflected participants' own perceived confidence across three domains of bedside echocardiography and was not assessed externally or used as a measure of objective competence. As questionnaires were anonymous, pre- and post-session responses were unpaired. Self-reported confidence scores were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Results Nine students completed the pre-session questionnaire, and seven completed the post-session questionnaire. Mean confidence scores were higher among post-session respondents (9.86/15; median, 10) than among pre-session respondents (3.67/15; median, 4), with a statistically significant difference between groups (U = 0.0, P < 0.001). Mean knowledge scores were also higher among post-session respondents (4.71/5 vs. 4.22/5), although baseline scores were already high. Qualitative feedback was positive, with students particularly valuing the clinical relevance of the teaching and the integration of echocardiography into realistic emergency scenarios. Participants identified additional supervised scanning opportunities as an area for future development. Conclusions This preliminary evaluation suggests that a short, simulation-based bedside echocardiography teaching programme is feasible to deliver within an undergraduate prep-for-practice placement and acceptable to participating final-year medical students. Higher confidence and knowledge scores were observed among post-session respondents; however, the small sample size and unpaired questionnaire design prevent conclusions regarding individual learner improvement or intervention efficacy. Larger studies incorporating paired responses, objective assessment of ultrasound competence and longitudinal follow-up are required to evaluate the effectiveness and retention of this educational approach.

articles.title: Accuracy of Ultrasound for Fatty Liver Assessment.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is increasingly prevalent, particularly among individuals with obesity and Type 2 diabetes. Early identification of MASLD is critical, yet access to formal imaging is often limited in primary care. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) with the Ultrasound Fatty Liver Index (US-FLI), a semi-quantitative scoring tool, has demonstrated strong diagnostic accuracy but remains underutilized and is rarely included in standard POCUS training. This pilot study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of US-FLI when performed by a novice POCUS user to explore its potential role as a screening tool for MASLD.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In a prospective convenience cohort (n = 65), US-FLI scores from a novice POCUS user were compared to radiologist-interpreted abdominal imaging. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value (NPV), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve were calculated.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Fifteen patients (23%) had confirmed fatty liver disease on standard imaging. The novice user achieved a sensitivity of 0.87, specificity of 0.32, positive predictive value of 0.28, and NPV of 0.89. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54-0.67). Raising the US-FLI threshold improved specificity but lowered sensitivity: ≥3 balanced sensitivity (0.73) and specificity (0.62), whereas ≥5 maximized specificity (0.96) at the expense of reduced sensitivity (0.27).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: POCUS using US-FLI may serve as a rapid, noninvasive screening approach with high sensitivity and NPV, suggesting potential utility for ruling out MASLD in primary care settings. Larger studies in more diverse patient populations are needed to further validate these findings.

articles.title: Pediatric Anaphylaxis in a Tertiary Pediatric Emergency Department: Observation Duration and Biphasic Reactions.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Biphasic reactions are an important consideration during post-treatment observation of children with anaphylaxis; however, real-world pediatric data on observation practices and the timing of these reactions remain limited. This study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics, management practices, observation duration, and occurrence of biphasic reactions among children presenting with anaphylaxis to a tertiary pediatric emergency department (PED). Methods: This single-center retrospective observational study included children aged 0-18 years who presented with anaphylaxis to a tertiary PED between January 2014 and December 2024. Potential cases identified through ICD-10 codes and PED intramuscular adrenaline administration records were reviewed to confirm the diagnosis according to established criteria. Demographic and clinical characteristics, suspected triggers, treatments, observation duration, and biphasic reactions were evaluated. Results: Seventy anaphylaxis episodes in 68 patients were analyzed. The median age was 93.5 months (IQR, 50-156). Food (32.9%) and insect stings (28.6%) were the most common suspected triggers, followed by drug/vaccine-related triggers (18.6%) and allergen immunotherapy (11.4%). Adrenaline was administered in 94.3% of episodes, and intravenous fluid therapy in 50.0%. Central nervous system involvement and age-adjusted hypotension were more frequent among episodes receiving intravenous fluid therapy (p = 0.004 and p < 0.001, respectively). The median PED observation duration was 5.5 h (IQR, 2-8). Biphasic reactions occurred in three episodes (4.3%), all within three hours after initial symptom resolution. Conclusions: In this tertiary PED cohort, adrenaline administration was frequent, and biphasic reactions were uncommon and occurred during the early observation period. Given the small number of biphasic reactions, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive and are insufficient to determine the optimal observation duration.

articles.title: Association of a Triage-Based Emergency Alarm System with Waiting Times and Clinical Outcomes in a Pediatric Emergency Department.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Pediatric emergency departments (PEDs) experience abrupt fluctuations in patient volume that can prolong waiting times and compromise timely care for critically ill children. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether implementation of a triage-based emergency alarm was associated with time to electronic documentation of initial physician evaluation and clinical outcomes during the 2022 COVID-19 Omicron wave in Taiwan. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective before-and-after observational study of PED visits from 1 April to 31 October 2022. The emergency flashing-light alarm was implemented on 1 August 2022 to alert physicians to triage level 1 patients requiring immediate evaluation. Propensity scores were estimated using age group (<5 versus 5-17 years), sex, and availability of additional physician staffing support; 1:1 matching yielded 7467 pairs. The matched-pair structure was retained in bootstrap confidence intervals and permutation tests for waiting-time comparisons. Results: The analysis included 19,624 visits (10,814 before and 8810 after implementation). In the matched cohort, median waiting time among triage level 1 visits was 11.0 min (IQR, 6.8-17.2) before and 8.2 min (IQR, 5.7-12.5) after implementation; the post-minus-pre difference between subgroup medians was -2.82 min (95% CI, -3.48 to -1.80; p < 0.001). Among triage level 2 visits, medians were 12.4 and 11.8 min, respectively (p = 0.088). Hospital admission and PICU admission or planned admission were more frequent after implementation. Conclusions: The alarm was associated with a shorter median time to documented initial physician evaluation among triage level 1 visits. No statistically significant difference was detected for triage level 2 waiting time in the matched-pair analysis. Residual differences in triage mix and secular trends preclude causal inference.

articles.title: GFAP Use in Emergency Medicine-A Narrative Review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Traditional clinical assessments for neurological emergencies, such as the Glasgow Coma Scale, are often subjective and may be confounded by factors like intoxication or sedation. While computed tomography (CT) remains the diagnostic standard, it may lack sensitivity for mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) and pose a risk of radiation exposure. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an intermediate filament protein primarily produced by astrocytes in the central nervous system (CNS), has been shown to be a potential objective marker of neuronal distress, even when macrostructural imaging may appear normal.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: This narrative review synthesizes recent evidence on the molecular biology and pathophysiology of GFAP in acute CNS injury. It evaluates GFAP's clinical applications across major neurological emergencies-including TBI, stroke, and sepsis-while comparing its performance to other major biomarkers and identifying the technological and operational hurdles for routine emergency department (ED) implementation.

abstract.label: EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS
abstract.text: Following CNS insult, astrocytes undergo reactive astrogliosis, leading to GFAP upregulation and proteolytic cleavage into breakdown products (GFAP-BDP) that provide a unique signature of structural disruption. GFAP exhibits favorable kinetics in the circulation, with a rise within one hour and a peak at approximately 20 h. In TBI, GFAP is FDA-cleared for CT decision-making and demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.88-0.89) within the first 30-60 min of injury. Some studies also support its role in distinguishing intracerebral hemorrhage from ischemic stroke according to distinct temporal release patterns and serve as a potential biological marker of CNS involvement in sepsis-associated encephalopathy; though its use is still investigational and requires further validation. Compared with other biomarkers such as S100B, UCH-L1, NSE, and tau, GFAP offers greater CNS specificity and more reliable signals for identifying structural lesions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
