This review highlights key operational characteristics, identifies current challenges, and provides evidence-based insights to inform future research, policy development, and technological innovation aimed at improving PSAP performance and public safety outcomes globally.

articles.title: Penetrating neck injury with concealed glass foreign body transfixing the skull base: a case report of a diagnostic trap.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Penetrating neck injuries (PNIs) caused by glass carry high mortality due to occult deep penetration, transparency of foreign bodies, and bleeding‑induced obscuration. External absence of visible glass often misleads clinicians to underestimate injury severity and omit preoperative imaging, creating a life‑threatening diagnostic trap. This case uniquely clarifies that prolonged preoperative hypotension (SBP < 60 mmHg for ≥ 2 h), rather than vascular repair strategy, is the decisive factor for irreversible cerebral injury.

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 34‑year‑old man fell 1.9 meters onto broken glass, sustaining a 13.0 cm left posterior neck penetrating wound with no externally visible glass. Despite pre‑transfer transfusion, he arrived in hemorrhagic shock (BP 52/32 mmHg, Hb 51 g/L, lactate 8.1 mmol/L), with preoperative hypotension (SBP <60 mmHg) lasting more than 2.5 hours before hemostasis. Non‑contrast CT identified a 10.5 cm × 3.0 cm hyperdense glass fragment transfixing the skull base to the maxillary sinus with comminuted fractures. CT angiography showed complete non‑opacification of the left internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and sigmoid sinus. Emergency surgery removed the foreign body and ligated the lacerated internal carotid artery to achieve hemostasis. Postoperatively, the patient remained comatose; imaging confirmed diffuse cerebral ischemia and herniation. He died after family refusal of further intervention.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In PNIs, absence of visible glass externally does not rule out deep transfixing injury. Early non‑contrast CT is mandatory to avoid diagnostic errors. In patients with major cervical vascular disruption and hemorrhagic shock, prolonged preoperative hypotension (SBP <60 mmHg ≥2 hours) predicts irreversible global cerebral ischemia unresponsive to successful hemostasis. Emergency physicians must prioritize early CT and expedite definitive hemorrhage control.

abstract.label: CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER
abstract.text: Clinical trial number: not applicable.

articles.title: Trauma scoring systems for evaluating trauma center triage criteria in older adults: a retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Standardized trauma assessment is essential for early clinical decision-making; however, it remains challenging in older adults because age-related physiological changes may obscure injury severity. Accurate triage is critical to ensure timely access to trauma centers (TCs). While triage decisions must rely on immediately available clinical findings, advanced trauma scoring systems are typically based on diagnostic data obtained later in the course of care. Although these tools are not suitable for real-time triage, they are established predictors of mortality and may provide an objective basis for evaluating TC qualification criteria. Because current national TC qualification criteria do not adequately account for age-specific factors, they may contribute to undertriage in older patients. This study aimed to retrospectively identify the trauma scoring system most suitable for evaluating TC qualification criteria in geriatric trauma patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients admitted to the emergency department of a single clinical hospital with a TC between 2017 and 2020. Among 155,320 ED admissions, 6,541 trauma patients aged ≥ 65 years were identified. Injury severity and physiological status were assessed using the coded Revised Trauma Score (RTSc), Injury Severity Score (ISS), and Trauma and Injury Severity Score (TRISS). A predefined subgroup of patients meeting national TC qualification criteria (TC group 65+) was analyzed separately. Predictive performance for in-hospital mortality was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: TRISS showed the highest discrimination for in-hospital mortality (AUC 0.888), followed by ISS (0.867) and RTSc (0.687). In the TC group 65+, the mean TRISS-predicted survival probability was 34.58%, whereas observed in-hospital survival was 48.72%. The estimated undertriage rate was 73.47%, suggesting that current national TC qualification criteria may perform inadequately in older trauma patients.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Current national TC qualification criteria may contribute to undertriage among older patients, potentially delaying access to advanced trauma care. Among the evaluated scoring systems, TRISS demonstrated the highest discriminatory performance for in-hospital mortality and appears to be the most suitable retrospective reference standard for assessing TC qualification criteria in geriatric trauma patients.

articles.title: Low-volume body bag cooling for severe exertional heat stroke in the emergency department: a case report.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Exertional heat stroke (EHS) is a life-threatening emergency in which delayed or inadequate cooling substantially increases the risk of death and permanent neurological injury. Core temperature reduction to below 39 °C within 30 min is the therapeutic target, and cold-water immersion achieves the fastest cooling rates (0.15-0.35 °C/min) but is frequently unavailable in emergency departments (ED) due to equipment and space limitations. Body bag-based tarp-assisted cooling with oscillation (TACO) has been proposed as an alternative using universally available materials; however, clinical evidence supporting its emergency department use remains limited.

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 57-year-old immunocompromised male construction worker (acute myeloid leukemia, status post umbilical cord blood transplantation, maintained on prednisolone and tacrolimus) presented with EHS following 90 min of outdoor labor in ambient conditions of 36 °C and 65% relative humidity. On ED arrival, rectal temperature was 42.0 °C, Glasgow Coma Scale score was 4, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and heart rate was 183 beats/minute. Body bag-based TACO was initiated immediately upon arrival using 15 L of tap water and 15 kg of ice. Endotracheal intubation for airway protection was performed concurrently, demonstrating patient accessibility during cooling. Target temperature (rectal temperature < 39 °C) was achieved in 39 min at a cooling rate of 0.085 °C/min. Glasgow Coma Scale score improved to 14 within 7.5 h of admission. The hospital course was complicated by bacteremia requiring prolonged antimicrobial therapy. The patient was discharged ambulatory on hospital day 42 without neurological sequelae.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Body bag-based TACO required substantially less water (15 L) than the water/ice volumes reported in TACO studies (114-151 L) using materials available in any ED. Although the cooling rate achieved (0.085 °C/min) fell below published benchmarks, the patient achieved complete neurological recovery, suggesting that immediate initiation of cooling may help offset a suboptimal rate. While a single case cannot establish equivalence to cold-water immersion, body bag-based TACO offers a practical, low-cost option for initiating cooling when standard infrastructure is unavailable, and merits further comparative evaluation.

articles.title: Heat alerts and emergency department utilization: evidence from San Diego County, California.
articles.journal_full: Environmental health : a global access science source

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Extreme heat poses a significant risk to human health, underscoring the importance of early warning systems in mitigating such impacts. However, evidence regarding their effectiveness remains limited, particularly for emergency department (ED) visits. This study aimed to assess the associations between heat advisory and warning issuance and performance and ED visits in San Diego County, California, and to further examine differences by cause and demographic characteristics.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Daily adult ED visit data for the warm season (May-October) were linked to historical heat alerts and high-resolution gridded temperature data. ED visits were modeled using Poisson regression with ZIP code fixed effects, controlling for temperature, seasonality, and temporal factors. Main analyses evaluated associations between alert issuance and ED visits across 2012-2023, while secondary analyses examined differences by alert performance, classified as true positive, false positive, false negative, or true negative based on temperature-based criteria in effect during 2012-2016.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Heat advisories were associated with a 2.1% increase in all-cause ED visits (95% CI: 0.4, 3.9), as well as larger increases in neurological (13.5%; 95% CI: 1.3, 27.1) and heat-related visits (21.8%; 95% CI: 1.6, 46.1), while warnings were exclusively associated with increased heat-related ED visits (35.8%; 95% CI: 3.5, 78.3). In subgroup analyses, associations with all-cause ED visits were more pronounced among females and older adults, with warnings associated with a 12.7% increase among those aged 65 years and older (95% CI: 6.8, 18.8). During 2012-2016, heat alerts exhibited high specificity but limited sensitivity, and their performance had minimal overall influence on ED visits. Results were robust across alternative model specifications.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Heat advisories and warnings were associated with limited changes in ED utilization, primarily confined to heat-related conditions and to females and older adults.

articles.title: Bowel ischemia following extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR): case reports and narrative review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) is a life-saving strategy for refractory cardiac arrest (CA), but the mortality rate is still high. Bowel ischemia is associated with the clinical outcomes, and few studies on bowel ischemia following ECPR have been reported.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We reported 2 cases of bowel ischemia following ECPR. And we searched literature to describe the incidence, clinical features, and outcomes of bowel ischemia following ECPR. Demographic features, risk factors, clinical features, diagnostic methods, treatment and outcome were analyzed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We described 2 patients developed bowel ischemia with recurred hematochezia at different phases post ECPR, conservative treatments were not effective, one patient received colectomy after extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) weaning and recovered, and the other died without surgery. Our literature search found 3 publications. Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia(NOMI) was more common for bowel ischemia following ECPR, and the incidence of NOMI in ECPR patients seemed higher than that in conventional CPR patients. Postmortem findings demonstrated signs of bowel ischemia within hours of ECPR. The incidence of bowel ischemia following ECPR could not be identified due to the variability among the studies.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Bowel ischemia may initiate early post ECPR, or occur insidiously during the therapeutic process, thus clinicians should have a high suspicion and low threshold for CT scan and endoscopy. Surgical timing for advanced bowel ischemia should be individualized.

articles.title: Healthcare and cost burdens associated with potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults: a matched cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The adverse effects of potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) use in older adults are one of major public health burdens. This study aimed to examine the association between PIM use and healthcare utilizations and costs among older adults.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We used the Korean National Health Insurance Service-Elderly Cohort Database in 2015-2018 with matched cohort design. A propensity score derived from 16 variables, including age, sex, index year, Charlson Comorbidity Index scores, income decile, residential status, nine main comorbidities and number of comedication, was used for 1:1 matching. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to compare the risk of hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits 1 year after the index date between PIM users and non-users. In addition, hospitalization- and ED visit related costs were evaluated using a two part model consisting of logistic regression and generalized linear model with logit link.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 3,896 older adults aged ≥ 65 years at index date were included, comprising 1,948 PIM users and 1,948 matched non-users. All the matching variables were well balanced with absolute Standardized Mean Difference (aSMD) < 0.1. Females were 52.77% in non-users and 54.65% in users. The mean age was 73.26 (sd: 5.97) in non-users and 73.14 (sd: 5.98) in users. The results indicated that PIM users were associated with higher risk of hospitalization than non-users (adjusted HR [aHR]: 2.18, 95% CI: 1.81-2.63) and were more likely to visit the ED (aHR: 3.08, 95% CI: 2.01-4.72). Furthermore, the total healthcare costs for PIM users were 40% higher among PIM users than non-users (adjusted Cost Ratio [aCR]: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.35-1.54). Among PIM users, increasing numbers of PIMs were associated with higher total healthcare costs, as well as higher hospitalization- and outpatient-related costs.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: PIM use was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization and ED visits, as well as higher healthcare costs. These findings highlight the importance of regular medication review and optimization of prescribing in older adults. However, PIM use should be considered within the broader context of multimorbidity and frailty, rather than as an isolated risk factor, when developing strategies to improve health outcomes in this population.

articles.title: WSES-PSOGI-SICO evidence-infomed guidelines on surgical emergencies in patients with peritoneal surface malignancies: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and structured expert consensus.
articles.journal_full: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Peritoneal surface malignancies (PSM) are primary or secondary neoplastic deposits involving the peritoneum and are commonly associated with colorectal, gastric, appendiceal, gynecological, pancreaticobiliary, and other intra-abdominal or extra-abdominal cancers. Malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) is one of the most frequent and clinically consequential emergency presentations in this population, yet diagnostic and therapeutic pathways remain heterogeneous. We aimed to develop evidence-informed recommendations for emergency management of MBO in patients with PSM by integrating a systematic review, meta-analysis and a structured international expert consensus process.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This systematic review, meta-analysis, and Delphi consensus followed PRISMA, Cochrane, and relevant MOOSE reporting principles. PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to June 2025 (English language). Five predefined PICO/PIRT questions addressed: (1) the diagnostic role of CT, plain abdominal X-ray, or Gastrografin-enhanced X-ray in PSM-related MBO; (2) nonoperative medical management versus surgical or endoscopic therapy; (3) surgical versus endoscopic treatment after failure of nonoperative management; (4) bowel resection versus stoma or bypass in surgical candidates; and (5) endoscopic stenting versus endoscopic ultrasound-guided bypass with lumen-apposing metal stents in endoscopic candidates. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently and in duplicate. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for comparative non-randomized studies and MINORS for non-comparative studies; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses (REML) produced odds ratios (OR), mean differences (MD), pooled means, or pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CI); heterogeneity was summarized using I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals. Evidence profiles informed statements voted on by the WSES-PSOGI-SICO expert panel during the 2025 WSES Congress.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: No comparative diagnostic study evaluated abdominal X-ray or Gastrografin-enhanced X-ray in PSM-related MBO; two small retrospective CT-based series supported contrast-enhanced CT for mapping obstruction and excluding urgent complications, but no diagnostic meta-analysis was possible. For medical versus procedural treatment, medical management was associated with lower morbidity (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07-0.39) and shorter length of stay (MD - 9.48 days, 95% CI - 12.65 to -6.32), while success, mortality, and overall survival remained inconclusive. For surgery versus endoscopy, surgery showed higher clinical success (OR 2.57, 95% CI 1.47-4.50), whereas endoscopy shortened hospital stay (MD 3.35 days, 95% CI 1.46-5.23); mortality did not differ (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.70-1.49). Among surgical options, resection showed a signal toward higher perioperative mortality than bypass or ostomy (OR 3.55, 95% CI 1.45-8.68). Endoscopic stenting showed a pooled clinical success rate of 0.71 (95% CI 0.62-0.79), whereas evidence on LAMS was limited to one retrospective study. All guideline statements reached 100% agreement among voting participants.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Despite the low certainty of available evidence, integration of systematic review findings with expert consensus provides a structured international framework to support decision-making in emergency presentations of PSM-related MBO. These consensus-based recommendations are intended to assist clinicians in harmonizing care across peripheral and referral hospitals, while emphasizing individualized multidisciplinary judgement and the need for future higher-quality evidence.

articles.title: "I really like the idea of a partnership": A qualitative exploration of patients' perspectives on pharmacist and physiotherapist collaboration for musculoskeletal care.
articles.journal_full: Canadian pharmacists journal : CPJ = Revue des pharmaciens du Canada : RPC

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Acute musculoskeletal (MSK) injuries are one of the most common reasons for health care visits, yet many patients face barriers to timely primary care access. This study explored patients' perspectives on pharmacist-physiotherapist collaboration to inform the development of a framework to improve access to acute MSK care.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A qualitative study consisting of 2 rounds of semi-structured focus groups with adults who had received care from a pharmacist and/or physiotherapist in Nova Scotia was conducted using the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability. Discussions focused on experiences and expectations regarding collaborative care for acute MSK injuries. Transcripts were coded deductively using the Acceptability, Practicability, Effectiveness, Affordability, Side effects/safety, Equity (APEASE) criteria and analyzed inductively to develop themes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eight participant data points were coded from 2 focus groups (July and August 2024). Participants expressed support for pharmacist-physiotherapist collaboration, citing benefits such as reduced emergency department use and faster access to care. Suggested implementation strategies included the use of pharmacy-based clinics, mobile units, and virtual care, especially in rural communities. Identified barriers included poor communication, unclear role definitions, limited integration within the health system, and gaps in affordability and accessibility.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Patients supported structured collaboration between pharmacists and physiotherapists to improve timely, coordinated MSK care. Key recommendations included public education, integrated services, and clarified professional roles. Addressing communication, privacy, and affordability concerns is essential to delivering equitable, patient-centred care.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Patients supported collaboration between pharmacists and physiotherapists for MSK care and identified challenges to be addressed in developing a collaborative framework.

articles.title: Lower limb necrosis in an adolescent: a report on an overlooked case of snakebite at a rural hospital in southern Togo.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Snakebite is a significant yet underestimated public health issue in sub-Saharan Africa. Delayed presentation and a lack of antivenom are the main factors that limit appropriate management. Here, we present the case of a patient who was treated at a rural hospital in southern Togo for wet gangrene of the right leg resulting from a neglected snakebite.

abstract.label: OBSERVATION
abstract.text: A 12-year-old Togolese adolescent with no known medical history was admitted to the emergency department for treatment of a chronic wound on his right leg. The questioning revealed that he had been bitten by a snake one month earlier while working in the fields and had been treated with traditional medicine. Physical examination revealed extensive wet gangrene of the right leg, with both leg bones exposed. A transfemoral amputation was performed. The postoperative course was favorable.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Managing snakebites is challenging in our country due to delayed presentation and a lack of appropriate treatment.

articles.title: Easy as 1-2-3! Point-of-Care Ultrasound Estimation of Parapneumonic Effusion Size Using Intercostal Spaces in the Pediatric Emergency Department.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: There is limited evidence on the ability of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to quantify and characterize pediatric parapneumonic effusions. This study aimed to evaluate the agreement between lung POCUS and radiology ultrasound (RADUS) or chest x-ray (CXR) in determining effusion size and complexity in children presenting to the pediatric emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We studied patients aged younger than 18 years diagnosed with parapneumonic effusions at the Hospital for Sick Children between June 1, 2018, and December 1, 2024. Included patients had undergone a lung POCUS demonstrating a pleural effusion and a RADUS or CXR within 36 hours of their POCUS examination. Patients with suboptimal POCUS images were excluded. Using previously described criteria, we determined whether an effusion was "drainable" or "non-drainable" using the number of involved intercostal spaces as an estimate of effusion size. Our primary outcome was the rate of agreement between the POCUS estimation of effusion size to that of RADUS (or CXR if RADUS was unavailable) using Cohen Kappa statistic. We also compared the rate of agreement between POCUS and RADUS for effusion complexity and the time taken to complete both imaging modalities.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eighty-five cases were included in this study. POCUS agreed with RADUS substantially in its ability to quantify (κ=0.76) and characterize (κ=0.65) parapneumonic effusions. There was also substantial agreement between POCUS and CXR for estimating effusion size (κ = 0.71). The median time to complete POCUS was significantly shorter compared with RADUS (6 vs. 14 min; P=0.003).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Using a simple method of counting involved intercostal spaces, our results support the use of lung POCUS for quantifying and characterizing parapneumonic effusions in the pediatric ED. Future research is needed to evaluate the generalizability of these findings and their impact on clinical outcomes.

articles.title: The impact of remote monitoring on clinical outcomes in defibrillator patients during the COVID-19 pandemic: An interrupted time series analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Remote monitoring (RM) has become the standard of care for managing patients with defibrillators. Early in the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, there were abrupt constraints to in-person device clinic access. The effect on overall device clinic access and clinical outcomes in the defibrillator population with and without RM during this time frame is uncertain.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to examine the effect of the early period of the COVID-19 pandemic on health care access and clinical outcomes in patients with a defibrillator with either an RM or non-RM model of care.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Administrative data from the province of Alberta, Canada, were evaluated between March 17, 2018, and July 17, 2021, to observe and compare secular and pandemic-associated trends in overall visits, emergency department visits, cardiovascular hospitalizations, and all-cause mortality in the period before (prepandemic) and after March 16, 2020 (intrapandemic), between RM and non-RM patients with defibrillators. We applied interrupted time series analysis, and the significance for statistical tests was set at 5%.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 4604 adults with defibrillators, 80% had RM. The onset of the pandemic was associated with an immediate increase in virtual care visits that was much greater in the RM group. Clinical outcome trends in both groups were essentially unchanged although we observed a 2-fold higher baseline mortality in the non-RM group that minimally declined after the pandemic.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: During the early period of the COVID-19 pandemic, RM patients had significantly improved access to virtual device clinic care compared with non-RM patients. However, clinical outcome trends were essentially unchanged.

articles.title: Individualized Profiles of Burnout and Sensory Processing Sensitivity in Nurses and Their Associations with Mindfulness and Psychological Well-Being.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Nurse burnout is a widespread problem associated with adverse outcomes for both patients and healthcare organizations. Despite evidence that burnout risk is heterogeneous, most profiling research has emphasized burnout symptoms and work characteristics rather than individual susceptibility. Sensory processing sensitivity may help explain why similar work demands are experienced differently across nurses.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: This cross-sectional study included 405 registered nurses working across all units of a tertiary hospital. Participants completed validated self-report measures of burnout, sensory processing sensitivity, mindfulness, and psychological well-being. Latent class analysis was applied to identify profiles based on burnout and sensory sensitivity indicators. Model selection was guided by information criteria and interpretability. Between-class differences in mindfulness and psychological well-being were examined using analysis of covariance adjusted for age and gender, and associations with work-unit context were evaluated using multinomial logistic regression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Three latent profiles were identified, representing low, moderate, and high burnout. Higher-burnout profiles were characterized by greater sensory processing sensitivity and higher burnout levels, alongside lower mindfulness and psychological well-being. Nurses working in inpatient, procedural, critical care, and emergency units were more likely to belong to higher-burnout profiles. Mindfulness and psychological well-being were inversely associated with membership in higher-burnout profiles, independent of demographic factors.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Joint modeling of burnout and sensory processing sensitivity revealed distinct and interpretable nurse profiles that reflect differential vulnerability to occupational burnout. These findings point to the combined role of individual sensitivity and work-unit context in burnout and well-being among nurses.

articles.title: Predicting massive transfusion and mortality in severely injured patients presenting to the emergency of a level 1 trauma center from the Indian subcontinent.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Early management of traumatic bleeding in patients with massive hemorrhage and coagulopathy significantly reduces mortality in severely injured patients. This study aimed to identify independent predictors of massive transfusion and mortality to facilitate early risk stratification in trauma care.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective observational study (August 2017-August 2018) in severely injured trauma patients of all age groups with an injury severity score (ISS) ≥16 who presented to the emergency department (ED) of a level 1 trauma center. Data on injury characteristics, clinical findings, laboratory results, and transfusion details were collected from electronic hospital and blood center records. Multivariate analysis was performed to identify predictors of massive transfusion, 24-h mortality, and inhospital mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 986 severely injured patients were included in the study of whom 104 (11.8%) underwent massive transfusion. The median age of the cohort was 29 (0-92) years predominantly males (83.4%). The median ISS was 17 (16-54) and Glasgow Coma Scale 10 (3-15). Head trauma was the most common injury overall, whereas blunt abdominal trauma predominated among patients requiring massive transfusion. Multivariate analysis revealed that shock index >0.9, pulse pressure <25 mmHg, and pulse rate >120 bpm as predictors of MT. Age >56 years, activated partial thromboplastin time >37.8 s, ISS >25, mean arterial pressure < 65 mmHg, and INR >1.4 were found to increase inhospital mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Tachycardia, pulse pressure <25 mmHg, and shock index >0.9 were predictors of massive transfusion in ED. Patients receiving fresh frozen plasma showed survival benefits at 24 h and during the length of hospital stay. These easily obtainable variables can be used for aggressive resuscitation of severely injured trauma patients and can be included in massive transfusion protocols.

articles.title: A Textual Mapping Analysis of Mass Trampling Incident Emergency Drill Scripts Based on ICN Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Version 2.0.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To evaluate the alignment of mass trampling incident emergency drill scripts with the International Council of Nurses (ICN) Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Version 2.0 and to identify areas of higher and lower textual coverage of competency items.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Crowd crush incidents are increasingly frequent worldwide and pose severe risks of mass casualties. Despite the importance of systematic and standardized emergency drills, there is limited evidence on the extent to which existing drill scripts address core disaster nursing competencies, particularly in high-risk mass gathering scenarios.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We mapped 24 provincial-level emergency drill scripts from a mass casualty exercise in China against the ICN Version 2.0 framework. Two researchers independently reviewed each script line by line and deductively coded the content against the eight domains and 33 competency items of the ICN Version 2.0 framework. Coverage rates were calculated and summarized using four descriptive categories: high, moderate, low, and no textual coverage.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Domain-level coverage represents the proportion of competency items appearing in at least one script. It was high for Assessment (100%), Incident Management (100%), Preparation and Planning (80%), and Communication (75%). Law and Ethics (67%), Intervention (50%), and Safety and Security (40%) met the criterion for moderate coverage. No domain fell within the low-coverage category, and no Recovery-domain item was represented in any script (0% domain-level coverage). Several competency items related to post-drill evaluation, education and training, psychological support, isolation, decontamination, and recovery were infrequently represented or absent.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The drill scripts showed relatively strong textual representation in Assessment, Incident Management, Preparation and Planning, and Communication, but less comprehensive representation in Law and Ethics, Intervention, and Safety and Security, while Recovery was not represented. Future drills should strengthen underrepresented competency-related content that can reasonably be demonstrated during immediate response. Competencies involving organizational planning, education and training, post-exercise activities, and recovery-phase activities may require complementary assessment beyond script review to support a more objective and comprehensive evaluation.

abstract.label: IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT
abstract.text: This study may help nursing managers understand how disaster nursing core competencies are represented in emergency drill scripts and identify competency areas that warrant further attention. The findings may provide a reference for targeted improvements in disaster preparedness planning, training, drill design, and subsequent competency assessment.

articles.title: ED Initiated Buprenorphine and Outpatient Referrals for Opioid Use: A Literature Review.

abstract.text: This narrative review aims to evaluate whether starting buprenorphine in the emergency department (ED), along with intervention and referral, can improve short-term outcomes for adults with opioid use disorder. Eight studies were reviewed, including randomized trials, cohort studies, implementation research, clinical guidelines, and quality-of-life assessments. Data were collected on patient characteristics, illicit opioid use, side effects, ED setting, study design, treatment engagement, and repeat ED visits. The results showed a consistent pattern: patients who received buprenorphine with referral in the ED were more likely to participate in outpatient treatment programs. They also experienced reductions in withdrawal symptoms and relapse after discharge. These findings highlight the importance of ED-initiated buprenorphine before discharge. This approach can also help reduce health care costs and address the economic crisis related to opioid use disorder.

articles.title: A Painful Presentation: Lipschütz Ulcer in an Adolescent With Recent Mononucleosis.

abstract.text: Lipschütz ulcer is a rare, nonsexually transmitted genital ulceration most commonly affecting nonsexually active adolescent females after systemic viral illness, particularly Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Because these lesions often resemble sexually transmitted infections, they frequently prompt extensive diagnostic evaluation and aggressive treatment despite their self-limited course. This report describes a 13-year-old female patient who developed acute, painful vulvar ulcerations after infectious mononucleosis. Comprehensive infectious and autoimmune workup was negative. The patient was hospitalized and treated with antibiotics and topical therapies before clinical improvement occurred. This case highlights the potential for diagnostic cascade, unnecessary antimicrobial use, and avoidable health care utilization in a benign postviral condition. Greater awareness of Lipschütz ulcer may help clinicians reduce unnecessary interventions, minimize psychosocial distress, and promote evidence-based supportive management.

articles.title: Pharmacotherapy Management of Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity in the Emergency Department.

abstract.text: Calcium channel blocker (CCB) overdose is a life-threatening toxicologic emergency characterized by profound cardiovascular instability. Emergency medicine personnel play a critical role in the early recognition, hemodynamic stabilization, and ongoing monitoring of these patients. This review provides a clinically focused discussion of the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and emergency department management of CCB toxicity, with particular emphasis on intravenous fluids, atropine, calcium salts, vasopressors, hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic therapy, intravenous lipid emulsion, methylene blue, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. This review highlights the priorities in the monitoring and titration of therapies, underscoring the importance of a structured, multimodal approach to treatment. Early recognition and timely escalation of care are essential to improving outcomes in this high-risk population.

articles.title: "Growth From Failure": A Qualitative Study of NICU Nurses' Psychological Experiences Following Failed Neonatal Resuscitation.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: This study investigated the emotional responses and underlying psychological processes experienced by nurses in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) following unsuccessful neonatal resuscitation.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Nurses, particularly neonatal nurses, experience substantial psychological pressure and multifaceted challenges in the aftermath of resuscitation failure. Although existing literature has examined nurses' emotional responses to neonatal death, a significant gap persists in understanding the distinct psychological experiences of neonatal nurses following unsuccessful resuscitation attempts.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a descriptive phenomenological study. Purposive sampling was employed to recruit 14 NICU nurses from a tertiary hospital in Chengdu, Sichuan Province. Participants were selected based on their firsthand experiences of neonatal resuscitation failure and participated in semistructured, face-to-face interviews. The interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step method.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: NICU nurses described their personal experiences following failed neonatal resuscitation. Four themes emerged concerning nurses' experiences and growth following resuscitation failure: (1) physical and mental exhaustion; (2) communication challenges; (3) reflection and support needs; and (4) achievements and growth.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This study revealed the complex psychological experiences of NICU nurses following resuscitation failure. These findings highlight opportunities to support nurses' professional growth and improve team culture and care systems. Consequently, establishing a multidimensional support system is important to support nurses involved in neonatal resuscitation.

abstract.label: IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT
abstract.text: Nurse managers and hospital administrators should establish a comprehensive, multidimensional support system to improve nursing competencies. This system should prioritize standardized training in the theoretical knowledge and practical skills needed for emergency care, while also strengthening nurses' capacity to provide humanistic care.

articles.title: Career Compromise, Perceived Organizational Support, and Professional Identity in Nurses: A Latent Profile Analysis and Mediation Study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To characterize unobserved patterns of nurses' professional identity (PI), identify factors related to profile membership, and determine whether perceived organizational support (POS) statistically accounts for part of the association between career compromise (CC) and PI.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional electronic questionnaire was completed by 2288 nurses recruited from 10 hospitals in Henan Province, China, between August and November 2025. The assessment tools utilized comprised a general information questionnaire, the Career Compromise Scale, the Perceived Organizational Support Scale, and the Nurses' Professional Identity Scale. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was employed to derive the PI subgroups. Group differences and profile correlates were evaluated with univariate analyses and multinomial logistic regression, respectively. The assessment of the indirect connection between CC and PI via POS was carried out utilizing Pearson correlation and SEM.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The classification of nurses' PI resulted in three latent profiles: low-PI (30.4%), moderate-PI (43.4%), and high-PI (26.2%). Holding a position in nursing management and earning a higher income were associated with an increased likelihood of belonging to the moderate- and high-patient impact groups. Conversely, the likelihood of nurses in acute/critical care units or emergency departments being part of the moderate- and high-PI groups was lower. After accounting for various factors, having more than 10 night shifts monthly was not significantly related to high-PI group membership. According to the SEM, CC was positively linked to POS (β = 0.901, p < 0.01) and PI (β = 0.463, p < 0.01), and POS had a positive link with PI (β = 0.382, p < 0.01); the standardized indirect effect amounted to 0.344.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Nurses' PI was represented by three profiles. Membership varied by income, management role, department, gender, hospital level, and hospital type, whereas monthly night-shift frequency did not independently differentiate the high-PI profile after covariate adjustment. POS also accounted for a significant portion of the positive CC-PI association.

articles.title: Phubbing and Caring Behaviors Among Emergency Nurses: The Mediating Role of Emotional Exhaustion.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Phubbing (phone snubbing) in high-pressure emergency department (ED) settings is associated with nurse-patient interaction challenges and patient safety concerns; however, its underlying process remains unclear.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Grounded in the job demands-resources model, in this study, we explored the relationship between phubbing and caring behaviors among ED nurses, tested the mediating role of emotional exhaustion, and identified potential intervention targets to inform nursing management practice.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: A multicenter cross-sectional study.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Between March and June 2025, 512 ED nurses from 18 hospitals across five geographic-economic tiers in Sichuan Province, China, were recruited via stratified multistage cluster sampling. Data were collected using the Chinese versions of the generic scale of phubbing (GSP), caring behaviors scale-24 (CBS-24), Maslach Burnout Inventory-General Survey (MBI-GS), and a demographic questionnaire. Common method bias was assessed using Harman's single-factor test and the marker-variable technique. Hierarchical regression and bootstrap methods were used to test the mediating effect of emotional exhaustion.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The mean GSP, CBS-24, and emotional exhaustion scores were 4.28 ± 0.88, 4.52 ± 0.46, and 3.18 ± 0.82, respectively. Hierarchical regression showed that, after controlling for demographics, phubbing was negatively associated with caring behaviors (β = -0.203, p < 0.001), explaining an additional 5.2% of variance. After emotional exhaustion was added, the direct association of phubbing decreased to β = -0.138 (p = 0.002). Emotional exhaustion was negatively associated with caring behaviors (β = -0.267, p < 0.001), explaining an additional 6.8% of variance. Bootstrap analysis indicated that emotional exhaustion partially mediated the relationship (indirect effect = -0.089, 95% CI [-0.126, -0.056]), accounting for 43.8% of the total effect.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Phubbing is significantly associated with lower caring behaviors among ED nurses and is indirectly associated with lower caring behaviors through emotional exhaustion. Emotional exhaustion is a potential intervening node for nursing managers.

articles.title: Clinical evaluation of oral fluid point-of-care testing for drugs of abuse compared to urinary point-of-care testing at a large-scale music festival.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Urinary point-of-care testing for recreational drugs is commonly used in clinical settings. An oral fluid-based point-of-care test is a less invasive alternative, but the reliability and clinical applicability in a real-life acute care setting is unclear.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To assess the concordance of oral fluid point-of-care testing compared to urine point-of-care testing for recreational drugs in a prehospital clinical setting.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This study was conducted during a large-scale dance music festival in October 2023. Urine and oral fluid samples were collected at the event medical station from volunteers with a suspected drug intoxication. Participants aged 18 years and older were included if both samples were provided and at least one substance tested positive. The percentage of positive oral fluid test results per recreational drug were compared with those of the urine point-of-care test.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 78 patients were included. For most drug substances, positivity rates were similar between the two test types. Methamphetamine/3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine was the only substance that showed significantly more positive results in oral fluid compared to urine (p < 0.001). For all other substances, the differences between the two tests were small, with slightly higher positivity rates (on average 3.9 %) detected in oral fluid.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Oral fluid point-of-care testing shows potential in specific scenarios but requires further validation. It is a less invasive alternative to urine point-of-care testing for recreational drugs in a clinical setting. Nevertheless, it is important to consider the differences in test characteristics, such as detection window. Further research is needed to evaluate the reliability in other populations and settings.

articles.title: Effectiveness of combined management of automated red cell exchange and therapeutic plasma exchange in a patient of sickle cell disease presenting with acute chest syndrome and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

abstract.text: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a severe complication of sickle cell disease (SCD) that demands prompt medical attention. Approximately one-fifth of patients with a history of ACS progress rapidly to respiratory failure within 24 h, often leading to multiorgan failure. A 23-year-old male with a history of SCD and multiple vaso-occlusive crises presented to the emergency department with fever, chest pain, and breathlessness. Diagnosed with SCD 8 years prior, he had been on hydroxyurea 500 mg daily but had discontinued the medication 3 months back. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for urgent management and placed on noninvasive ventilation. The chest X-ray revealed new right lung consolidation. As the clinical condition deteriorated, he was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation in the prone position. Routine management included intravenous (IV) morphine, antibiotics, and IV fluids. The patient urgently required a transfusion of two packed red blood cell units due to a critically low hemoglobin level of 4.1 g/dl, followed by automated red cell exchange (RCE). Automated RCE improved the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and prone ventilation was no longer necessitated. He was suspected of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis due to fever, splenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperferritinemia. He was treated with therapeutic plasma exchange of 1.2 plasma volumes, followed by IV immunoglobulin. Hemodialysis was performed to treat acute kidney injury. His condition gradually improved, and he was extubated.

articles.title: Effect of high ratios of plasma and platelets to red blood cell transfusions during early resuscitation on the mortality of severely injured trauma patients.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Recent studies have suggested that increasing fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) and platelet (PLT) transfusions can improve survival rates in patients requiring massive transfusions. This study evaluated the impact of different ratios of plasma and PLT to red blood cell transfusions on the mortality of severely injured trauma patients who received blood transfusions during resuscitation.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective observational study was conducted in the emergency department of a trauma center from August 2017 to August 2018. Patients aged ≥18 years, having injury severity score ≥16, and who required ≥2 packed red blood cell (PRBC) unit transfusions in the first 4 h of presentation to the emergency were included. Four groups were identified based on the FFP:PRBC and PLT:PRBC ratios. The patients were grouped into only PRBC, low (<1:1), balanced (1:1), and high (>1:1) ratios.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eight hundred and fifty-two patients met the inclusion criteria, with a mean age of 36.1 ± 14 years. Males constituted 85.7% and 89% had blunt injuries. The 24-h mortality was higher in the low ratio (LR) group of the FFP:PRBC ratio (13.6%) and the PLT:PRBC ratio (16.1%). The overall inhospital mortality rate was higher in the high PLT: RBC ratio group (45.3%) but comparable in the LR and high FFP:PRBC ratio groups. Multivariate logistic regression showed high FFP:PRBC (odds ratio [OR] = 0.9, P < 0.0001) and PLT:PRBC (OR = 0.28, P < 0.0001) ratios reduced mortality at 24 h.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: High FFP:PRBC and PLT:PRBC ratios reduced 24-h mortality but not overall hospital mortality in severely injured patients who received multiple transfusions. Prospective trials are necessary for further evidence.
